TaE MUSIC OF LABOUR. The birds may sing in the country-side, But I think in the city's throrg There is many a sound of labour That is pleasant as any song. The workman whistling cheerily As he goes to his work at morn Is jist as sweet and as musical As the whistling birds in the corn. When the bricklayers tap with their trowels Vs Woks tu the growing wa'lls When the chip ! chip I chip I of the masons fri a rytbmical cadence. falls; Whs.s the earpenter's busy hana Mar Ilion& with a laugh or a word, 'LA the music of labour, and jest as sweet As the song of the wildwood bird. The sigh of the summer wind is soft. And gay is the chattering stream. But the engine throbs to &noble tune Through the mighty tongue of steam. And there's music in the click, click, cllck Of the mystical telegraph; In the chiming bells in the lofty tower. Lithe school-girl's innocent laugh. In the kindly voices of greeting men. In the playing of girls and boys; Oh the streets are full of pleasant sounds I hat fretfully we call "noise." Bu , think if all this wonderful life Went silently to and fro! It never a sound fell on the ear. And the tumult was all a show : How we should miss the spirit and stir How we should drearily sigh Over the busy but dream-like crowd ' " '
Passing us..eilently by! Oh! the tree/ere • tap," awl the mar,on'e
Tne hammer, the wheel, th 3 bell. Are the stirring songs tha- labour sing.. And we all of us love them well.
Tarittits.

Idleness is the dead sea that swallows up all virtues, mncl the self-made sepulchre of a living man. A great step is gained when a child has learned that -there is no necessary connection between liking a thing -and doing it. Among the-jtomans the gift of, a ring was a badge of liberation from slavery. Married people can best ex- plain whether it is so amongst the moderns. Satan selects his disciples when they are idle, but Christ chose his while they were busy at. work, either mending their nets or casting them into the sea.— / Faremion. No habit is more difficultly acquired than that of ac- knowledging our errors; and yet this habit is the best feature in an amiable character, and the strongest proof of a sound understanding. ' • The tissue of the life to be We weave with colours all our own, And in the field of destiny We reap as we have sown.— Whittier. Our forefathers had clocks put on the outside of • churches that they might net be late in getting to ser- vice; we put the -clocks inside of the churches lest we be late in getting out.—Rev. H. A. Tupper. On the road of life one mile-stone more! In the book,of life one leaf turned o'er! Like a red seal is the setting sun On the good and the evil men have done,— Naught can to-day restore !—Longfellow. Little Alice A—, dressed and prepared for a walk, was skipping back and forth-through the entry, waiting for her Mother to get ready to go out: Her little cousin said he was going out too. ."No," said Alice, " you_can't go—you are not dressed up." Her uncle laughingly re- marked that the pride stuck out quite larly. No," -answered Alice, "it isn't my pride, it's my new moreen • skirt that sticks out so." •• Lord M—, with no very large portion of either wit or wisdom, had a very exalted opinion of his own powers. When once in a large company, and expatiat- • ing about himself, he made the following pointed re- mark:—" When I happen to say a foolish thing I always burst out a-laughing."" I envy you your happiness, my Lord," said Charles Townsend, for you must, cer- tainly live the merriest life of any man in Europe." He was a burly Yorkshirernan, and walked about his post very smartly, and looked as if he was determined , both to obey the orders he received on mounting guard and to have,implicit obedience rendered him in the carrying out of his duties": About u. o'clock p.m. some- body was heard approaching his post, and the sentry, bringing his rifle sharply down to the " charge " de- manded, "Who comes there ?" A muffled voice through the gloom replied, "Friend." "Advance, friend, and give the countersign." "I've forgot it—quite slipped my memory—'pon my word." "Well," said the sentry, "if tha'rt a soldier thyself this knows what orders is, and tha doesn't pass here a fut till tha says Welling- ton ? " . _

Archbishop Cranmer had a niece whom he married to a gentleman every way her equal, and the ceremony was solemnised with much pomp and splendour, the rest of the day being passed in amusements and the receiving of presents, of which the Archbishop's was the most notable one, and which lie concealed from view under his robes. This both the bride and. her newly-made hus- band were most impatient to see. The husband thought it must be some grant of lands or employment of honour, the wife some rich diamond necklace or other precious ornament, but the Archbishop persisted in con- cealing his present till they had both promised him never to wear it at the same time, and then he pulled out—a fool's cap. Many were the rencontres between Will Speir and the Earl of Eglinton, who condescended to familiarity with him, and in return allowed the same latitude of expres- sion to the wayward Will. The vagrant one day made a demand on his Lordship for a bottle of ale. "Deed, Will, gin ye kent it," replied the Earl, "I have not a farthing in my pocket just now; but just gang in there, to Leezie Paterson's, and I'll tell her to gi'e ye't, and I'll return in a few minutes and help you to drink it." The Earl, faithful to his promise, returned in a short time, and taking his seat opposite to Will. aYe may be a proud man this day, Will," said his Lordihip. "An' for what ?" queried the wit. "Sitting drinking wi' an Earl." Hech, hech, man! great cause to `be proud, sitting aside an Earl that hasna a bode in his pouch to bless himsel' wi'." ' LIFE-PRESERVING APEARATIIS.—Life-preserving appa- ratus for enabling an exploring party to carry with them an adequate supply of oxygen gas, or vital air, has been invented by• M. Rouquayrol. It consists of a vessel of sheet iron, capable of resisting the pressure of from twenty-five to forty atmospheres. Air is forced into it by pumps, of which the pistons are fixed, and the cylinders movable. The apparatus is fastened on the back like a soldier's knapsack. A bellows-like contri- vance is placed above the vessel or reservoir, which . allows the air, though so greatly compressed, to enter the lungs at the ordinary pressure of the atmosphere. A small external valve, formed of two leaves of India- rubber, which are kept in contact with each other by ,the pressure of the atmosphere, opens to allow the ex- pired air to escape. It is asserted that a man thus pro- vided can breathe with ease under wale; as proved by • experiments on rivers, and at the bottom of the sea.— .Tke World qf Wonders. A LOCH FYNE PROPHEF.—The herring is good cur- rency—the Loch Fyne variety being silvery. to look at and luscious to the taste. and from box or barrel so good to eat that he does not require to be branded for the Baltic. They breakfast on him in the west end of Glasgow and dine on him in the east end; the day after he is caught he is carried direct to Liverpool, Manchester, and Lon- don, and is everywhere popular. But the broken clans • cannot always lay hands on him, for the herring has oc- cult habits which as yet baffled inVestigation. Nor is 'local experience an infallible guide. Experience will < come down to the herring quay, eighty years of age, • toddling with a stick and an ancient sou'wester and will declaim to inexperienced youngsters of sixty, "Hooch, ay, which! Ye canna get a herrin' whateffer ? Ye'll no 'be aware that she'll sweem away sometimes for no reason that no man knows; and will neffer come again. She hasna, come doon from Campbeltown yet? Eery goot whateffer ; if she'll no come now, she'll neffer come. t Go down into your poaties and look for her at the Kyles die Pute, an' if she's no there she's at Ballantrae, or no onywhere the year, but just sweemed back to the deep sea.—The English Illustrated _Magazine. A laughable anecdote is told of the late Mr. James Johnston, M.P. for Sandwich, who was in Parliament at . the commencement of the present century. On his first taking' his seat in the House he was said to have formed a "maiden" speech, in the course of which he expected 'to rival Demosthenes; but it so happened, that though the speech was transferred from his head to the lining of his hat, yet the perspicuity of utterance fled. He rose, essayed to speak, but in vain; and he re-seated himself, in silent dismay, without articulating a word. The meirMers of the Eccentrics' Chib, of which Mark Supple was the chairman taking advantage o this his unfortunata failure, caused papers tobe printed, circu- -1 AAA, and, as was then the fashion In London, cried through the streets of Westminster and the City, on the top of which appeared in large type, "The Maiden ;Speech of James Johnston, Esq., M.P. for Sandwich, as -delivered ,yesterday in Parliament." The rest of the paper was blank; and scarcely had the Members re- -turned to their respective laomes before the squib was cried in all the principal streets of the metropolis. The lady of the hon. gentleman heard the outcry as she sat at her windowin Great George-street, and exulting in the consequence and popularity of her husband, in- stantly called for her footman, and desired lie would purchase some of the papers of the poor man in the stafeet He having obeyed her commands, immediately presented them to the lady, who, on viewing the blank paper, exclaimed with great violence. "Why, Richard, you are a fool—you have brought nothing !' No, my lady," drily replied the servant, "it is my master, for he said nothing..."

noble and atttactive everyday bearing comes of goodness, of sincerity, of refinement, and these are bred in years, not in moments. Re that loses his conscience has nothing left that is worth keeping. Therefore, be sure you look at that. And in the next place look to your health, and, if you have it, praise God, and value it next to a good con- scienae; for health is the second blessing that we 'nor- ' lab are capable of—a blessing that money cannot buy— therefore value it, and be thankful for it. OLD-TIILE Trrzes.—Here are a few titles used by au- thors in the seventeenth century in England A Most Delectable, Sweet-perfumed Nosegay- for God's Saints to Smell at ;" "The Snuffers of Divine Love ;" "Hooks and Eves for Believers' Breeches ;" " Shoes for D.Warfs in Holiness ;" "Crumbs of Comfort for the Chickens of the Covenant;" "Seven Sobs of a Sorrow- ful Soul of Sin; or the Seven Penitential Psalms of the Princely Prophet David; whereunto are also annexed Willia.re Humuis' Handful of Honeysuckles, and Divers Godly and Pithy Ditties, now Newly Augmented ;" "The Spiritual Mustard Pot to make tile Soul Sneeze with De- votion." BUYING A Caracrrs.—A good story is told at the ex- pense of a late Pennsylvania oil millionaire, who thought he would take advantage of his rapid accumu- lating wealth to give his daughter the benefit of an " eddication." Be dressed her up in gorgeous silks, and her arms, neck, fingers, and ears were laden withrthe most costly gems. He concluded to take her to an Eastern seminary, which he did, much to the desire of the young miss, who was just old enough to commence to "put on frills." They arrived at the seminary in due time, and the principal was instructed to spare no pains nor expense, for was he not an oil king, and could well afford to spend "a million dollars on' my darter." "Spare no expense; buy her anything she wants, I'm rich, and the gal must have an eddication." The young miss remained in school for just one year, yet had made but little progress in her studies. The old man thought he would make her a visit, and he was very much chagrined when the principal of the seminary informed him that the girl was getting along very well in her studies, but she did not have the capacity necessary for a very marked improvement. "Didn't have the capa- city !' fairly yelled the old man. " Didn't I tell you I was an oil king, and that you should spare no expense. Why the didn't you buy her a capacity ?" The story is a very old one, but sometimes resurrecting "chestnuts" creates a little fun. A GREAT WHIG Horse. My father-in-law, Lord Tankerville, was an old Whig, and a friend of Lord Grey, , and he took me on a visit to Howick, where the old Earl lived in patriarchal retirement amidst his numerous sons, daughters, and sons-in-law. Two of the latter, Lord Durham and Mr. Ellice (commonly called "Bear Ellice "), .both clever and ambitious men, had great influence with Lord Grey, and used it without mercy. - He was one of the most striking figures I ever saw, the very type of a grand seigneur and of an intellectual man. Whilst I was at Howick I was struck with two peculiarities of the family, one of which we§ that all the sons and daughters called their parents by their christian names, " Charles " and "Mary," which had a strange effect; the other was the taste of the whole family for argument. They were always in a state of discussion, even as to the distance between Howick and Alnwick, and the shortest road to and from each, which one would suppose they had veri- fied long ago. Lady Georgiana was very ergreeable, and played beautifully on the harp, an instrument then much appreciated. As I suppose I was looked upon as a mere boy by the party, politics and future onslaughts on the Tory Government were freely spoken of without a4ne in my presence; and I remember one day Lord Grey breaking out and declaring that the three greatest rascals in the world were Lord Castlereagh (then dead), Brougham, and Talleyrand, and I recollect this explo- sion• the more, because when he formed his Government three months later he was obliged to make Brougham Ins Chancellor, and to receive Tallevrand as the Ambas- sador of France.—Lord Malmesburls Autobiography. FALSE IDEAS OF SEA LIFE.—The ocean is the theatre of more interest than boys would care to follow. We laugh with Marryatt ; we read Cooper for his "plots ;" we find much that is dashing and flattering to our patriotism in the "Toni Bowlings" and "Will Watches" and "Tough Yarns" and "Topsail Sheet-blocks ;" in the sprawling and fighting and drinking school of sea yarns; but when we turn to Dana and Melville, we find that the real life of the sea is not to be found between yellow covers adorned with hatching cuts; that all the romance does not lie in coCked hats and epaulets, but that by far the largest proportion of the sentiment, the pathos of the deep, the bitterness and suffering of the sailor's life, must be sought in the gloomy forecastle of the humble coaster, in the deckhouses of the deep-laden cargo steamer, in the crew's dwelling-place on board the big ship trading to Australia and India and China. It is be- cause only two or three writers have kept their eye steadfastly on this walk of the marine calling, and it is because all the rest who have written about the sea have represented the sailor as a jolly, drinking, dancing, skylarking fellow, that the shore-going public have come, to get the wildest, absurdest notion of Jack's real cha- racter and professional life. For one who reads Dana and Melville, thousands read Marryatt and Michael Scott, and Chamier, and Cupples, and Neale. It is in these books that we find Jack always on the broad grin, al- ways smart in pumps for cutting capers, always yarning and smoking, and lounging, unless drubbing the French. "Pass the grog," he says— Pass the grog! pass the grog! your sailor le a jolly dog, Ever laughing, ever gay, sings at night and works by day; Cares no more for wounds and wealth Than doctors for their patients' health. Yes, it is always passing the grog, and singing all night, -with lovely Sue to join in the chorus! And this great maritime nation has for generations accepted all this sort of thing as true of Jack's calling, just as on the stage they dress up a man meant to play the part of a merchant sailor in the dress of a naval blue-jacket. But it is the nautical novelist who has misled the public, who, knowing perfectly what is right, has deliberately melodramatised the unfortunate sailor, whether mercan- tile or naval, until readers look with incredulity upon the truthful portraits offered them by such men as Dana and Melville, and refuse to regard any representation of a nautical man as correct unless he is constantly swear- ing, constantly getting tipsy, constantly speaking a language crowded with marine expressions; and unless he makes his bow in a tarpauling hat at the back of his head, a laniard round his neck, an immense collar down his back, and a pair of feet scarcely visible in the bell- mouthed trousers which run extravagantly tight to his hips.—W. Clark Russell, in Contemporary Renew. A 'FARMER'S INTERVIEW WITLF MR. GLADSTONE.—AN
AMUSING; EPISODE.—On the occasion. of the recent pri-
vate visit of Mr. Gladstone to the old house of Panmure, near Carnoustie, once the favourite residence of the

' Maules of Panmure, a very amusing episode occurred. ' As the visit was quite a private affair, every precaution • was taken to prevent the public getting access to the grounds, or intruding on the privacy of the Earl of ' Dalhousie and his guests. Notwithstanding this a. con- siderable number of the residents of the village made ' their way to Panmure in the hope of catching a glimpse ' of Mr. Gladstone, and amongst them was a retired farmer, a pawky old man, and a genuine specimen of the old school of Scotch farmers. He walked briskly up to the gate, and was about to pass through when the gatekeeper barred his progress and sharply intimated that there was "no admittance." "What d'ye say ?" exclaimed the astonished farmer. "Will ye no' lat a body in?" "No," was the reply; "no strangers are to be allowed within the grounds.' "But I maun hae in to see the great man, an' I winna tak"no ' for an an- swer." But the' lady was firm, and would not yield. A cibwd of visitors from the seaside village had by this time gathered round the gate, all equally anxious for admittanoe. While the portress was holding a parley with the fresh arrivals, the old man slyly slipped out of sight, walked along the road for a short distance, climbed the boundary wall, and thus obtained access to the grounds. Doubling the porter's lodge, he walked leisurely up the carriage drive towards the mansion. He had not gone far when he was met by a "gentleman" in high authority, who, amazed at the old man's audacity, levelled his eyeglass, and after surveying him frbm head to foot haughtily demanded—" What do you want here ?" " Weel, frien' " coolly replied the farmer, "I've come to see that' great man you hae wi '• you the day. Whaur do you think he might be enow ?" The gentle- man saw he had a tough character to deal with, and, after a moment's reflection, he concluded that it would be best to get him quietly cornered, to prevent the pos- sibility of a scene. Accordingly he led him to a retired part of the policies, and told him to wait there, and the Premier would pass that way shortly. But the old far- mer was too impatient 'to wait, and, disregarding the injunctions of the high dignitary, he struck a bee-line for the Mansion House. His perseverance met with its due reward, for before he had gone far he encountered the Earl and• his guests. Advancing briskly up to the Earl, the old man held out his hand, and greeted him with " Hoo's a' wi' you the day, my lord? I've just come to see that great man, and I winna gae awa or I shake hands wi' him." The Earl smiled, shook the old man by the hand, and then introduced him*.to Mr. Glad- stone as an old tenant on the estate. The Premier shook hands with the worthy farmer, hoped he was well, and so forth. "Man, but I'm prood to see you, Maister Gladstone! Man, fiyou're a clever chiel; we hav'na mony like yon, but a young birkie there," alluding to Dalhousie, "that's promising weel. "Man, but I'm glad I to see you looking sae weel and he.aity. An' this is the mistress and your dochter, I suppose. Hoo are ye n-rern? You maun just excuse me, but we're a' saeprood to see you." Thus the honest old farmer went on, shak- ing hands all round, while every one was highly amused. At last he bade them " Gude day," after giving a parting shake tolfir. Gladstone's hand. He was so elated at the honour Conferred upon him that lie told the story to all his friends, and he was heard to declare in a burst of en- thusiasm 4' That he would not wash the hand that had grasped the porn of Mr. Gladeterte for the nexi, three days." lIIRIFT.—The latest official retorns of Provident Societies in England arid Wales show a memiawehlo of six millions and funds amounting to thietv-eigh t m Mons of pounds, The ROYAL CLOTIIIYG CLUB. er 57, South John-street. div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. OCTOBER 18, 1884.
NOTES ON AGRTCULTURE,
CULTURF,

A stag was killed on Exmoor recently weighing 14 scores when perfectly dressed, and Without the head, skin, and slots. Thirteen hundred and eight wolves were killed 'last year in France, mainly on the borderland of Belgium and Germany. The reward amounted to £4,150. 4t the Kelso ram sales recently held Lord Polwarth's lot of Border leicesters excited lively competition. The highest price was £73, given by a Wark farmer: The Shorthorn bull Gay Baronet, a roan yearling, which stood second at the Northumberland tow, has been bought from the Duke of Northumberland by Mr. Win. Graham, Eden Grove, Fennel. Two very 'fine young Shire stallions, named " Malt- ster " and "Admiral Melton," have been recently sold by Mr. J. F. Crowther, Knowl Grove, Mirfield, at good prices, and a few days ago were shipped at Liverpool for Buenos Ayres, their destination. The Hereford bull Emperor has been purchased by Mr. Hudson,'Montana, at £3OO, from AP4danis Earl. Mr. Malcolm, of Poltolloch, Argyllshire, has secured six Hereford calves of the Horace and Lord Wilton blood for exportation to his farms at Knocklava, Jimbaica. The grand Shire stallion Meister has been purchased by Messrs. Torrome, Son, and Co. from Mr. Crowther, of Mirfield. This stallion descends in a direct line from Honest Tom, 1,105. It has already been shipped to South America for Senor Huorgo, who owns a large stud.

Weaning foals should be fed with oats and bran when takeh from their mother's milk; it will keep them grow- ing through the first winter, which is most essential. The good start lays the foundation, in bone and sub- stance, for a good horse. A colt neglected the first-winter never recovers its proper shape, nor does it attain the size and strength which naturally appertain to its:breed. A five-year-old Clydesdale mare, of high breeding and good quality, but not a prize-winner, was lately sold for £240; a three-year-old mare, of similar qualifications, realised £125; a yearling filly, a leading prizewinner at several of the most important local allows in the West of Scotland, drew £125; and another yearling filly, of good breeding, but not a prize-winner, made £ll5. These are all registered in the Clydesdale stud book. Scotch Liberalism is generally unimaginative, but the gathering at Aberdeen was distinguished by §uch sym- bolic displays as a large shorthorn bull, drawn in a wag- gon, and labelled "Mr. Gladstone," followed by a lean ox, on which a ragged urchin rode, ticketed "Lord Salis- bury ;" while Lord Randolph Churchilrwas rePresented by a monkey, and the Conservative working men by a contingent of donkeys. 'Twout.nN'T Coma—A farmer's wife living at Orms- kirk was pestered by a patent churn agent, who was anxious to demonstrate that the machine would make ' butter in ten minutes. Upon his third or fourth call, she filled the churn, and the agent worked at it for ten minutes, then very briskly for ten more, and then per- spiringly for ten more. He confessed that he was at a loss to know what was the matter, until the lady re- marked, "I guess I churned all the butter out of that milk this morning." The agent" flew.". - BEEP OF' IdonsEs.—An authority says it is always best to feed a variety of food in the ration of a horse. As a simple food oats are best, but oats and corn are still better; and oats, corn, and barley better still. And whatever food, one pint of linseed me.al per day to a horse will be found to pay well in health and conditio'n. One of the best combinations as a food for horses is 800 pounds of corn, 800 pounds of oats and 100 pounds of flaxseed, evenly mixed and all ground together. WATER FOR FATTENING CATTLE.—HINTS TO FEEDERS.— Many experiments have been made by agriculturists in Germany for the purpose of discovering whether pure water, taken in large quantities by animals' which are being fed for fattening, is favourable or otherwise, to the process. The conclusion to which the German scientists have come on this question is that water introduced in large quantities into the digestive organs increases the elimination of carbonic acid by the animal, and conse- quently hinders the formation of fat. The result of this opinion is that when cattle are to be fattened for the market no more water should be given to them than is strictly necessary for diluting the food of the animals, and quenching their thirst. It is judicious not to give water to animals which are to be fattened, except whbn a certain quantity of oilcake, bran, rye, flour' or barley meal has been added to it to make a drench, and thus inerease the nutritive power of the food. Milking cows also • benefit by this method of sweetening the water, but water ought to be given to them without Stint. The ingestion of a large quantity of liquid is the first and indispensable condition for the plentiful production of Milk.

NORTH LANCASHIRE FARM NOTES.—Showery weather has set in and banished our second summer, and the high winds have given the country a very autumnal ap- pearance. Grass lands, are fast losing the green hue, swedes and mangolds are drooping at the top, and the work of lifting the potato crop has been delayed. In sowing cabbage-seed last spring, for the sake of economy we mixed the seed with common turnip-seed, known as Scotch hardy, the turnip plants being afterwards re- moved when the cabbage plants were singled. In places a few of the turnips were left in, where the cabbages were missing, and on raising the turnips several of them weighed upwards of 201bs. I am told that this kind have keeping properties equal to most swedes. Can any of your readers verify this? Here and there you see manure led out on to the ploughed lands for next year's spring crops. I cannot think that autumn manuring for spring crops is sound practice. It may appear a sav- ing to get out manure in a time when work does not pre4s, and to find it done when the busy time comes on; but in a district where the rainfall vanes from 50 to 60 inches, the manure must and does lose much of its fer- tilising properties; and now, when on all sides iou hear the question propounded, "What is to be done ?" surely that loss ought more than to stand against the score of convenience.—W. "No DISSENTER'S NEED APPLY."—.The writer of the notes in the Mark Lane Express says :—A correspondent has sent me the following paragraph :—" A farm belong- ing to Mr. T. C. Daniel, Stordleigh Court, Tiverton, was recently advertised to be let by tender. The highest bidder was Mr. Yendell. He gave as references Lords Poltimore and Fortescue, and finally it was agreed he should have the farm • but before the lease was signed, in a final interview with Mr. Daniel he was asked if he was a Churchman. To which he replied no, he was a Wesleyan, but supposed that times were past for that to make any difference. To his surprise, however, he subsequently received the following letter from Mr. W. Easton (Taunton), the agent Dear Sir,—After due consideration, Mr. Daniel has come to the conclusion not to accept your proposals for Pilemore. All his other tenants are Churchmen, consequently he has decided not to make an exception in this case. Thanking you for your tender for the farm, I remain, &c.' " Why did not .Mr. Daniel put "No Dissenters need apply". in his adver- tisement? He certainly ought to be compelled to pay any expenses that Mr. Yendell may have incurred in ten- dering -for the farm. Such intolerance as he has ex hibited is happily now as rare as it is discreditable. It is such arrogance as his that makes "landlordism" stink in the nostrils of ,the people.

Perfectly clean milk is what is wanted by consumers and by factories,•yet it is not always obtained. Many of the milkmen furnish milk to their patrons which is so filthy that should one attempt to take it with bread the "taste of the barn" would be so strong that he who made the attempt would be disgusted. Such milk can be used in tea or coffee and the filthy taste not be de- tected, but the filth is thext none the less, and who wants to eat that kind of filth? Filthy milk is neither fit to vat nor fit to manufacture into butter or cheese. We have seen butter and cheese that tasted of the filth of the barn. Now, in order to secure perfectly clean milk, great care must be exercised in removing all filth from the sides and from the udder of the cow before milking. The stable must be kept neat and clean. A foul smell- ing stable will taint the milk during the process of milk- ing. The best milk can only be obtained by observing the most scrupulous cleanliness in all the operations; the cows should not be overheated by fast driving, nor by being chased by dogs, nor should they be excited by being beaten or frightened while being milked. All milk coming from animals in heat should be separated from the rest of the milk, and also all milk taken from dis- eased or inflamed udders. The cow should also have clean, pure water to drink and wholesome food:to eat. A milkman who can furnish a first-class article of milk is deserving .pf patronage.

- - TEE HORSE ENTERPRISE OF CANNOCK.-A few particu- lars of this grand young horse, which was the champion at the last exhibition held at the Agricultural Hall, will be especially interesting to Fylde farmers. Only a few years ago there was no recognised name for the.famous breed that is now known throughout the world .as the Shire Horse. But the long-continued period of over- sight, we might say, is a thing of the past, and the splen- did result we have now before us is this rapidly improv- ing breed,' the interests of which are so well looked after by the energetic members of the English Cart Horse Society. Enterprise of Cannock, on the last occasion at their show, fully maintained the reputation of the "Shires," for a more symmetrical big horse could scarcely be desired. In every particular he is first-rate. Size, action, soundness, colour, bone, and muscular power are all perfect and finely developed, forming in their entirety a truly noble lairse of most pleasing con- tour. The credit of having bred this distinguished horse belongs to Mr. Thomas S. Minton, of Montford, Shrews- bury. Enterprise of Cannock was exhibited at the Lon- don Horse Show last winter by the Cannock Agricul- tural Company, and won all the principal prizes, includ- ing the Champion, Challenge, and President's Cups, Abe whole haring an aggregate value of £2OB 10s. This fine perforinaneewas followed up by his owners disposing of him to •Sar Henry Allsopp, Bart., for the handsome price of 1,000 guineas.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

ROOT-PEENING FRUIT TREES is practical with the view of checking over luxuriant growth and increasing a dis- position to form flower buds, without which fruit can- not be expected. The operation may be conducted any time from now till the trees commence to grow in the spring, but the best period is no doubt that which has proved most suitable fof moving the trees entirely where necessary. There are overwhelming proofs that October, as we stated last -week, is the time. To root-prune a tree the soil must be ,moved 'by cutting a trench all round, and at regular distance from the stem of the tree. For instance, a tree 6ft. or Bft. high should be cut abOut twe feet away from the stem, and as deep as the roots penetrate. ' All the ends of the roots will present a jagged appearance from having been cut with the spade. 'Before the soil is replaced in the trench the roots must be gone over with a sharp knife, and a clean cut made at the end of each, which will enable them to heal much (Recker and 're-establish themselves by form- ing fresh roots. There is another method of interfering with the roots of fruit trees that is productive of fruit- ful results—i.e., the feising of them near the surface in the case of trees of -Jong standing. The nearer with safety the roots of • trees, are to the sun &influence, the larger the crop and finer the produce. Roots that have penetrated downwards, or have been buried low down, are in a cold medium, and in consequence the tree makes late growth, and the buds are rarely properly matured, so that year after year there is very littje fruit produced. The roots of trees in, a cultivated piece of ground are likely to be worse treated than those in an orchard, where.the grass is allowed to grow. In the first there is constant addi,tion.made to the soil by the 9.pplication of manure to the 'cropg,' so that the roots in a few yea'rs will be several inches. deeper than when they were first planted. , In the ,course of cultivation the surface roots are destroyed by the spade, so that it becomei a matter for consideration whether we are justified in digging to any depth under fruit tree's—whether the miserable crops of vegetables we get from under such trees al e an equivalent for the destruction Of roots of the tree and the loss of fruit thereby. For our part we would select to leave under the branches untouched, beyond a slight forking or boring to maintain it clean, and dig or trench the remainder as deep as it is necessary. We are ac- quainted with a very healthy row of trees that is treated something like this; every other year a celery trench is formed on each side, and in the process of earthing up all the root' are cut that extend beyond the limits of the breeches. In raising the roots of trees, the soil must be moVed from amongst them, and as the trees requir- ing this -treatment are genefally of large size, it is re- quisite to commence at a greater distance from the stem than in the .case of trees requiring- only root-pruning. Much care should be exercised to preserve all the roots, and when the soil is being replaced round them their points should be directed -upwards. This will be a fit, tihg opportunity to improve the quality of the soil where necessary, but it is a mistake to place good 'soil at too great a depth, as that would only induce the roots dovrnwlards and defeat the object in view. THE FRONT .GenoEN.—The grass plot, which is fre- quently much neglected, should now have a share of attention when other work is not pressing. If cutclose with whatever means may be at command, it will main- tain a fleet appearance for the winter. Its appearance may be also improved if it receives a good beating with the back of the spade occasionally,hut not at such times when it is so wet as to give it a plastered appearance. The asters and other annuals growing in the beds or borders should be removed, now that they look shabby, so as to admit more light and air round subjects that are of a more perman,ent nature, and likely to maintain' a respectable appearance for some time yet. It is also wise to remove portions of vigorous growing plants:that are encroaching on their weaker neighbours. Notice should now be of those plants that are out of place, either by being too near the path on account, of their height, or others that grow too dwarf for the posi- tion they now occupy, so that they may be re-arranged at the proper time. When plants are first received the grower may not be acquainted with their habits, or they may assume proportions different to what he may have been used to in a different soil and locality, so that fresh ,arrangement is forced upon him, if he maintains any- thing like uniformity and studies the well-being of the plants.

Tax Wisnow.—Arum lilies (Calla Ethiopica), if planted out as previously advised, will have made good growth, as the season has been most fdvourable for them. Being of an exotic nature, they should not be leftin the ground any longer. Much of the soil may be shaken from them, and all the suckers, removed and placed in other pots. All should have the smallest size pot they can be got into, and fine, moderately-dry soil should be used for potting, so that it may work the more readily amongst the roots. Supply them with a soaking of water before being placed indoors, and preserve them at all times in a moderately-moist state, and they will re- ward you by throwing up their trumpet-shaped flowers one after another for several weekg. Plants that may have remained in their pots the whole of the season would be benefited by being turned out and some of the sour soil removed, and the plants placed in clean pots, treating them in every respect like the others.

The Pres—ent time of the year is one of the best that can be selected for putting into proper condition the floors of the houses. It is surprising how few perman- ent poultrY houses there are which can be regarded as at all satisfactory. They are generally either the earth alone, brick, or cement, none of which can be in any way regarded as really good, though of the three, if properly covered with a layer of fine soil or ashes, the brick is about the best. Cement is much too culd, and if by any unforeseen occurrence water finds its way into the house, unless the floor is laid so that it will run away, it stands about for the cement will not allow it to percolate through. But it is necessary if a brick floor is used to keep it thickly covered with ashes or fine earth; this to be constantly renewed, or the moisture from the droppings charges the bricks and the inter- stices between them with ammonia, and when that is the case, the atmosphere of the house soon becomes charged with the effluvia, which can never be got rid of until the floor is renewed. Earth is objectionable for the same reason; but can be more easily renewed, and, as we have already stated, cement is too cold, even if it is kept covered with sand, or ashes or soil. It is surprising how few holises there are in which the floor stands sufficiently above the ground. We have been inewell-built poultry houses, in which the floors within were just on a level with the ground without. The result of such an arrangement is that the floor can- not fail to be damp. It may not be wet, but it will be damp. Always should a floor be six inches above the ground without, . for that provides perfect dryness within, so far as the earth itself is concerned. Wherever possible, it is better to let permanent wooden houses be raised upon a bed of brickwork, say, two rows in height. If when one row Of brick has been laid, this is well coated with tar, and allowed to harden somewhat before the other row is laid on, the brick will be damp proof; that is, no damp will be communicable up to the wooden walls of the house through the brickwork. In stone or brick houses the same plan will be adopted with advan- tage. The floor will then be laid within this brick, and I there will be no danger of the gradual rotting of the I lower part of the woodwork, of which there is always I a danger when that material is carried level with the ground. In places where sand is plentiful, either sea or land sand, we should do nothing more than fill the inside up with it. If raked over daily, dug over once a fortnight, and renewed twice a year, there.is no better I flooring to be obtained. It is a perfeat deodiser, and water cannot•remain on it. Next to that we should place fine dry ashes. But if neither of these are avail- able, then it is better to dig out the earth within the house other three or six inches, fill this up two-thirds with broken slag, or brick, or coarse gravel, and when that has been well rammed down, lay on top a compost of cinders, ashes, fine gravel, quicklime, and water. This makes a splendid permanent floor, only needingto be covered with a little sand or earth, and cleaned regularly. The runs should be looked at now, whilst the weather ,is open. For covered runs and sheds, we like gravel best of all, but the open runs must be natural. Where space is abundant—on farms, for instance—if any of the , outlying houses have been standing in one position for I two or three years, and they can be moved, it is worth consideration whether they might not with advantage be placed somewhere else. Fowls use the ground near their house more than any other. It is the centre round which they radiate, and in process of time the earth there must get charged with the droppings from them. Often disease and non-success is due to this cause, when no 'reason can be assigned for them. If a run is looked at carefully, it will be seen that the earth by the house and the strip next to the fence, if there be one, is worn most of all. The advantage of the movable house sys- tem is that fresh ground can constantly be given, to the benefit of both the birds and, the ground, but even with the more permanent erections, if it be possible they should be reinoved every two or three years. For this reason we prefer medium-sized houses. The runs which are to be devoted to breeding stock should have a rest, if that can be arranged, so as to be fresh when the pens are mated up. Fenoes should be repaired, and where shade is not very plentiful, Virginian creeper or some such rapid growing runners may be planted near the fences, so that they can be trained along them. We need only now mention the perches and 'nest boxes. For the former, we should urge the abolition of all flat, narrow perches, and the adoption of a fir pole sawn in two, or a three-inch pole of another kind. This is the best time to make such alterations. Nest boxes also ought to be prepared, whilst, they are not so much in use. Let them be well lime-washed when the house is so treated, which ought also fo be now done. If the nest boxes need renewal or to be repaired, this is the time for that to be done. ha,fact; the object of the poultry keeper should be to get ready for whatever may be required later on. _

div.head: SEASONABLE HINTS.
div.p: SEASONABLE HINTS.

When the runs of the fowls are limited, those who keep the more active breeds are often troubled by their flying over the fences, and if there are several pens near each other, a "battle royal" is sure to ensue, often ter- minating in the serious injury, if not the death, of the combatants. Cocks kept together from the Arst, or, if

not running with hens, may have a tussle now and I again, but that is soon ever. When separated, or mated with hens, it is not so easily settled, and to prevent this, if not exhibition birds, it will be better to cut their wings, and so prevent their flying. This can be done without injury to thd appearance of the fowls. If one wing is cut right across, excepting the three first-flight feathers, which fold together outside, the bird will be unable to fly. There is a wing lock sold, which is very effective also, but, for. ordinary purposes, cutting the wings is the simplest plan.

EFFECT OF ALCOHOL ON LONGEVFIR.—The effect of alcohol upon longevity is most decidedly injurious. In intemperate persons the mortality betlveen twenty-one and thirty years is five times as great and between thirty and forty years of age four times as great, as that of the tenterate. It becomes gradually less with ad- vancing years, but at every age the abstainer has the advantage:—

intemperate Person. Chance of Living. Az 20-15.6 years. „ 30-13.8 „ „ 40-71.6 „ „ 50-108 „ „ 60— 8.9 „ —The Book of Health, for October. A correspondent of Nature, writing from Cheltenham, asks for an explanation of the "total failure" of the crop of' parsley this yen'i and last year. The parsley comes up well, grows to about one inch in height, then begins to dwindle and get yellow, and the whole summer re- mains about half-an-inch high, the only green part being the crowd. All the market-gardeners are said to be making the same complaint, only one having a crop, which was sown in freshly cultivated earth. Examina- tion of leaves and roots under the microscope has re- vealed no cause to Natures correspondent. A report: from the Meteorological Office states that during the past summer the ocean temperature in the course of the Gulf Stream was abnormally high. The conclusion is based on a comparison of returns made'by 28 ships, containing 116 recent observations, with the official data in the chartB of. the Atlantic sea-surface temperature. Bearing in mind the influence which the Gulf Stream exercises, or is supposed to exercise, upon the climate of Europe, a decided hddition to meteorelo- gical science May be expected, from such comparisons, the coincidence between the heat of the past summer and the abnormal heat of the Gulf Stream being remark- able. Ship-masters may well be encouraged to continue such observations during their voyages. The publication of a new work on The Origin of the World" is promised,immediately by M. Faye, the emi- nent, astronomer and president of the French Bureau des Longitudes. According to a synopsis which M. Faye has communicated to the Paris Academy of Science, M. Faye reviews the various cosmological Systems from the earliest times to Laplace, and after describing the progress of astronomical science since Laplace's day, presents a new theory "more in accordance with the enlarged astronomical knowledge of to-day, and more in harmony with the present state of science in general than this theory of Laplace." M. Jules Guerin and his opponents, the advocates of the "importation "hypothesis respecting Asiatic cholera, have latterly been (debating their respective opinions again before the Paris Academy of Medicine. All the old arguments were gone over, but MM. Rochard, Brouardel, and others remained faithful to their belief in personal importation, and consequently in the efficacy of quarantine, notwithstanding the recent experiences of Italy. Probably the most important fact announced was that contained in the statement by Dr. Guetin that he had authoritative evidence that epidemic diarrhcea was prevalent in Toulon for months before the true choleraic epidemic' appeared. This fact is quite in accordance with previous experience and was rightly described by Dr. Guerin as one of till strongest possible supports of the non-importation opinions which he holds upon the subject. AN ENORMOUS RAILWAY ENOINE.—" There has just been completed in a railway engine shop at Wilkesbarre, Pennsylvania," says Iron, 'a locomotive which it is anticipated will be able to pull a train on the New York division of the Lehigh road at the rate of 80 miles an hour. The engine, we are informed, weighs nearly 100,0001 b., and the tender, when filled with coal and water, 70,0001 b. The engine, it is stated, will develop from 1,400 to 1,500 horse-power. The great speed ex- pected with this engine is said to be attained by con- structing the cylinders with the steam and exhaust entirely independent. This is done by using fewer plain slide valves (known as gridiron valves) on each cylinder. The valves are worked by a peculiar arrangement of valve gear, in which the motion is taken from the con- necting-rod, and working entirely on true centres; there being no sliding surfaces, the steam valves being in- dependent of the exhaust, and rice versa, and the point of cut-off or expansion can be obtained without the corresponding back pressure and over compression, as in the link motion. The point of compression can also be changed without altering the point of cut-off or ex- pansion, so that the same-sized cylinder will give much more power at a given pressure than can be obtained by the link. To get the full benefit of this, the engine carries 1601 b. boiler pressure, the boiler being constructed of steel, especially for the purpose." TILE NEW AUSTRALIAN SILVER MlNEs.—The discovery, of silver mines round about Silverton, extending some 60 miles long by 30 miles wide on the borders of South Australia and New South Wales, is exciting great atten- tion, and schemes are. on foot for making railways from Jerowie, Morgan, and other points in New South Aus- tralia, as well as in New South Wales. Sixty veins have already been discovered, and so richly charged with sil- ver that in one case a mass of two tons has yielded 10,000 ounces of pure silver. Silverton, the centre of this silver land, 32 degrees S. lat. and 142 deg. E. long, is situated about 300 miles from Adelaide, and twice that distance from Sydney. Fortune hunters are, of course, rushing thither in thousands, in spite of the heavy ex- penses of travel, and the still heavier ones of living in a country hitherto unpeopled, and which, unless wells or springs are discovered, may entail on them terrible Suf- ferings for want of water. In any case South Australia, so long labouring under a depression of trade, is congra- tulating herself on the sudden influx of visitors, and for- tune. The land about Silverton is rising to quiet fabu- lous prices. Silver discoveries are also reported from Emmaville,,New South Wales, whence Mr. W. E. David, Government Geological Surveyor, states that six assays made in a sample of the mineral at Tent Hill yielded sil- ver at the average rate of 492 ounces to the ton, and gold at the rate of at least la minces. One assay gave as much as 81 ounces of gold, others merely a trace. Fur- ther discoveries of silver ore are announced from Welling- ton Vale, 12 miles from Emmaville. MUSICAL Pircd.—Mr. John Brinsmead, London, writes :—ln the time of Beethoven, Bach, and Handel the then newly-invented pianoforte was in most respects inferior to the harpischord, from which it borrowed its pitch and shape, but during the past half century the orchestra of the drawing-room has developed strength , and capabilities that enable it to resist a strain previ- ously deemed impossible, and the pianoforte now vies with the brilliancy, power, and shades of tone colour of a small orchestra. For this reason the pianoforte maker not only increases the length and thickness of the strings of his instrument, but also raises its pitch as high as possibte, so as to still further increase its brilliancy, despite the protests of vocalists who find themselves un- able to sing to such a pitch without injury to the voice. The pitch most suitable for the human voice is undoubt- edly the French diapason normal, the number of vibra- tions of pitch C being only 518 per second, and that is nearly half a tone lower than the so-called Philharmonic pitch used in England and America, the only two nations that venture to retain it. That the musical pitch should be lowered is Universally acknowledged, and it is to be hoped that a change so beneficial may be intro- duced in England at the Inventions Exhibition next year, if not before, it being certain that manufacturers of musical instruments will not make the alteration till the military bands have set them the example.

All who have had the care of children, or who have been called to use moral influences with their fellow- men, know that law and its sanctions are instruments inferior to love and mercy; that it is easier to melt than t,o break, to draw than to drive, and that persuasion triumphs where correction and admonition have utterly failed.

It should be the aim of young men to go into good society—we mean not the rich, nor the proud, nor the fashionable but the society of the wise, the intelligent, and the good. When you find men who know more than you do, and from whose conversation you can gather information, it is always safe to associate with them.

A sympathetic spirit is one of the, chief pre-requisites to all good conversation. No matter what natural gifts a man may have, what depth of thought, or breadth of knowledge or brilliance of expression, if he do not in- terest himself in other people, share in their feelings, and be as ready and glad to listen cordially as to talk freely, he will never be a good converser.

POISONING • MISTRESS.—At Durham Assizes, on Mon- day, Margaret Powell, domestic servant, was charged with mixing three and a half grains of blue vitriol with her mistress's tea in order, as she stated, to-spoil the tea and annoy her mistress. Ihe latter bad quarrelled with the girl about nine weeks before the present offence was committed, when blows were exchanged. A few days afterwards some liniment was found to have been mixed with the lady's tea, and she narrowly escaped drinking it. The bluish tint of the mixture led to the diycovery that vitriol had been used. The prisoner was sentenced to twelve months' imprison- ment.

REMARKABLE SCENE IN WESTMINSTER A 138 EY. —On Monday a singular scene was witnessed M Westminster Abbey. About 500 persons of both sexes knelt around the tomb of King Edward the Confessor, and engaged for some time in prayer, the day being the Feast of St. Edward. A special celebration was held in the neighbouring Roman Catholic Church of St. Peter and St. Edward, Westminster, where the Rev. George Akers, after preaching about St. Edward, invited the congregation to join the clergy in a pil- grimage of devotion to the shrine of the saint, and to implore his intercession for the conversicn of England to the ancfent faith. In response the entire congregation accmpanied the clergy to the abb.y.

PRESTON DOCK AND RIBB.LE NAVIGATION. On Saturday afternoon the first sod in the construction of the Preston Dock and other works in connection with the improvement of the navigation of the River Ribble was cut by,Mr Alderman Gilbertson, chairman of the Ribble Come mittee of the Corporation, in the presence of a large con- course of spectators including Mr Tomlinson, M.P., Major- General Feilden, 31:P., the members of the Town Council, Jsc., Jae. The ceremony took place on the Penworthan side of the river, just below Castle Hill. A pontoon bridge had been thrown across the river by Mr T A Walker, of Great Gborge-street, Westminster, who had already a large staff of men at work upon the necessary preparations. From the bridge stretched a roadway of planks to the ceremonial ground; and at the end of this was a grand stand of five tiers for the ladies, who filled every seat. Previous to the ceremony of cutting the sod, Mr Alder- man Gilbertson was presented with a silver-bladed spade and • carved mahogany barrow, both mounted with silver. Among the gentlemen present at the ceremony were the following, who had been received by the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) in the Guild Hall, and who went to the ceremonial ground in a procession of carriages : —Lord Alfred. Churchill, Sir Edward and Lady Watkin, Lieutenant-General Feilden, Captain Hesketh, Colonel Mounsey, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr Sidebottom, M.P., Mr Tomlinson, M.P., Captain Met- son; Messrs F C Hulton, L Rawstone, C B JaCSOD, W As- croft, JP., Dr Gilbertson. J.P; Mr R G Underdown, general manager of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway; Messrs E Ross and T Sidebottom, railway direc- tors; Mr Gilbert, secretary of the West Lancashire Railway Company; the Mayors and Town Clerks of Accrington, Burnley, Blackburn, Blackpool, Chorley, Clitheroe, Darwen, and Wigan; Mr J Elaydock, chairman of the Great Har- wood Local Board; nearly all the members of the Preston Town Connell, and many other gentlemen from other Lan- cashire towns. After the ceremony had been performed by Mr Gilbert- son, that gentleman requested Sir Edward Watkin to be "good enough to cut a sod." Sir EDWARD WATILIN having complied, then addressed the Mayor as follows: It has afforded me very great plea- sure to be here on this very auspicious occasion. You have taken a•bold step with reference to these works, but they will be the making of Preston, profit to the merchant, higher wages to the working-man and prosperity, I believe, to everybody. (Hear, hear, and cheers.), Mr. GILBERTSON then addressed the assembly. He said: Whatever may be said about this undertaking it is one of great magnitude, one which, if carried out successfully, will in a great measure conduce to the prosperity of the town and trade of Preston. It may *kt least be said that it is based on a sure haste—the regular ebb and flow of the tide twice a day. Those natural operations bad been going cm from the very earliest times, and were not likely te cease in our day. (Laughter and applause.) But we are not engaged in speculations of that kind; our business is to make Pres- ton a tidal port, and we are all well assured that the works we are now inaugurating will be successful., We might be asked —What are you going to do with the tide ? and I may say that when we have got it up to Preston in greater volume than at present we are .going to bottle it, as it were, and not to let it go back except in minimum quantities. We are going to take it prisoner, and make it float the ships which •we certainly think will come up to Preston in large nums hers. (Cheers.) It is a great and expensive operation, but we have taken the best advice, and are well assured that it will be a successful operation. That means that we shall have Preston a seaport which the largest vessels will ha able to reach easily and safely, and take up positions in the dock, I hope, with full cargoes. We have the very greatest confi- dence that the gentleman who has invited us here to-day will carry out the work successfully. and with the least pos- sible delay. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. Gilbertson concluded by calling for &roe cheers for the contractor. Mr. WALKER briefly responded, and cheers were afterwards given for the Mayor and Mr. Gilbertson, which closed the proceedings, and the procession returned to the Guildhall, where about 250 guests were entertained at a collation by Mr. Walker, and several complimentary speeches were delivered. About 400 men have since been set to work on the under- taking. In connection with the ceremony of cutting the first sod of the Ribble works at Preston. it will be interest- ing to take a brief glance at the proceedings which have led to the practical commencement of a work which its promoters hope will have an important effect on the future prosperity of the town. We need not go into the earlier history of the Ribble navigation, for we have in a comparatively recent issue fully leak with that. Suffice it to say that there was for a long time a strong feeling that the Ribble navigation should be in the hands of the Corporation, and that the rights and works- of the Navigation Company should be purchased by them. Negotiations were entered into with the company, and On the 28th of October, 1882, the Corporation offered to purchase the rights of the company for £72,500. The offer was discussed, and at length accepted, by the company, and the purcha3se was completed in the follow- ing March. In the Session of 1883 the Ribble Naviga- tion, Prestbn Dock, and Borough Extension Act was obtained, and in March last Mr. E. Garlick was appointed engineer, and his plans—a modification of those lodged in Parliament—were adopted. At a recent meeting the Ribble Committee was authorised to advertise for ten- ders; they did so, and that of Mr. Walker, Great George- street, Westminster, was accepted. The details of 'the contract were discussed in the Council Chamber on the 3rd of September, and fully reported in our issue of the 6th. After the discussion which took place at the special Council meeting on September 3rd, it will be readily understood that the works embraced in' the contract now under execution do not cover the whole scheme for which Parliamentary sanction has been obtained. The tenders of Mr. Thomas A. Walker, of Westminster, which have been accepted, include the construction and com- pletion of the diversion of the river, the river. entrance for the dock, with entrance gates, timber staging, tidal basin q acres, locks, lock gates, a 40 acre dock, training walls, and other works for £439,359 9s. 11d., and the deepening of the river diversion down to the rock for the additional sum of £17,241 Is. 3d., the two contracts thuO embracing an expenditure of close upon half a million sterling. The work to be done includes the diver- sion of the present river to the Penwortham side of the valley, commencing west of Penwortham Bridge. This diversion, which is the first portion of the work to be proceeded with, will cross part of the Holme, skirting the foot of the hill north of Penwortham Church, and join the present river course again west of the Chain Caul. A flood bank is to be constructed along the south Side te prevent the flooding cif the adjoining land. The sides of the river diversion are to be pitched with rubble, and it is to be excavated as far as the rock. Up to the present all that has been done beyond preliminary pre- parations is the arrangement of a pontoon bridge across the river for purposes of general convenience. As a pre- cautionary measure the site of the diversion will be banked round to prevent the river from getting into the works, as it might otherwise do at flood tides. The dock, which is to be 40 statute acres in extent, will be in the centre of the Ribble valley, between the new river and Ashton brow. It will be 3,240 feet long, 600 feet wide, and will afford 6,565 lineal feet of quayage. The jetty, which is not included in the present contract, and which it is not intended to proceed with until circum- stances require it, would give 2,000 additional feet of quayage. In the original scheme there was also included a 25 acre timber pond, but that is not confirmed in Mr. Walker's Contract. Between the dock and tidal basin there will be a lock 66 feet wide and 550 feet long, which, for the purpose of preventing a waste of water as much as possible, will be divided into two chambers, 325 feet and 225 feet long respectively. The quay walls will be 39 feet 6 inchee deep, and will stand 9 feet above high water at the ordinary spring tides and allow for 30 feet 6 inches of water. It is to be founded on the red sandstone rock, which will be exca- vated to a depth of from 5 feet to 10 feet. The walls are to be of concrete, composed of nine parts of sand and gravel to one part of Portland cement, to be faced with concrete of a superior quality, and surmounted by a granite coping 3 feet by 2 feet. In width the walls will range from 17 feet at the bottom to 10 feet at the top. They 'still batter 1 in 24, and are to be stopped at the back. The graving docks, which were provided for in the original scheme, are not included in the present con- tract, but the entrance is to be made, and also trenches for the hydraulic machinery. In a general sense the lock walls will be similar in character to those of the docks. Longoidge stone will be used for the principal portions, and millstone grit for the sluice openings and for the skirtings and apron sills. The floor is to be covered with concrete 2 feet thick. There will be the usual complement of mooring posts, and capstans (not included in the present contract) to be worked by hydraulic machinery, and preparations for coal hoists ta be constructed afterwards. The gates, 66 feet wide, are to be constructed of greenheart timber., Generally speaking; the locks will be about the same depth as the dock. The tidal basin, ai acres in extent, will be 40 feet deep; the entrance widening from 66 feet to 90 feet at the bull-nose. There will be 29 feet of water on the sill, the top of the lock gates will be 3 feet and that of the entrance 4ates 5 feet above the water. There will be a full provision of mooring posts 50 feet apart, steps, and ladders.

A DEorarcriyE FIRE, believed incendiary, occurred on Tuesday, at Cooper's corn mill, near Newry. The entire premises and an immense quantity of grain were consumed. THIRTY THOESAND PEOPLE STARYING.—An account of the distress in Sunderland. owing to the depression of trade, states that there are 10.000 men unemployed in that town. Most of these have been out of work all the year, and, in- cluding their families, it is estimated that 30,000 persons are at present in want. A leading pawnbroker has taken in pawn this year 1,500 wedding rings and other articles of Jewellery, besides nearly 3,000 watches. DISAPPEARANCE OF FOOT AND MOTITIL DISEASE —A state- ment of considerable public interest was made by the Chan- cellor of the Duchy of Lancaster on Monday. Mr. Dodson, who spoke froth the bench of the Lewis Quarter Sessions, said there bad been no fresh outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in England during the last three weeks, and there had been no outbreak in Scotland and Ireland for some months. So far as the Privy Council were aware there was not a case ot foot-and-mouth disease now in the United Kingdom. Should any fresh case occur the Privy Council hoped that local authorities would act with promptitude and vigour.

div.head: APPLICATIONS FOR INCREASE OF SALARY.
div.p: APPLICATIONS FOR INCREASE OF SALARY.

In the minutes of the House Committee it was stated that Miss Mackie, the infant school mistress, had applied for an increase of salary. Her \ present salary was £2O year and rations, and the committee recommended that it be increased by £5 a year.—lt was stated that the,e was also an application from Mr Shearer' and that the Board bad resolved to consider all , applications for increase of salaries at the end of Octobar.—lt was consequently agreed that these ap- plications should be left over.

NRW CLOCK. The School Committee recommended that the tender of Mr. A. Blae.khuret, Sankey-street, for a new turret clock to be put up at the schools be accepted. This tender which amounted to £44 10a was the lowest that had been received. —On the motion of Mr. DARBISHIRII the minuted were con' firmed.

VACCINATION CASES. A letter was read from the Local Government Board slat' lug that on their examining the returns for the period Jail —December, 1883, recently received from the vaccination officers of the Warrington and Newton districts. The Board found that of the 970 and 324 children whose births bad been registered in thoie districts during that period 140 and 130 respectively are unaccounted tor as regarded vac' cination. It was requested that the Guardians would ob- tain from each of the vaccination officers and forward to the Board an explanation of his omission to account for these cases. The Board would also be glad to be furnished with any observations which the Guardians- might desire 0 make with reference to such explanation.—The CLERIC said he had written to the officers about the matter, and had re- ceived a reply from Mr Cooper in which he stated that from the details which he sent he (the clerk) would see that there was a good excuse in most of the cases, and that eince send' log the returns five pf them had been vaccinated. lie might say with regard to the children who were ill that although 'some others were under the doctor yet there were no certificates of postponement sent in. Mr Cooper also re' tarred to the number of arrears in the district when be was appointed and the progress which he had made with thew, and also the amount of opposition with which he had had tc: • contend. The Clerk suggested that they inform the Local, Government Board that they had applied to the vaccination officers for explanations, and that he enclose their replies .-- This was agreed to, and the meeting terminated.

A LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY MYSTERY:"... , On Monday morning a coffin. containing some human re" mains, was found near an embankment close to flushoY; Station, on the London and North-Western Railway; it is supposed that a murder has been committed ii"" coffin was covered with quicklime, and has the appearance of having been buried in a garden. The mystery' has since turned out to be a hoax. Dr. Clark!, of Bushey, and a London pramitioner, examined 40/ bones on Tuesday, and came to the conclusion that 00. were not human remains but those of an animal. .01.' Brett, the medical officer of health, was at first of opinion that they were the remains of a child about 12 years old, t, Dr. Clarke reserved his opinion until be had made a caring' examination. STREET NOMENCLATURE IN DUBLIN —A circular harg been issued, signed "The Executive of The Irish Republie can Brotherhood," addressed to the Corporation of Dublin, stating, with regard to re-naming the streets, "We vr3fo you not to use the names of any of the men of 17(38 or 1803, of Thomas Davis, or of the men ef 1848 except GOA Duffy or Darcy M'Gee. Let the proposer and eeconder of the changes look well to this warning, as we will hold then, , responsible, and take such action with regard to them oe their conduct shall deserve; for we will not permit such name i as Wolfe Tone, Robert Emmett, John Mitche",, John O'Mahonv, &c.. to be dragged through the gutters byr the cowardly, swaggering mountebanks, their abettors,. r their dupes. They who are loudest in this matter have not-121:E in common with the men upon whose memory they want trade, and they will not be allowed to appropriate ao9 the glory of men whose conduct they are afraid to imitate-
