FOREIGN NEWS.
r--0-k-O'Vi--U-P- -A -QUEBEC PARLIAMENT

HOUSE—FRIGHTFULT EXPLOSIONS. QUEBEC, SATURDAY—About one o'clock this afternoon an explosion occurred at the new Parliament buildings, des- troying a considerable portion of the masonry and windows. The shock was felt throughout the city, the windows of houses in the neighbourhood of the explosion being shat- tered. The explosive is supposed to have been dynamite. At the time of the occurrence the workmen engaged in the building were absent at dinner, and only one was slightly injured. A second explosion took place at three o'clock. but without causing any damage of consequence. The car- penters state that they observed a box lying all the morn- ing close to the wall of the building where the first explo- sloe oemrred, but supposed that it had been placed there by one of the plumbers. After the explosion no trace of the box could be found, but it is believed to have contained dynamite and an infernal machine. The second explosion took place about 30ft from the first. The Parliament build- ing is stated to have been so badly cracked by the first shot that it is feared that one half of it will have to be rebuilt. After the first explosion men were sent all through the buildings to search foe suspicious-looking boxes, but found nothing. The cause of the second explosion is as mysteri- ous as that of the first. QUEBEC, SUNDAY.—An investigation into the circum- stances attending the dynamite explosion at the new Par- liament Buildings here is now proceeding. It appears that the first explosien made a hole about 121 t. high and sft. wide in the will on the third storey, directly over the right entrance to the Assembly, and close to the spot where the Speaker's chair would be located. The second explosion was in the north-eastern corner of the same building, the corner-stones forming the support of the buildings being badly bulged. It is doubtful whether it can be repaired without letting down the whole wall. Two persons were slightly injured by the explosion. A number of military are patrolling the grounds. The building had been com- pleted with the exception of part of the roof. The Cabinet has decided to oiler a reward of a thousand dollars for infor- mation which may lead to the apprehension of the perpe- trators of the outrage. All places where explosives are kept are being guarded. It is said that the Government were warned of this outrage some time ago. The police have now replaced the troops who were stationed on guard round the new Parliament building. It is stated that the authori- ties believe themselves to be in possession of a clue to the perpetrators of the outrage. The damage is greater than at , first appeared, and it is feared that the building cannot be completed in time for the winter session. The rtiontcalm Market, situated a quarter of a mile distant, was shaken to its foundations by the explosion. The powder magazines, the military store depot, and the cartridge factory are still guarded by the military. QUEBEC, MONDAY.—It is rumoured that four strangers lately employed on the new Parliament building had been acting in a sueoicious manner ; and it is also stated that three or four of the workmen had been heard to say that they would soon have their grievances redressed. The bole caused by the first explosion is larger than was at first re- ported. The cost of repairing the damage caused by the second explosion will be greater than that occasioned by the first. It is now thought that the entire wall of the north-west portion of the building will have to be removed, entailing an exnense of 25,000 dole. OTTAWAS, SUNDAY.— Owing to the dynamite outrage at Quebec. extra police have been placed round the Parlia- ment House here. The Marquis and Marchioness of Lans- downe are staying at Halifax. QUEBEC, TUESDAY.— An impression gains ground that the explosion was the work of a dissaffected employe. QUEBEC, THLRSDAS.—A copper cap, supposed to belong to an infernal machine, has been found among the debris caused by the recent exolosione at the Parliament Houses. EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN.
THE NILE EXPEDITION-THE REPORTED MAS- SACRE OF COL. STEWART.

- DONGOLA, THURSDAY.— The steamship Nassef-el-Khein has arrived here, having made the passage from Sarras in 17 days.--Saturday.—Sir Charles Wilson and Major Slade have arrived here from Wady Haifa by camel. The jour- ney occupied seven days.--Sunday.--Native merchants say that General Gordon, Colonel Stewart, and Mr. Powell are still at Khartoum, and that provisions there are plen- tiful. WADY HALFA, SATURDAY.— Twelve Nile boats reached Shellal on the Bth inst, having been either towed, rowed, or pushed up with poles. They were easily propelled by four Arabs in each boat. The boats were despatched the same day for Wgcly Haifa. The cable across the river has now heel completed. Lord Wolseley has returned here from Sarras. Assn:Kee, MONDAY—Lard Northbrook arrived here this morning. His Lordship is slightly indisposed, and will not land. He will start for Cairo to-morrow. Colonel Scott- Moncrieff has b,en summoned by teleeraph to Lord North- brook, and will return to Cairo with his Lordship on the 17th inst. Eight hundred and sixty-three men of the Camel Corps leave here to-day in the steamers Masur and Damietta, which are towing four barges. CAIRO, SATURDAY.—The Mudir of Dongola telegraphs this morning, re-transmitting the following message from the Sub-Mudir at Ambukol —"A: certain Fake, Walad Ah- met has :arrived here, stating that he has heard that after General Gordon's return to Khartoum a steamer with 40 men board, partly Europeans and partly Egyptians, besides five negroes and three servants, arrived at Salamat, where she ran aground, but did not founder. The population being much alarmed, several persons went ashore to reassure the natives, and to purchase camels to cross the desert to Merawi. The Sheikhs Soliman and Abu Noman, and the uncle of Faki Osman, agreed to see to their conveyance. Those on board were so pleaeed that they presented one of the sheikhs with a gold swori, and the uncle with a silver sword. 'The sheikhs requested them to leave the steamer and accept their hospitality; this was accepted, and the party entered the house, where they were all massacred. The sheikhs after- wards returned to the steamer and killed most of those on board. Of 40 persons, only 14 were spared, and these were taken prisoners."—Lord Wolseley has ordered be Mudir of Dongola to proceed to Merawi, with all the troops at his disposal, in order to release, or, if necessary, to ransom the prisoners in the hands ot the rebels. The Foreign Office on Monday morning received from Major Kitchener news from Debbab, which, if correct, would conclusively prove Colonel Stewart was alive. One of Major Kitcheners's runners, who has come in with details of the massacre, spoke with a survivor, who stated that the Greek Consul at Khartoum was in command of the steamer, and not Colonel Stewart. If Colonel Stewart had been on board he would have held that position. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—Lord Wolseley telegraphs that a native who saw the steamer which ran aground when within one day's journey of Merawi states that there were no Europeans of importance on board. Official telegrams from Suakirn report that it is now too late to utilise the Suillim-Berber route on account of the Amarars not having received the supplies and reinforce- ment which they had applied for. Dowame, MONDAY.—The Kudir is despatching to-day to Ambukol 100 men belonging to his army, mounted on dromedaries, in order to keep the road open in the vicinity of that place. The Mudir himself will leave shortly in a Private steamer. THE FINANCIAL SITUATION.

CAIRO, SI7NDAY.—A special Cabinet Council was held to-day, when the Khedive communicated a letter from him- self to Nubar Pasha, declaring that the Egyptian Govern- ment would consider itsdf responsible for the indemnifica- tion of Nubar Pasha and the Minister of Finance in case the international tribunals should grant the seizure of their private property, on account of the suspension of the sink- ing fund.

div.head: TIIE MAHDI ATTACKING.
div.p: TIIE MAHDI ATTACKING.

CAIRO, TUESDAY.—A small caravan from Kordofan has succeeded in reaching the Selima oasis. The travellers re- port the Mandi, hearing that Khartoum supplies were fail- ing, was gathering a strong force to invest the town. MOVEMENTS OF THE MAHDI. DONGOLA, TaIIRSDAY.—The tribes in this neighbourhood report that the Mandi has left El Obeid, and is marching in a south-westerly direction. They further allege the Mandi to be discouraged by the failure of his plan, and more par- ticularly to have lost heart since the death in the battle of Korti of his lieutenant and relative, Sheikh Mahomed, whom he appointed Ameer of Dongola. THE CHOLERA.

ROME. MONDAY.--:iiitTet;ven —fresh cases of cholera have occurred in Naples and 48 deaths. At Genoa there were three fresh cases and four deaths occurred. The other pro- vinces give 93 cases and 51 deaths. Mannin, SaTurtnay.—The epidemic seenas to be dis- appearing. The publication of bulletins will be discon- tinued. PARIS, MONDAY.—AI Marseilles on Saturday three deaths were reported, and none on Sunday. No more bulletins will be issued. On Sunday no deaths occurred it Toulon, but one on Monday. FRANCE AND CHINA. PARIS, SATURDAY.—AdiniraI COI/Ibet telegraphs: At Tamsui landing parties from admiral Loop's squadron. have made a reconnaisance of the posts from which the Cninese torpedoes are fired. A line of torpedoes forms the only de- fence of the harbour of Tamsui, but the shal'owness of the water preventing the approach of large vessels, and the nearness of the torpedoes to the coast render dredging opera- tions dangerous. The Chinese torpedo post is defended by a large number of infantry, ambuscaded behind dense thickets. In the reconnaissance six persons were killed, including a naval lieutenant. I have taken steps for establishing an effective blockade of Tamsui, and other ports. M. Tirard, minister of finance, has informed the Council of Ministers that he has succeeded in equalising the Budget without making any reductions in the sinking fiend. General Briere de Lisle canno, follow up his success at Kep, owing to the fall of the river. It was yesterday re-asserted that he had applied for further reinforcements. SEVERS DEFEAT OF THE CHINESE. PARIS, WEDAESDAY.—The following despatch has been received from General Sriere de Lisle, dated Chu, Upper Lu- chuan, October 13, 3 p.m. : " Colonel Donnier, after a brilliant engagement, carried on the 10th instant the heights commanding the fortress of Chu, which forms the paid d'appui of the large entrenched camp, which is defended by five casemated forts. The Chinese, who were very numerous, suffered a heavy loss, and endeavoured on the following day to assume the offen- sive, but our artillery fire strewed the ground with their bodies. After having lost all their positions the Chinese fled in the direction of Langson, and appear to have halted near Plan Truong Khamh. We had 20 killed, including one officer, and 90 wounded, of whom two were officers whose injuries are slight. Our troops are animated by the greatest ardour. The Chinese by whom we were opposed formed

part of the best troops of the Empire. They are perfectly armed, and manceuvre in European style. Their losses are very serious, amounting to about 3,000 killed, including their Commander-in-Chief. Colonel Donnier states that he considers the Chinese invasion as absolutely arrested in the direction of Langson. General Negrier is progressing very well." The Minister of Marine has received an exact return of the French loss in attacking 'LIMBO. Sixteen men were killed, including a naval lieutenant, and 17 seriously wounded, one being a midshipman. Thirty-two were , slightly wounded, including a naval subaltern and midship- man. nous, THURSDAY.—The Temps this evening publishes a telegram front Hanoi of to-day's date stating that after the recent French victory the Chinese army completely die- 1 Persed, abandoning its killed and wounded and an immense quantity of provisions. The Chinese generalissimo and a large number of mandarins were killed. John Thomas Appleby, chief cashier of the Middles- borough branch of the North-Eastern Bulking Company, has been sentenced to eight months' imprisonment for steal- ing £382 from his employers. On Thursday the Conservative candidates for Birming- ham visited a new Conservative Club in the soburb of Sparkbrook, and were presented with addresses of welcome. Lord Randolph Churchill. in reply, recommended a large extension of those political clubs, which formed admirable centres of instruction and organisation for their party. THE UNITED STATES ELECTIONS. NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY,—The Republicans have car- tied the State of Ohio by a majority of from sixteen to twenty thousand votes. The victory causes great rejoicing among the Republicans throughout the country. The returns from West Virginia indicate that the Democrats have proved successful by about five thousand votes. The Republicans are exultant at these results ; but the Democrats represent that they were expected, and will not affect the November elections. THE TRANSVAAL. DURBAN, MONDAY —The Transvaal Volksraad has adopted the proposal of the Executive Council to withdraw the pro- clamation placing Montsioa's territory under the protection of the Republic. THE MERIDIAN CONFERENCE. WASHINGTON, MONDAY.—The Internation Prime Meridian Conference re-assembled to-clay, and adopted a resolution in favour of Greenwich as the standard meridian. The repre- sentatives of France and Brazil did not vote, and the San Domingo delegate voted against the resolution. WASHINGTON, TUESDAY.—The Prime Meridian Confer- ence to-day resolved that longitude be counted from Green- wich in two directions up to 130 degrees, east longitude being designated plus, and west longitude minus. CANADA.

ST. JOHN'S (NEWFOLTI•TD—LAND), SUNDAY —The steamer Neptune, which sailed frnin Halifax in July last on an exploring expedition to Hudson's Bay, with the object of opening the direct summer line of traffic between the North-West provinces and Liverpool has returned here. She has established seven stations of observation to test the navigability of those waters, the stations to remain there one year. FIFE? HOUSES BURNT. NEW YORK, SaTllßDAY.—lntelligence received here from Paita, in Peru, states that a great fire has occurred in that town, by which fifty houses, including the Spanish and Por- tugese Consulates, have been destroyed. The damage is esti- mated at $250,009. THE ARGENTINE REPUBLIC. BUENOS AIRES, WEDNESDAY.—The Apostolic delegate has received his pas9ports from the Argen,ine Government for having associated himself with the agitation carried on by the Catholic clergy against the Secular Elementary Education Act. THE RED SEA LITTORAL.

.... - ADEN, OCTOBER 9.—The British India steamship Abys- sinia, specially chartered for the purpose, left here on the 4th inst. to convey from Berbera to Suez the Egyptian gar- rison, which is being withdrawn as arranged between Major Hunter and Noailli Pasha. The French at °belch find it difficult to carry on work owing to the beat and scarcity of native labour. The HaLbob tribes have been threatening Massowah, and some of the Bashi Bazouks forming the garrison of the town have deserted. Vice Admiral Hewitt intended to leave Aden on September 28 in the Euryalus to reassure the garrison, but was prevented by hearing that Commander Molyneux had rendered the required aid.

PESTH, THURSDAY.—In the Chamber of Deputi2s to-day during the debate on the Address M. Tisza delivered a speeh in which be expressed his satisfaction at the intimate relations existing between Austria-Hungary and Germany, the object of which was the preservation of peace, the main- tmance of good relations with neighbouring States, and es- pecially with Russia. THE JEANNETTE EXPEDITION. PHILADELPHIA, THORSDAY.—A vessel which has arrived here from Invigtut brings intelligence that the Governor of that place has many relics of the Jeannette and her crew in his possession.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

We take the following from The Evineer :—" That the rejection of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill last session was net at all likely to deter the promoters from making further efforts to secure the object they have in view, has never been a question of doubt, and the project is now again promi- nently before the public of Manchester and the district. As an evidence of the earnestness with which the project is being supported in Manchester, a town's meeting called for the purpose has by an overwhelming majority authorised the Corporation to levy a rate towards meeting the expenses of obtaining parliamentary sanctiou for an amended scheme in which it is intended to avoid the objections that proved fatal to the bill last session. It will be remembered that the opposition which proved successful before the House of Commons' Committee was based mainly, if not entirely, upon the evidence as to the injury which might result from the training walls proposed to he constructed in the estuary of the Mersey. After a careful investigation of several alternative schemes that have been put forward to overcome the objections to the original project, it has been decided so to alter the line of the propcsed canal from a point near Runcorn that it will avoid the estuary of the Mersey altogether. The chief feature in the new scheme will consist in the abandonment of the training walls in the estuary and the construction of a locked channel on the Cheshire side from Astmoor March. The channel will pass through the southernmost span of Runcorn bridge, and proceeding outside the line of the quay wall of the existing docks at Runcorn and Weston Point, it will by a bold sweep be carried past the mouth of the Weaver; it will then traverse the marches and at short distances the foreshore of the estuary, passing well inside Stanlow Point, and finally terminate in a set of locks above Eastham Ferry, from which point there is only a short distance to the existing Sloyne Deep, to which a channel will be formed by dredging. The carrying out of the new scheme, it is estimated, will involve an extra outlay of about a quarter of a million, and it will also I slightly lengthen the course of the canal; but as a set off it is claimed that the deviation of the coarse will enable the I canal to tap a larger trade than would have been possible with the original proposal. The locks originally proposed to be built at Runcorn will be removed to Eastham, and the water in the channel is to be maintained at a depth of 26ft. at low tides, whilst at high tides from 30f1. to 40 ft. of water will be got. This is briefly what the promoters propose to bring before Parliament as their new scheme, but whether it will enable them to escape opposition on the old ground or pos- sible injury to the navigation of the Mersey is a point that is open to some doubt. It woald seem not improbable that the question may be raised whether the proposed new channel, although it avoids the estuary, may not have the effect of abstracting water which would otherwise flow through the estuary, and thus have a prejudicial influence. That the promoters will not again have to encounter serious opposition is scarcely to be expected, and the action now being taken by the Bridgewater Navigation Company is a further complication which will not lessen the difficulties with which they have to contend. The proprietors of the Bridgewater Navigation are, in fact, putting forward a counter scheme for improving the water-way from Manchester to the sea, certainly not on so ambitious a scale ae the pro- posed ship canal, but of a sufficiently important character to secure for it a considerable following of support from those who doubt the practicability of the larger scheme. IThis project contemplates the deepening and widening of the rivers Dwell and Mersey, the shortening of the course by making two channels to avoid the present devious warps and bends, and the entire removal of several of the existing locks and weirs, which would be reduced in number from eleven to six. The remaining locks would be doubled in length; breadth, and depth, and the navigation so improved as to admit craft drawing 10 feet of water or vessels up to 400 tons. The port of Runcorn is now the terminus of the Bridgewater Navigation, and at present it is only capable of carrying vessels of 50 tons, craft of i greater tonnage having to unload at the above port. That the proposed improvement would im- mensely facilitate the water transit of goods between Man- chester and the sea there is no doubt, and in addition to allowing coasting vessels to come direct to Manchester it would, in all probabirty, develope a special trade between Manchester and Liverpool in vessels constructed solely for this traffc, and which might,be built up to 500 tons. This action of the Bridgwater Navigation Company is naturally regarded by the promoters of the ship canal as simply a scheme for increasing the value of their property, which will have to be purchased in the event of the ship canal being constructed. This no doubt is a result that the proprietors of the Brida•water Navigation have in view in the event of their property being required, but it hat not been the main oblect that has induced them to undertake the improve- ment. Tne work, which the company already possesses Parliamentary power to carry out, has, in fact, been in con- templation for a considerable time past, and two years ago the plans were laid down, but held in abeyance in conse- quence of the ship canal scheme being brought forward. The proprietors of the Bridgwater Navigation have, how- ever, now fully decided to proceed with these improvements, independent altogether of anything that may be done with regard to the ship canal, and schedules are now being pre- pared for the land that will be required." The Mayor of Manchester has officially intimated that he cannot legally entertain the demand for a poll with reference to the Manchester Ship Canal Scheme.
It is stated that Dr. Trench intends announcing his resig- nation as Archbishop of Dublin and Bishop of Glendalough and Kildare at the visitation to be held on the Bth prom.

div.head: THF, EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1884.
div.p: THF, EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1884.

THE REFORM AGITATION. LORD HARTINGTON AT CHATSWORTH. An important franchise meeting was held on Saturday at Chatsworth, the historic seat of the Cavendishes. The peeps of Derbyshire attended in thousands, and though an attempt to obtain the exact numbers failed, the attendance, to judge from the vast assemblage at the meeting and the nnnaerous excureionists in other parts of the extensive grounds, must have amounted to between twenty an 4 thirty thouland. For nearly three hours the large audience stood in the open air exposed to a severely cold wind to listen to the speeches of Cabinet Ministers and local members of Parllpment. The Marquis of Hartington, in a remarkably effective address, criticise the motives of the Conservative leaderh in pretmding to be sincerely in earnest in their de- sire for the extension of the franchise to county housholders. With regard to the redistribution scheme, he said that was a scheme which had been prepared for the use of a committee of members of the Government which was appointed to con- sider the question. It was an attempt to put into a practical and definite shape the principles laid down by Mr. Glad- stone himself in his speech on introducing the Franchise Bill. Neither the committee of the Government nor the Cabinet were pledged to the scheme either in its principles or in its details, but he was not ashamed to say that it was a plan which had been under their consideration,and, added the Marquis," I am not ashamed that all the world should know it." Lord Hartington emphatically protested against the claim of the House of Lords to dictate the time and the circumstances under which an appeal to the people should he made. The Government resisted the creation of this new precedent, because it was a claim to the exercisa of a power unaccompanied by responsibility. The resources of he Con- stitution were not yet exhausted, and it was his conviction that, however near we might be to a Parliatnentary deadlock, that deadlock would be avoided. That was his conviction, and because it was his conviction he was not the less anxious that the House of Lords should yield with- out loss of honour and dignity, without further loss of tem- per and time, and, above all, without further risk of the dis- turbance of our constitutional institutions, of which this country had long and, he believed, ever would, remain proud. Sir W. Harconrt followed with a speech which, like that of Lord Hartington, was received with great en- thusiasm. He contended that the public opinion of England would prevail, Lord Salisbury notwithstanding. The House 4. Commons had conceded everything that reason could demand, but they would not surrender the vital principle of the Constitution. They would not place the authority of the House of Commons under the feet of the House of Lords. Mr. Mundella and other members of Parliament ad- dressed the assemblage, and a resolution was passed pledg- ing the Liberals of Derbyshire to an unwaveridg support of the Government in its determination to carry the Franchise Bill in the autumn session. LORD SALISBURY, SIR R. A. CROSS, ti:c.

The Marquis of SALISBURY addressed a meeting of Con- servatives at Kelso on Saturday on the subject of the Franchise Bill. He accused Sir Wm. Harcourt of USittE quotations from his speech unfairly in order to mislead, and regretted that the great question had been degraded by Mr. Chamberlain and others into matter of personality. He had never said that the peers had the right to say when a dissolution of Parliament should take place, but they were bound constitutionally to see that the liberties of the people were preserved, and not sacrificed to a Caucus or to the will of the Minister of the day. The position of the Peers was quite clear. They did not object to the extension of the franchise, but they said it must be accompanied by a fair re- distribution scheme. He did not know if the scheme pub- lished in the Standa,e/ was that of the Government, bat if so it was not likely to be satisfactory, and the amiable plc- tare of Lord Hartington, by which they were to be induced to pass the Franchise Bill, did not look like business. They had heard a good deal about blank cheques, but this is not a case of blank cheques. The Lords are asked to give the Government a blank cheque, and in exchange they give us a cheque without ,t signature. Mr. Chamberlain has need many threats—he had said they would march on London. He hoped Mr. Chamberlain would head the column, and a good account of him would be given. He (Lord S slisbury) did not believe the House of Lords would recede from its position, and he was quite sure that it ought not to do so.— The Hon. Edward Stanhope, M.P., having spoken, Colonel MILNE HOWIE, M.P., moved, and the Earl of DALICEITE/ se- conded the following resolution, which was carried by ac- clamation :—" That this meeting, while cordially concur- ring in the extension of the franchise to the county house- holders, desires to support the House of Lords and the Con- servative party in their endeavour to complete the measure of reform now proposed by an equitable redistribution of political power." A Conservative demonstration was held on Saturday in the circus at Wigan, in support of the House of Lords and their action with respect to the Franchise Bill. The demon- stration was arranged by the Wigan and Smalls-West Lanca- shire Conservative Associations, and it was stated that 14,000 tickets had been issued. The building can only ac- commodate between three and four thousand persons, and it was therefore decided to hold an outdoor meeting. It was not, however, found necessary to take this step, as ticket-holders were all crowded into the building. The Earl of Crawford presided, and he was supported by Mr. Gibson, Q.C., M.P., Sir R. Cross, M.P., Lord Gerard, Colonel Blackburne, M.P., Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, M.P., Mr. Ecktrsley, M.P., and Mr. F. S. Powell, all of whom took part in the proceedings and addressed the meeting, condemning the home and foreign policy of the Government, and supporting the House of I Lords in their demand for a Redistribution Bill along with the Franchise Bill. Mr. Gibson, M.P., said the Government had brought in the Franchise Bill to cover their mistakes in other directions. The present Government was one of pre- tence, of great inefficiency, and of great expense, and would without doubt be driven from office when an appeal to the country was made. Sir Richard Cross, M.P. criticised the Ministerial methOd of testing the feeling of the constituen- cies by demonstrations, and remarked that the Conservatives could play at the demonstration gave equally as well as their opponents. The sooner they Ind a general election the better, for the verdict of the country would surely be in favour of the Conservative policy. Sir Richard followed Sir Stafford Northcote's example in asserting, with perhaps a little characteristic exaggeration, that Lord Salisbury, when he induced the House of Lords not to pass the Fran- chise Bill, was acting with the connivance of the Conserva- tive leaders in the Commons. Sir Theodore Martin and Mr. Cecil Raikes, M.P., spoke at a crowded meeting at Llangollen on Monday night, the latter dwelling on the importance of minority representation, especially in Ireland.
LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT NORTHWICH.

only that the Franchise Bill should be passed, but that at the earliest possible moment some reform must be made in the House of Lords. (Cheers.) The resolution was carried without a dissentient. Mr JAMES Toantnesps moved a resolution condemning the action of the House of Lords in throwing out the Fran- chise Bill. If, he said, they looked to the outcome of the legislation of the House of Lords during the last 55 years, they would see that that House had been systematically opposed to social and religious liberty in every form. (Ap- plause.) Mr. I. S. LEADHAM seconded the resolution. Refer- ring to Lord Salisbury's statement that it was the duty of the House of Lords to control the constitution of the House of Commons, he said that was a principle foreign to the letter and spirit of the Constitution as it had been handed down to them. (He tr, hear.) Lord Salisbury said the House of Lords were the guardians of the people's interests. (Laughter). He always supposed the guardianship of the people's interests was imposed upon the people's representa- tives. (Cheers.) Ler-I Carnarvon was not content with the House of Lords being the guardians of the people's in- terests, but said it was the duty of the Lords to see that the people did not oppress their representatives or their repre- sentatives delude the people. (Laughter ) Lord Egerton, in the intervals of tea and ices, the other afternoon—(laugh- ter)—attempted to warm the enthusiasm and spirit of the slender gathering by another text. He said it was consti- tutionally right of the Lords to appeal to the people. Now, as he understood the Constitution, no man had a right which was not linked with a responsibility. What responsibility would the House of Lords have in the event of an appeal to the country? As Mr. Gladstone justly said, if the House of Lords enjoyed the privilege of appealing to the country and were defeated, they would have nothing to do but to go home to their armchairs and repair to their usual forms of enjoyment. As the Constitution saddled the right of appeal with responsibility, that right rested with the responsible Ministers of the Crown. (Hear, hear.) He would have no compromise which involved the slightest iota ef surrender. If they once surrendered that principle they practically conceded the whole of the ground for which Lord Salisbury had been contending. (Hear. hear.) If they conceded to the House of Lords the right to dictate to the House of Commons the time it should dissolve, there would be an end to the possibility of continuing to pass Liberal measures for the advancement and improvement of the nation. If it happened that a Tory Government was returned all would be plain sailing, its measures would be supported by the House of Lords and the Government would enjoy unrestricted freedom and power. If they con- ceded that principle to Lord Salisbury, they would abandon Ithe privileges and liberties which their forefathers had ob- tained for them, and transfer the government of this country from the House of Commons to the House of Lords. (Cheers). Mr. G. W. LATHAM said that was a dangerous county in which to touch on the hereditary principle. The peers were hereditary; that was common to the peers of England, but in that county the members of Parliament were hereditary as well—their Egertons, their Tollemachee, and on from Legh to Legh, with now and then an Egerton Legit for change. (Laughter.) The parsons were hereditary in some cases, and now the chairmanship of the quarter sessions had been made an hereditary institution. The Duke of Portland said man made the House of Commons, but God made the Peers. (Laughter.) All he could say was, that he was very sorry for such handiwork. (Laughter.) He was no enemy of the Peers, he did not care about the stars and gar- ters—(laughter), they might enjoy them if they liked, but he desired that they should not direct the affairs of this na- tion. (Cheers.) There were a host of measures which must soon be made into law, for the country was crying out for them. They knew that the House of Lords, if allowed to exist without having their wings clipped, would prevent any of those measures being passed in their integrity. (Cheers ) " You have not yet entered into that rest and inheritance which the Lord your God has promised you." (Cheers.) The resolution was passed with acclamation. On the motion of Mr. T. SNAPF, of Liverpool, seconded by the Rev. F. MINTON, vicar of Middlewich, it WAS resolved te send copies of the resolution to the Premier and Lord Salis- bury. SIR S. NORTHCOTE AND LORD R. CHURCHILL AT BIRMINGHAM.—RIOTOUS PROCEEDINGS.

On Monday Sir Stafford Northcote, M.P., and Lord Ran- dolph Churchill, M.P., began to address a series of meetings in Birmingham. These meetings have direct reference to the present crisis, but indirectly, so far as Lord Randolph is concerned, are intended as a preparation for his candidature at the next election, when he is to contest Birmingham in 11 the Conservative interest. How far the meetings will be I persevered in is at the moment of writing this uncertain, seeing that the inauguration of them has been marked by disorderly proceedings, for which both parties must share the blame, and which the Liberals, no doubt, chiefly regret, as they will be the greater sufferers. The country, however, cannot allow the questio a at issue to be obscured by this collision at Birmingham. Sir Stafford and Lord Rindolph arrived at the railway station separately, and were each both cheered and hooted as they drove off, the former to Perry Hall and the latter to an hotel, demonstrations' however, not being any indication of what was to follow. Lord Ran- dolph spoke a few words from his hotel window, inviting the people to attend in their thousands that evening, when a demonstration was to be held in support of the House of Lords. The crowd, after giving three cheers for the Mar- quis of Salisbury, Sir Stafford Northcote, and Lord Ran- dolph Churchill, and a similar number of groans for Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Chamberlain, and Mr. Bradlaugh, quietly dispersed. The programme for the evening deeponstration included arrangements for five separate meetings, which were to have taken place in different rooms at Aston Park, a well-known popular resort in the suburbs of Birmingham. The fact that a counter demonstration had been announced to take place on some vacant ground adjoining, at an earlier hour in the afternoon, gave rise to some fears that the result would be a violent collision between the two rival factions, and events proved these apprehensions to be only too well founded. . . . .

. ..... At the counter demonstration there were about seven or eight thousand persons present, including not only the members of trade unions in Birmingham, but in the Mid- land Counties. It was originally intended that there should be speeking from only one platform, but as the attendance exceeded the expectations of the promoters two other gather- ings were improvised. The principal speaking took place nearly in the middle of the waste land, the chair being taken by Mr. Raddis, who was supported by several of the local representatives of the working classes ins the Trades Council and municipal offices. A resolution to the follow- ing effect was put:—" That the conduct of the managers of the Tory party in first of all inviting Liberals to be present at the lower grounds and at the same time making elaborate ticket and other arrangements to prevent the at- tendance at the falsely called 'public' meetings was an in- sult to the people and a frauduleot attempt to misrepresent the opinion of the midlands." One c,f the speakers said the Conservatives had issued two sets of tickets, one white and the other red. The former were given to the Liberals as invitations to attend the meeting in the great hall at night (at which Sir Stafford Northcote and Lord Randolph Churchill were announced to speak), and the others to the Conservatives, but it was understood that the presenters of the white tickets if they bore the badge used by the Liberals—a piece of blue ribbon (the Liberal colour in Birmingham) with the heed of Mr. Gladstone marked in gold—should not be admitted. It was further suggested that, if this refusal was denied, access to the lower grounds should be gained by getting over the wall—a sen- timent which was met with the response, " We will !" The resolution was carried with enthusiasm. A further proposi- tion, condemning the action of the House of Lords, was also carried, and everything appeared for the moment to pass off with ordinary quietness ; but no sooner had the meeting began to break up than there was heard a Cry,! "Over the will !" This cry had no sooner been uttered than several ladders were placed against the wall of the Lower Grounds. The wall is about Bft high, and a foot in thickness. Running along the top of it is a coating of jagged glass. This was not a sufficient impediment, for in less than two minutes half a dozen men had scrambled over, several, no doubt, suffering some personal injury from the adventure. Their example spread like wildfire amongst the crowd, who brought planks, which they placed against the wall. The few county police—not more than seven— who were near were simply powerless, and as there was no resistance on the other side, for the reason that the Conser- vatives were enjoying themselves in other parts of the ex- tensive pleasure grounds, in a quarter of an hour some hun- dreds had by this means gained admittance. By this time (about half-past five o'clock) the excitement became much more intense, and now, not content with scal- ing the wall of the ground both in Bevington-road and Witton-road, a portion of the masonry of the wall in the former thoroughfare was demolished, leaving a gap through which the crowd swept. It was estimated by the Conservative party that about 130,000 persons were at the Aston Grounds, the main portion of whom were admitted by duly authorised tickets. The Conservatives had arranged to hold meetings in the great hall, which bolds seven or eight thousand people; the skat- ing rink, which holds about the same number; and at plat- forms erected in the grounds, the time fixed being seven o'clock. There was a great pressure at the doors of the large hall an hour before that time, and several windows of the conservatory leading? to it were broken. When the doors were thrown open a rush was made on all sides, and it was noticeable that many who demanded admission were wear- ing opposition badges. Those who had charge of affairs en- deavoured to keep out the opposing element, but without success. The attacking party availed themselves of planks and other materials with which they battered in the doors, and in the end gained admission in large numbers, which were reinforced every minute, the supporters of the Conser- servative side being utterly overwhelmed. A scene of vio- lence and confusion then ensued. The opposition rushed over the reporters' tables and carried the platform by storm. Chairs were thrown indiscriminately amongst the audience, and a regular free fight ensued, in which the whole of the property on the stage was broken. At one time tits Conser- vatives were belabouring their opponents with pa ts of the wreckage, and almost cleared the platform, but they were powerless to restore anything like order, and although it is stated that no one was seriously injured, many persons were badly bruised, and the demonstration terminated in the greatest confusion. The Skating Rink also was the scene of much disturbance, the platform being completely carried away, but without injury to anyone. The other meetings were abandoned. Sir Stafford Northcote and Lord Randolph Churchill appeared on the platform in the ball and said a few words, which were drowned by groans, but the Conser- vative leaders were afterwards conducted to a quieter place, where they briefly addressed their supporters. Sir Stafford said their opponents had prevented them from hearing what they could not answer by argument, for wherever Comer-

vative meetings had been held during the recess but one opinion had been expressed in reference to the present crkis. They all desired an extension of the household suffrage, but there was unfortunately one party desirous of keeping up the agitation for another purpose, as was shown at Hanley by the suggested £lOO,OOO subscription. Lord Randolph Churchill said the Radicals by their manoeuvre , had brought a great stigma and slur on Birmingham. In no; other place would any audience have refused to listen to so able a statesman as Sir Stafford Northcote. He did not blame the Radicals so much as Mr. Chamberlain and his nayrrnidoms, Messrs. Schnadhorst and Nuttall. The Town Hall,which the Conservative party could have packed the next night, would be empty, and Mr Chamberlain regarded it as his own property just as much as he did his suburban residence. Mr Chamberlain no doubt represented 5,000 who had disturbed 25,000 that night, but the poll would show that Messrs Chamberlain, Schnadhorst, and Nuttall would not always win. Mr. Schnadhorst has taken an early opportunity of re- plying to some of Lord Randolph Churchill's personal attacks after the disturbance at Aston Lower Grounds on Monday evening. Referring to the statement that Mr. Chamberlain had "prevented" the Birmiogham Conserva- tives from engaging the Town Hall for a meeting, Mr. Schnadhorst says the hall was engaged five months ago for a Liberal meeting to be held on the day subsequently chosen by the Conservative leaders, and that was the only reason why they could not have it. The Liberals of Bir- mingham bad no desire to do or say anything which would be disrespectful of Sir Stafford Northcote personally, for on previous visits to the town he and also Lord Salisbury had been listened to by Liberals with patience and respect. Even Lord Randolph Churchill, who had heaped scorn upon them, had been treated with fairness and courtesy. The meeting at Aston was intended to deceive the public, for tickets by the ten thousand were issued to people of both parties, who would all have been counted as supporters of the House of Lords. The Liberals had adopted a thorough- ly legitimate device to counteract that fraudulent attempt. They all regretted that certain things had happened, but he was glad to know that the damage did not exceed £5O. They could not answer for everything that occurred in the present excitement, for which excitement he held the Con- servatives entirely responsible.

Lord Randolph Churchill spoke at another Conservative dinner at Birmingham on Wednesday evening. He de- fende-i himself from the chanze of having insulted the work- ing men by calling them "the mob" and "the scam," and explained that the expression he need was only levelled at the supporters of Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Bradlaugh. His Lordship afterwards made a characteristic attaek on Lord Derby.

Mr. T. B. Potter, M.P., Mr. R.. Leake, and Mr. O'Connor Power, M.P., were present on Saturday at a great demon- stration, held at Rochdale. Mr. W. Angnew, M.P., in a letter, said when the peers could give the people the fran- chise they wouldn't. If they refused on the second time of asking they must be forced to give mach more than the franchise—Mr. Leake said the House of Lords on this as on many other occasions had proved itself to b 3 blind to the people's rights, and to its own interests. The Tories had now a possible inkling of what the Liberal redistribu- tion scheme must be, and he hoped they liked it—or rather that they did not because the less they liked it the more he should like it.—Mr. Potter said if the Lords succeeded in the present contest and placed their feet on the representa- tiVes of the people, it would not be long before they heard of the re-enactment of the corn laws in one shape or another to enrich the landed interest at the expense of the people. —Mr. O'Connor Power said the franchise agitation had re- sulted in the conversion of the rory party to the opinion that public opinion demanded the county franchise, and also to the inclusion of Ireland in the Bill, which was no small thing in connection with the party whose history was intimately associated with coercion in Ireland. A great demonstration of the Liberals of West Camber- land was held at Whitehaven. A procession was formed at the railway station, several hundred colliera belonging to Earl of Lonsdale's pits at Whitehaven marching in it, a eight never befere witnessed at Whitehaven. An open-air meeting was held, when sO.leelne were delivered by Mr. Thomas Burt, M. P., Mr. W. C. Gaily, Q.C., the Liberal candidate for Whitehaven, Mr. David Ainsworth, M.P. for West Cumberland, and others. An imposing demonstration was held at Exeter. Amongst the numerous speakers were Sir Thomas Dyke Acland, M.P. and the Earl of Morley. The first resolution approved of the Franchise Bill in the one part, and stranglv condemned " the majority of the hereditary portion of the Legislature in the other. The Earl of MORLEY confessed that he felt some delicacy in touching upon the latter proposition. Over his head, however, waved the words: "The People's Will : The Franchise Bill," and to this he was unreservedly faith- ful. His claim for the absence of violent language during the agitation on the Government side and his assertion that the Government are perfectly confident in the verdict of the constituencies, with or without redistribution, were signifi- cantly applauded. The resolutions, the second being one of unabated confidence in Her Majesty's Government, were of course carried with acclamation. The five Liberal candidates who were present (for St. Ives, East Devon, Tiverton, Devon- port, and Sheffield) were singled out for special encourage- ment on rising to speak. A great demonstration of Liberals of Perth and Perth- shire was held at Perth on Saturday. Mr. W. E. FORSTER, M.P., speaking at a franchise meet- ing held at Bradford on Saturday evening, said the Govern- ment must not bring in a Redistribution Bill which they themselves did not approve, nor had he any fear that they would do so. He could not see why Ireland should have a larger representation than Scotland and England, nor could he understand why the metropolis should have 50 per cent less representation than Ireland. He referred to the offer contained in the speeches of Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain, which he considered very reasonable. If the House of Lords would not be contented with information of what kind the measure of redistribution was to be, then the respensibility of the conflict must rest with them.—Mr. HERBERT GLADSTONE said he was confident that nothing would induce the Government to introduce a Redistri- bution Bill without the amplest and most certain security that the House of Lords passed the Franchise Bill first. . _

Huddersfleld declared its sympathy with the unenfran- chised householders on Saturday. A demonstration of 10,000 electors and non-electors from all parts of the sur- rounding district was made through the principal tenets, and afterwards a meeting was held in St. George's-square, at which about 20,000 persons gathered. In the evening crowded meetings were held in the Armoury and the Town Hall. Addresses were delivered by Mr. E. A. Leatham, M.P., Mr. W. H. Leatham, M.P., Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., Mr. C. Bradlaugh, M.P., and other gentlemen.—Mr. H. Gladstone characterised the publication by the Standard of the rough draft scheme as a "dirty trick,'" and said the key of the present situation was in the deep-rooted antipathy to reform which the Tories had. _

In many other parts of Great Britain the Government re- ceived hearty support. A meeting in support of the Franchise Bill was held on Monday evening in the Liberal Club, Prestwich. There was a crowded attendance. Mr. R. N. Phillips, M.P., pre- sided, and was supported by Mr. Robert Leake, M.P., Mr. Wm. Agnew, M.P., Mr. B. Armitage. M.P., Mr. Henry Lee, M.P., and Mr. J. O'Connor Power, M.P. Letters of apology ' for non-attendance were read from Mr. Slagg, M.P., Mr. Arnold, M.P., Mr. Briggs, M.P., and others. Sir Charles Dilke addressed a crowded meeting of the Liberal party at Oldham on Tuesday evening on the fran- chise and redistribution questions. Replying to a resolution of confidence in the Government, he said the Radicals of the great towns had no personal cause to regret the infatua- tion of the peers. The interests of the unenfranchised labourers suffered for the time, but Radical principles gained largely by the action of Lord Salisbury. The people of Oldham were appealed to recently to support the Lords because they had given them Magna Charts ; he (Sir Chas. Dilke) would rather quote the words of the peroration on the same cccasioa of their. Tory candidate's speech, when he said that "the earth was cracking around them on every side," for a moral earthquake would, in his opinion, be brought about if in November next they again rejected the Bill. On Wednesday night a county franchise demonstration took place in the Manchester Free Trade Hall, which was crowded to excess. The principal speaker was Sir Charles Dilke, M.P. Speaking of the franchise, he said he felt delighted at the new popularity of Liberal principles with the Tories, to which they had been so bitterly opposed hitherto; but if the Lords would act in November as they sometimes spoke, and show their liking for the franchise by passing the bill, the Liberal party would cease to inquire too narrowly into the cause of the miracle which bad been wrought. An address thanking Sir Charles for his support of the Extension of the Hours of Polling Act was presented to him by a deputation from the Liverpool Industrial Union. Sir Charles Dilke broke his journey from Manchester to London on Thursday at Stockport for the purpose of open- ing a Liberal Club which has been erected in St. Thomas's Ward in that town. Speaking in response to a resolution thanking him for his presence, Sir Charles Dilke urged the importance of popular representative organisation, and said that, having had experience of such organisations in the borough which he represented in Parliament, he had no hesitation in declaring that not only was it the true form of organisation in the interests of the party, but, what was of far greater importance, it was the true one in the inter- ests of Liberal principles. Sir Stafford Northcote spoke on Thursday at Liverpool In the afternoon, replying to a number of addresses pre- sented to him at the Conservative Club, he emphasised some of the new conditions under which the next elections would have to be conducted. In the evening there was a great meeting at the Circus. In his speech there he remarked that there had grown up in this country an organisation which crippled seriously the liberty of members of the House of Commons, and which was directed by men who bad ulterior objects in view which they hardly cared to disclose, but which were now becoming more clearly perceived, and were dietasteful to the great balk of the English people.

THE NEW BA-IKIIIIPTCZ ACT.—The following case has been mentioned as an example of the working of the new Bankruptcy Act in a remote district, where the Official Re- ceiver's costs for travelling formed the chief item in the ex- penses of realisation. The petition was filed on the 18th July, and the dividend of 12,3 in the £ paid on September 24th. Debtor's estimate of the value of his assets, £l2 10s 6d ; amount realised. £172 17s 7d. The payments were : Board of Trade and Court fees, £l6 103 sd; law costs, £8 15s 6d •, cogs of realisation, LT Ss id; preferential debts, £34 13 sd. Dividend, £lO5 193 21.

div.head: LIBERAL CANDIDATES FOR MID AND WEST
div.p: THE LIBERAL CANDIDATES FOR MID AND WEST
CHESHIRE.

A Reform demonstration was held at Northwich on Satur- day afternoon. Although the weather was cold, upwards of a thousand people, chiefly of the unenfranchised class, as- sembled on the Barons Quay" to protest against the action of the Lords in refusing the franchise to the county house- holders. The meeting was most enthusiastic. Mr J T Brunner presided, and amongst those on the platform were the Hon. R C Grosvenor, Mr James Tomkinson and Mr David Duncan, the Liberal candidates for West Cheshire; Mr I S Leadam and Mr Thomas Rigby, the Liberal condid- ates for Mid-Cheshire; Mr G W Latham, Mr Robert Verdin, Mr George Rooke, Mr T W Killick, Mr F Snape, Mr Alger- non, Fletcher, Mr Green, Mr Dixon, Mr A E Paterson, the Rev T B Lloyd, the Rev F Minton, and the Rev Thomas Carter. .
Mr ROBERT VERDIN moved a resolutim in favour of the Franchise Bill. .

- Mr THOMAS RIGBY, in seconding the resolution, said it was true that he had not hitherto taken much active part in political matters, or at political meetings. But his heart , had always been warmly in the Liberal cause, and be had endeavoured to promote it in an intelligent and proper man- ner. He was fully sensible of the honour which had been done him by the Liberal party in that division of the county in selecting him as one of their candidates. He was not so vain as to think the honour had been intended as a personal compliment, but he regarded it as an honour done to the class to which he belonged; it was an honour not only to him as a farmer, as one connected with agriculture. but as one belonging to the middle class of society, or, indeed, to t*.e lower half of the middle class. (Hear, hear.) It was an admission that a man need not be rich or titled before he could be thought of as a member of Parliament, and it was a declaration of fitness or of ability where it was thought to exist. (Applause.) It was desirable that tenant farmers should be represented in the House of Commons by men whose interests were in common with theirs, or who by ex- perience or training were at one with them in sympathy and who possessed the practical gauge of their case and its needs. (Applause.) He thought that, if elected, he could serve the class with which his life both in private and in public had been largely identified. Hitherto agriculture had been almost wholly represented in Parliament by owners of land, and although the interests of the two classes should be common there were some essential fea- tures which were divergent and distinct, and some which were antagonistic. (Hear, hear.) The Liberal party of that large agricultural constituency were the first to recognise the duty of watching the interest of the tenant farmer, and ha trusted their action would meet with the response it deserved when the time came to express it. (Cheers.) He believed the Liberal party were most acceptable to tenant farmers, as it was to them they were indebted most largely for the freedom they possessed. lie thought he could serve the cause of agriculture in the way ii required service, which was not open to him in any 'Hier Position, and he had, therefore, resolved to offer such service as he was able to render for the acceptance and in the interest of his brother farmers. (Cheers.) Mr. H. Duscax, in supporting the resolution, said he thought they would be in a stronger position to fight the House of Lords with two millions more electors at their backs, and for that reason he thought it might be well to accept the suggested compromise. Tne Hon it C CrnosvErron, who was greatly cheered on rising to address the gathering, said that he sympathised with them in the objects of the great meeting of that day. There could be no doubt the action of the Tory party with regard to the Franchise Bill had been of enormous assis- tance to the Liberal cause throughout the country. It had united into one solid phalanx all seCtions of the Liberal party. They were determined this Franchise Bill should be passed, and that a majority of 59 Peers should not dictate to the House of Commons as to when that measure of jus- tice should be given to the people. They, the Liberal party, considered the Franchise Bill as good as passed, but there had been the greatest enthusiasm whenever anything had been said about reforming or abolishing the House of Lords. (Cheers.) They were determined that an unrepresentative chamber of persons who bad hereditary rights should- no longer interfere with the action of their elected representa- tives. It was the opinion of the people of this country, not

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

_ On Wednesday night an enthusiastic meeting was held at Birkenhead in favour of the candidature of Mr. W. R. Kennedy, who has been selected as the Liberal candidate for the borough, FATAL COLLISION ON THE CLTDE.—On Saturcay. a col- lision occurred on the Clyde between the Sunderland steamer Roseville and the Dublin steamer Europa, and the result was the sinking of the Europa, with a loss of six lives, and the beaching of the Roseville. Oa Saturday last rive men belonging to a steamer which had attended npsn the Island of Coll, Inner liebrilestleft in a small boat for a telegraph station on the mainland. A gale was blowing at the time, and as the boat has not sines been seen it is feared that the men have been drowned.

A HEAVY COLLECTION.—At the opening services of the new place of worship of the Wellington-street United Presbyterian Church, in the West end of Glasgow, on Sun- day, the collections amounted to £12,500. This is said to be the largest collection ever made in any church in Scot- land.

An alarming explosion of gunpowder in process of manu- facture occurred on Wednesday morning at the works of Messrs. Shortridg4 and Wright, gunpowder manufacturers, Worsboro Dale, near Barnsley. A workman named William Wallace was frightfully burnt; several others were slightly injured. ALLEGED OUTRAGES BY Awnr.,LEnvxmc—A number of artillerymen have been arrested at Portsmouth, pending an investigatien being conducted by the military authorities at Woolwich relative to certain outrag•ts which were committed there on Wednes lay night, prior to drafts leaving to join the Poonah at Portsrneuth....

STRIKE OF CoLLlPus.—All the miners employed at the Llay Hall colliery, Flintshire, have struck work against a reduction in wages of 5 per cent. The proprietors have offered to effect a compromise by conceding Id per ton in the price of cod, but the men have peremptorily declined the offer, and have all been paid off. THE AUTUMN SESSION. Th,. Daily News announces that Mr. E. S. Howard, M.P., will move, and Mr. W. Sum- mers, M.P.. will second the address in the House of Com- mons, in reply to the speech from the Throne on the open- ing of Parliament. Lord Be!Wier will move, and Lord Law- rence will second the address in the House of Lords.

The Earl of Dufferin, the viceroN -designate of India, was entertained at a banquet in Belfast on Wednesday evening. In replying to the toast of his health, his Lordship said he had the good fortune to be united to the Fcreign Minister of Russia by the ties of personal intimacy and regard, and be Ives convinced that a more moderate-minded, wise, and unaggressive statesman did not breathe in Europe.

REPORTED SEIZURE OF DYNAMITE AT LIVERPOOL.—The Liverpool correspondent of the Press Association teie.zraphs that late on Wednesday night, as the passengers were land- ing from the steamer Lord Clive, from Philadelphia, the Irish detectives who are stationed in Liverpool, in searching the luggage of an Hungarian • steerage passenger, found nib. of American dynamite in 30 packages. The Hungarian was arrested.

THE INTERNATIONAL FORESTRY EXHIBITION, which was opened at Edinburgh on July Ist, was closed on Saturday evening. Pecuniarily, the undertaking has not been so profitable as was anticipated, but if there be any deficiency it will not be serious, and in all other respects the exhibition has been attended with success. It is only a question of Close now when a permanent School of Forestry will be established in Edinburgh.

, ALLEGED WILFUL STARVATIOX.—AI Grimsby Police Court, on Tuesday, Diz tbeth Briggs, widow, and Charles Briggs, mother and son, were charged with the wilful mur- der of Theresa Briggs, wife of the male prisoner. The evi- dence showed that deceased died of starvation and exhaus- tion, and it was alleged that the prisoners had deliberately and systematically kept her without food with intent to bring about her death—Remanded.

There came before the magistrates at Skibbereen, in c3unty Cork, on Wednesday, one of those injudicious prose- cutions which serve to intensify the popular feeling. Over forty persons were summoned by the police for c trrying tar barrels and displaying emblems on the occasion of the visit of the Baroness Burdett-Coutts. The solicitor for the de- fence described the prosecution as deplor tisle, seeing that the people were only paying honour to whom honour was due. The Bench dismissed all the cases.

THE Fos rsfaSTErt-GENEnaL 03 FEMALE grFFRAO2.-.. Mr. Fawcett, in addressing his constituents at Hackney, on Monday night, justified his attitude in reference to the en- franchisement of women, and said be felt Mr. Woodall's amendment was so just that it was absolutely impossible for him to vote against it. He could not see how the carrying of this amendment could possibly endanger the Franchise Bill. The claim of women to enfranchisement was just and expedient, and could not be permanently resisted. SIR P. CL-NLIFFE OWEN ON TECHNICAL EDUCATION.— Sir P. Cunliffe Owen, speaking at the City and Guilds of London Institute, South Kensington, on Saturday, said that in the matter of technical education they might learn a good deal from the trade syndicates of Paris which comprised manufacturers, foremen, and workmen. in addition to their. ternational juries there were juries composed of men of techsical ability connected with these syndicates, and they studied every particular object belonging to their trade, and drew up a set of valuable reports. The result of his ex- perience had been to confirm his opinion as to the honest work of the British manufacturer, and he would still back the old country against any in the world. He suggested that they should get up a series of exhibitions of drawings and different objects with respect to the various trades in. terested in technical education.

SHOCKING TRAGEDY ON THE HIGH SEAS. The barque John Gill, from Iquique to Falmouth for orders, arrived at the latter port on Friday, andireported that a shocking mur- der had been committed on board during the voyage. The John Gill left Swansea for Iquique about thirteen months ago, having shipped a crew at that port, amongst whom were two men who were found to be utterly useless. The mate did his best to teach them their work, but succeeded only in the case of one of them; the other became exceed- ingly troublesome, and was a great annoyance to all on board. About a month after they left Swansea the mate ordered this man to go about hie work, when the latter, who is reported to be a Scoteeman, and of very morose dieposi- lion' suddenly drew a knife, and before anyone could inter- feredrove it into the mate's body, inflicting such injuries that he died on the following day. The murderer, directly he had committed the deed, jumped headlong into the sea and was drowned. THE DEATH OF THE Hon. GILBERT LEIGIL—The body of the Hon. Gilbert Leigh was sent to England from New York, on Sunday, in the Britatmic. Mr. Grenrell, the former member for Salisbury, who was in Mr. Leigh's party, gives the following particulars of the death :—" Mr. Leigh disappeared on September 12. The body was found on the 21st. We had a camp ha the bottom of a canon. He saddled his horse, and left at two in the afternoon. As he did not return during the night we beeame alarmed, and in the morning went in search. We examined carefully, firing re- peated shots. There was no response. We found the horse two miles away. Mr. Leigh's coat was tied on its back. We found no other trace, though we searched censtantly for a week. When we went over the ground for the third time we found the bat, and soon afterwards the body. It was hidden in a hollow below a rock 80 feet high. The clothes were not torn. He must have been killed instantly. The skull was fractured, and the back of the thigh and the leg were broken. He was on his back, head upwards. The body was untouched by animals. It was three miles from the camp. I know exactly how the accident happened. We had hunted the canon repeatedly, and knew it perfect'y for miles. The rock was quite perpendicular, the lowest ledge being a hundred feet high. There is only one place where you can ascend, a mile and a half up the cation. He ascended there, and returned along the precipice. I fol- lowed the tracks for a considerable distance. The ground where he fell shelves rapidly. Be could not see the preci- pice below. I saw plainly the place where he slipped. There was a tree ten yards below. His rifle caught on this, which is on the very edge of the precipice. His death was not caused by carelessness. The place was simply a trap he fell into. It was very slippery and covered with loose stones. I have no doubt he was returning to his horse. He was very adventurous and plucky. He was going home next day. We lashed the trunks of two trees together. and placed the body upon them, and carried it over the mountains for 25 miles. We then had a wagon journey of 130 miles before we reached the railway." GALE AND SNOWSTORM.—WRECK AND Loss OF LIFE.— g OnTriday:morning a disastrous wreck occurred at the month of the South Esk, Montrose, Forfarshire. About one o'clock the powerful steam tug Storm King went out to tow into Montrose the steamer Petrel. A strong gale from the north was blowing, and as the vessels entered the river the tow rope gave way and the schooner went on the rocks. The tug, in backing to procure another rope, also went on the rocks a little ahead of the schooner. The crew of the tug at once launched and got into their small boat, but it was immediately swamped, and the occupants, four in number, were thrown into the sea. One of them, George Boetland, got hold of the tackling and reached the deck of the tug. He then gotithe master, Samuel Duncan, safely aboard. Tt& other two men were drowned. Meanwhile the Mincing-lane lifeboat was launched and pulled down the river and along- side the tug, which was then found to have struck on what is known as the "stone"—an outlying rock about ten yards from the shore. The lifeboat took off the two survivors from the tug and returned with them to Montrose at three o'clock in the morning. Meantime the schooner had got off the rocks, and again put out to sea. As she displayed distress signals, another tug went after and brought her safely to port.—The barque Sarnaning, owned by Messrs. Harrison, and Sons, Newcastle, and bound from Quebec for South Shields with timber, ran ashore midway between Marske and Saltbarn, on Friday morning. The sea was running very high, and the position of the crew was ex- tremely perilous. While the lifeboat was being Prepare,' the coastguardsman got the rocket apparatus on the scene, and they endeavoured for two hours to throw a line over the ship, but the force of the gale frustrated their efforts. The lifeboats Charles and Ann, from Saltborn, and two from Redcar meanwhile made strenuous efforts to reach the wreck, the crew of which clung to the rigging while the waves broke over the vessel. After three hours' arduous working, one of the Redcar boats succeeded in getting along- side by' the aid of a rocket line, and took off twelve of the crew, including Capt. Geddie, amid the cheers of thousands of spectators. Eight of the crew bad already come ashore in the ship's boats. The vessel is expected to become a total wreck.—During a heavy gale on Friday afternoon the schooner Eliza, of Penzance, from Porthcawl with a cargo of coal, was making for Padstm harbour, when she struck on the Doombar Sands. The lifeboat Aral, put off through a heavy sea, and saved the crew of five hands. The vessel remains on the bar and is likely to become a total wreck.
