div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c

" Clovie and Madge" by Mrs. Heaney; London: S. W. Partridge and Co., 9, Paternoster Row. This is a temper- ance tale, in one volume, by the wife of the Rev. G. 8. Reaney, formerly of Warrington. Mrs. Reaney is not new to work of this kind, having previously appeared before the public as the author of "Our Daughters,"" Found at Last," Stc; and the writing throughout reveals the practised hand. The object of the story is to show the insidious growth of the desire for strong drink amongst "the best and fairest," and at the sere time to demonstrate that the rich and cul- tured may become its slaves as well as the poor and illiterate. Clovis ", and " Madge " are types of their class—the for- mer being the ilaughter of a dissipved charwoman and the latter the petted darling of "a squire of high degree." But they are alike in gradually acquiring a taste for intoxica- ting liquor—the one through imbibing beer and the other through taking wine ; and the result is that in the end they are both degraded by the habit. We will not anticipate the reader by giving in brief the plot of the story, which is well told, and ends naturally and pleasantly in " Clovie " and "Madge" becoming teetotallers and leading Christian lives. Looked at merely as a story, Mrs. Reanev's work has per- t:lms too much preaching in it ; but she has had something more in view than simply to engage the attention of the 3 acing; she has felt it necessary to point the mare, and adorn the tale eS :he sent along, so as to make the most or her opportunity. Toe volume, which is one of some 200 pages, is handsomely bound and praphically illustrated. It 's exceedingly suitable 'as a presentation book :o the young.... . _ . _ _

. Cassell's "Encyclopedic Dictionary" has now reached the ninth part of the monthly-number issue of one shilling each. The more we see of it, and the more we become de- lighted with its many excellencies. The Tinzes might well call it "a work of immense utility, both an encyclooindia awl a dictionary." Indeed the diligent student will find it a reference library in itself, and if his means aie limited he cannot do better than invest in this direction. The article On letter "A," to take it as the instance of the fulness with which everything is treated, occupies over a page (three columns) of closely printed matter. The letter is (1) des- cribed as a vowel sound, (2) as an initial, (3) as a symbol, including the musical sign, (4) as used in composition, (5) as a p ,rt of speech, and (0) as an abbreviation. This thoroughness is not occasional but characterist'c. and the reader is farther aided by the pictorial illustrations which adorn them while they e!ucidste every page of the text. Every care is taken to ensure accuracy in r,iving the la•est nomenclature of science, while at the same time obsolete words and phrases are placed on record, thus linking the thirteenth with the nineteenth century. The quotations by w:y of illustration are numerous and apt, so that taking up a dictionary as interesting resding becomes a great fact, instead of as formerly a great joke. The sticklers as to spelling—and these are legion in these days of 'spelling- bees "—will find everything to their hearts content; for with the modern form other forms are given to indicate historic evolution. As to pronunciation, exactness, and clearness are aimed at and attained, the signs employed being simple, and therefore, readily remembered. Some faint idea of the way in which the " Encycloccedic Dic- tionary" towers above its predecessors may be gathered from the fact that it will contain 150,000 words—that is no less than 20,000 more than the new edition of the Im- perial Dictionary. And what an advance it is upon John- son's Dictionary (Todd's edition) which contAins 8,01:X7) only!

The second part of Cassell's fine-art ediricn of Long- fellow's Poetical Work is a charming number. It includes such celebrated poems as "The Village Blacksmith" and " Beware," and it is not too much to say that th 3 illustra- tions are such as the poet himself would have been de- lighted to see. " Cassell' a Magazine" for October is of wide and varied interest; there is something to please every reader. The serial stories" Within the Clasp" and "John Ford " are continued, and there are several complete tales and sketches. "The Care for Rheum itism," by a family doctor, is a valuable paper—worth its weight in gold to the chronic subject. " The Primrose Way," by Mr. G. Weather- is charmingly set to music by Mr. C. Baslett. " A Canoe Voyage Deem the Wharfe" is a readable sketch, and there is an article by Professor BlAikie Ou " A Battle that all must Fight." Volulle In Of "he Quivef " OM§ the current issue, A very fine frontispiece, "Fattier and Daughter," Nustrates a poem by the Rev. F. Langbridge ; and tilera AN Several striking illurtrations to " Overland to Cairo," by the Ven. Arthur Gore. " His Second Sell" and " For Cecil's Sake" are brought to an end is the present part; but the reader need not fear a lack of good serial stories. The programme of arrangements for the next volume of this popular magazine is of the most complete and exhaustive kind. Cassell's " Book cf Health," which. now reaches part 8, is, we are g!aci to see, beginning to be' quoted as an authority. The article on "The Influence of Stimulants and Narcotics," written as it is in a calm, judi- cial and scientific pint, will be read with great interest, and will be studied, as it deserves to be, for the statistics are most valuable. "Popular Gardening " loses none of its attractions. There is, amongst others, an erratic .11ustra- r ion of the vine in pot for the table. "The Rose and its Culture "is continued, and there are articles on Surbaban Gardening, Flower and Kitchen Garden. Greenhouse Plants, and the Vine and its Fruits. "Little Folks" is bright as ever, and is strong as usual in the number and variety of its illustrations.

The English Illustrated Magazine (Macmillan & Co.) sustains its high reputation. A pleasant article on "Loch Fyne" is beautifully illustratA; but mtny readers will be attracted by "The hors2—ancient and modern," and "Heidelberg," both of which are also amply illustrated. That tos-brief spiritual romance, Little Schoolmaster Mark," is brought to a pleasant close in the October number.

We have also to hand "The Season," better known as the fashion journal, "La Season." The success it has achieved in this country has led to an edition being issued entirely in English, and to a reduction of the price to one shilling. tu the same departnymt of literature we have ' Le Moniteur de la Mode," "Myra's Journal of Dress and Fashion," and 'Myra's Thre penny Journal," all issued by Meesrs band 4k, Son, Covent Garden, London. They are accomo pauied by the usual patterns and coloured plates.

div.head: GOLB-ORNE.
div.p: GOLB-ORNE.

INDEPENDENT METHCDIST CHAPEL.—An impressive Ser;e vice was held in the Independent Methodist Chapel on Surer day evening. The death of the wife of Mr. Robert Open- sbaw was referred to by the preacher, Mr. J. Bitchall, of Westhough ton. REFUSING TO Quir.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton and A. C. McCor- qaodale, Wm. Urquhart, of Newton, applied for an eject- ment order against Albert Jackson, of Golborne. The ap- plicant stated that Albert Jackson was the tenant of some property at Golborne. He had served a 'notice to quit" upon him, but the tenant refused to leave.—The Bench granted an ejectment order. DRUNKENNESS.—At tbe Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, Peter McLoughlin, 13 years of age, was summoned for be- ing drunk and disorderly at Golborne on the 219 t ult, and pleaded guilty.—The Bench remarked that defendant must have a bad sort of a character as he had been there so fre- quently. He would be fined 5s and costs.--Thoneas tins- worth was also fined 5s and costs for beiog drunk and disor- derly at Golborne on the 24th September. Aessume—Michal Joyce, a young fellow, pleaded guilty at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, to a charge of assaulting John Hill, a youth, at Golborne, on the 27th ult. —The camplainant stated that he was walking across a field between the Cricket field and Bank-street, when the de- fendant threw stones at him, and threw him down without any provocation. He hit the defendant with a stick in self defence' and the defendant" thumped" him in the face.— A fine of 2s Gd and costs was imposed. A SHOPKEEPER FlNED.—Benjamin Waterworth, an aged man, who keeps a small sweet shop in Golborne, was sum- moned at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, for having an unstamped and unjust weight in his possession on the let inst —Superintendent Weir stated that a 21b. weight was 1/ drachms light, and it was unstamped. lie did not think the defendant was aware of it, because when he (Superin- tendent Weir) entered the shop the defendant was buying some articles and the weight was being used. He had oelv summoned the defendant so that the weigbt might be seized.—The Bench said the weight would be forfeited and the cave dismissed. GOLBORNE Foornete, Ceum—One of the most intere,t- ing events in connection with the Golborne Football Club came otT on Monday evening, when the members assembled at the Legh Arms Hotel to present Mr. T. Berwick, the originator of the club, with a handsome pair of fish carvers, in case, and a photoeraph group of the first team. Tea was provided, to which about 30 sat down. Mr. Arnott was called upon to make the presentation. The photograph bore the following tastefully inscribed on a silver plate :—" Pre- sented to Mr. T. Berwick, by the members of the Golbornee Foothill Club, as a token of respect and esteem for the great interest he has taken is forming the above club." Mr. Ber- wick suitably responded, sincerely thanking the members who had subccribed towards the gifts, and said he hoped they wotld always stick together and never gain a victory by underhand actions. Several toasts were afterwards honoured, a very pleasant evening being spent. "CHEAP MEAT AND UNJUST WEIGHTS.—Bef ore Messrs. R. Houghton and A. C. McCorquodale, at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, John Wm. Green, a youth, described at I a butcher, was summ,med for having a number of unjust I weights in his possession on the Ist inst.—The defendant said he would plead guilty, but he did not know they were light —Superintendent Weir stated that the defendant car- ried on business as a butcher in Smithy-lane, Golborne. When he visited his shop he found the defendant's grand- father in charge of the shop. lie (Superintendent Weir) found the following unjust weights :—a 4lb weight ounce light; 21b, 7 drachms light; llb, 1 drachm light; drachm light; and a 2 ounce weight was also light.—The defendant said they were not his weights as he had borrowed them.—Snperintendent Weir said he did not know whose weights they were, but the defendant had them in his pos. session. The shop was known as the "cheap meat shop ;" and there were bills in the window bearing the words "Hello; look here for cheap meat."—The Bench imposed a line of 103 and costs, and said the weights would be forfeited. They thought they were dealing leniently with the defen- dant, as he mast have been aware whathe was doing.

A motion by Earl Lytton for an injunction to restrain Messrs. Swann, Schonntnshetm, and Co., and Miss Devev, from publishing letters of the late Lord Lytton to Lady Lytton, was on the paper for hearing before Mr. Justice Chitty on Wednesday. Counsel announced, however, that both sides had arranged that tbe motion should stand over till the first motion day in Michtelmo sittinl, on defendants undertaking not to publish the letters in the ' meantime.

- --- DISORDERLEY BEHAVIOUR. Henry Ice, of Havdock, was summoned at the Newton Town Hall on Saturday for a breach of the peace at Haydock on the 26th ult. The Bench ordered defendant to pay the costs, 6s 6d. SHOCKING DEATH OF LADY.—A lady met with a fear- ful death at Palnaerstown, nuar Dublin, on Sunday. She was driving in a trap with a gentleman, two other ladies. and a child, when the horse shied at the engine attached to a tramcar. The unfortunate lady struck her head against the projecting part of time engine and was thrown under the car, being literally cut to pieces, death being instanta- neous. The tram rails were covered with blood and brains. The child was thrown out, and the two other ladies fainted.

POOll-LAW CONFERENCE.—Tbe tenth annual Conference of members of Boards of Guardiaos in the North-western Poor-law District was held at Macclesfield on Wednesday, under the presidency of Mr. J. T. Hibbert, M.P. In a report which was presented details were given of the action taken during the year la ith regard to various bills affecting the poor laws; and it was stated that the effect of the Casual Poor Act of 1882 had been to reduce vagrancy very largely both in the north-western district and through- Out the country generally. DISCOVERY OF DYNAMITE AT DARLIScGTOSe.A9 two boys were blackberrying on Thursday, in a field closely adjacent to where the recent Houghton-le-Spring races were held they strolled under the grand stand, where they found a tin containing 16 charges of dynamite. The charges were pro- perly wrapped with copper wire and had a fuse attached, which had evidently been lighted. Mr. S. Smith, of the White Lion Hotel was near, and took possession of the dynamite, which he afterwards caused to be exploded in a field. Much excitement prevails in the locality, as it is sup- posed the intention might have been to blow up the grand stand.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1884.

THE Conservatives of Warrington were in the enjoyment of "high jinks " on Wednes- day in celebration of the opening of their new club. It is time they had a little recreation; they have been doleful enough all the bright summer. They certainly tried during the early part of the year to have what the Americans call a "good time." They be- came "fishers of men "; but they found the waters even as the waters of Walton reservoir. As Sir GILBERT GREENALL would say, they , had been fished by "another party" until they were empty, and the result was that, like the fishermen of old, they toiled all night and took nothing. Was it to be wondered at that some amongst them should begin to think there was something the matter with the bait, and that they should even go the length of proposing to change it? If the " Lion " itself could only have spoken at the luncheon on Wednesday, what a tale it might have told of the misgivings and heart-burnings of a few months ago! But the Conserva- tives of Warrington have apparently con- cluded that there is wisdom in the saying that it is unwise to swap horses whilst crossing a stream; and, after the proceedings of Wed- nesday, it may, We presume, be taken for granted that they have finally decided to make the best of Sir GILBERT as their nomination for the next Parliamentary race. This is something to be thankful for. When you know the pace of an animal at its best, there is a fair chance of calculating the beating that can be given it when it is all but out of the running. • To return to the club., We can sincerely congratulate 'the Conservative party on the commodious and handsome home they have provided themselves, and upon its being graced at its opening by so distinguished a politician as Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE. The leader of the Conservative party in the House of Commons is held, we do not hesitate to say, in high estimation by almost every section of thdLiberal party. It is the complaint of the Conservatives, as Sir STAFFORD himself once pathetically remarked, that he is lacking in " go ;" but they may take comfort in reflect- ing that if he were twenty years younger, and had more " go " in him, the chances are that, like Mr: GLADSTONE and Lord DERBY, he would be found within , the ranks of' the Liberal party. As-it is, with the conserva- tion of energy which accompanies advancing years, he will probably remain a Conservative —an instance, amongst many, of arrested de- ' velopment. Well, he is better as he is than a bushel of SALISBORYS, whose name 'has become a synonym of that which is hateful to honest men, or of your weather-cock CHURCHILLS who turn about with every wind that blows. Touching the latter, some surprise has been expressed that Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE did not open- ly rebuke Lord RANDOLPH for his frothy ravings after the break-down of the Tory demonstration at Birmingham; but if this was a little too much to expect, it is gratifying to observe that he took the oppor- tunity of doing this, indirectly, at Warrington. Speaking of the attack upon the Aston Park meeting, he said—" We must not allow our- selves to be tempted into an imitation of what was so wrong on their part." This is excel- lent advice; but it is exactly opposite to the course proposed to-be taken by Lord RAN- DOLPH CrruscHirm, who is pledged to a policy of retaliation. It is curious to observe how oeten Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE is at odds with his followers when there is any- thing being done which is obviously wrong. We have given one case in point, and another is suggested by the address which was presented to him at Warrington. That address proceeded to congratulate him

upon his resistance to the proposed "change of law for the purpose of admit- ting an avowed atheist into the House of Commons." How the right honourable baronet must have winced when he found. them treading on this particular corn so heavily but unconsciously ! It is notor- ious to all but Tories, who have no his- torical memory, that the leader 'of th Tory, party in the House of Commons was amongst the first to suggest that a change in the law was the proper way out of the Bradlaugh difficulty. It was not till "the fourth party" had snatched an ur,- expected victory that he was brought round to acquiesce in that which we do not doubt he still regards as a questionable proceeding. But it is his weakness as a leader that he sometimes consents to be- ing led astray against his better judg- ment; he is too prone to follow in a trck that has been made for him, HOW otheriiiise could he have come to jo:n in the petty sneer, as he did on Wednesday, at " the opinion of the public gathered together in the streets ?" This is the language of Lord SALISBURY and Sir MICHAEL HICKS- BEACH, and of other smaller if not meaner men. It is one of the straws which shows how the wind blows, like the unfortunate reference of Sir RICHARD CROSS to what he called " the wretched Franchise Bill." Hap- pily for the Liberals, these phrases have their use in holding working-men firm to the con- viction, that despite their protestation to the contrary, the Tories at heart despise them as much as they did when they jeered at them as "the swinish multitude" and butchered them at Peterloo. Still, the reactionists are being carried along in spite of themselves; they have throughout the country emulated the Liberals in establishing political clubs. They are undergoing a process of education, and by and-bye when the Two Millions have been added to the electoral roll ;hey will doubtless endeavour to persuade themselves that they never did anything to impede the progress of the Franchise Bill.

The riotous disturbances at the Tory meet- ings at Aston Park, Birmingham, on Monday, have brought, we regret to say, discredit upon the Liberals of the Midland Capital. We have no sympathy with mob law, and mob law was in full• swing on Monday evening. Liberals from the days of Milton onward have not fought the battle of free speech in order, as soon' as they are strong enough, to drown the voices of their opponents. There is a better way for rational men of -dealing with the bounce and bunkam of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL than by mobbing him when he tries to speak. It is true he has been im- pudent and reckless in his misrepresentations, and that he has used language of a most provoking kind. But better leave Billings- gate alone than shout it down. We do not for a moment think that responsible men among the Liberals of Birmingham have had any hand in breaking up the meetings at As- ton. It is nonsense for Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL to say that they owe those scan- dalous proceedings to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. The President of the Board of Trade too well knows the damage they are calculated to in- flict upon the Libetal party to counsel any- thing so mischievous. They are due rather to the indiscretions of Lord RANDOLPH him- self; he has been sowing the wind and has reaped the whirlwind. He has assumed to speak for the people of Birmingham, and the people have let him see, in a rough fashion, that he is not their mouthpiece. He talks about retaliatory measures, but that is a game he had better not, attempt to play. Politically as well as physically he cuts a small figure in Birmingham; if he has been badly handled by an angry giant that is no reason why he should challenge an encounter for 'which he is wholly unequal But his lordship has a way of losing his head now and again, and he has lost it over this matter. Amid so much that is almost tragical, it is highly diverting to picture him as con- gratulating the audience that would not hear him upon that." marvellous and enormous demonstration in defence of the House of Lords." ,He "thanked them too for their kind and hearty and courteous welcome," and he was quite serious—just as serious as he was an hour or so afterwards in denouncing the proceedings of the same meeting as utterly disgraceful and scandalous to the last degree.' What ideas he must have of propriety to condemn such things in a , Cabinet Minister, and in the same breath speak of them as "pardonable in a private individua'." The inference is that the mem- ber for Woodstock being neither a Cabinet Minister, nor likely to be, will be doing a pardonable thing if he incites the Tories of Birmingham to riot at a Liberal meeting. But, we repeat, he had better not try; those who have talked about breaking heads may get more of it than they like if they push matters to an extreme. We are mot, like Lord SALISBURY, desirous of seeing a display of violence.; but we may point to the fact that Birmingham is in no humour for tolerating the impertinences of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL.

PRoviszoN dealers will do well to take warning from a number of cases tried at St. , Helens the other day, several grocers being Ifined twenty shillings and costs for selling " butterine ' as butter. It seems to have become known to the authorities that there was extensive violation of the Adulteration of ; Food and Drugs Act, and Police-constable BROOKS was sent out disguised as a labourer to half a dozen shops to purchase " eight- penny butter." He was supplied in all cases. except two, with " butterine " instead of btitter, the shopkeepers in the two excep- tional instances remarking that it was " but- terine " that was sold at eightpence per pound. The samples analksed by Dr CAMP- BELL BROWN showed that about three-fourths of the article sold as butter was "fat derived from flesh." In one case this material was labelled not only as butter, but as butter of "splendid quality." It was urged on behalf of one of the defendants that the police authorities could not expect to get butter at eightpence per pound, and some comment was made on the sending of an officer " on a round of deceit and deception." But if one disguise is permissible as a means of bringing offenders to justice, why not another, or for that matter a dozen? It wouldn't avail a pickpocket to say that he would not have been guilty of a particular offence if he had known that the innocent- ' looking man he had noticed somewhere near the scene of his operations was" a policeman in disguise ; " nor should a like plea be made when the conduct of minor offenders I is in question. It is the duty of police authori- ties to see that those who are guilty of in- fractions of the law are made to pay the pen- alty of their misdemeanours; they are acting in the interests of the public, and are entitled to public sympathy and support. THE OUTBREAK OF DIPHTHERIA AT HALEWOOD.—Dr. Hale, the medical °lnner of health, has made the following report respecting the attack of diphtheria at Halewood , 1 he only cases of infection which have occurred in the die- , trict of the Rural Sanitary Authority since the last meeting I have been at Halewood, where an oatbreak of diphtheria has occurred. There have been three deaths in one house, and I expect the water has been the cause from a sanitary analysis I have made. I have requested Mr. Twist to for. I ward a sample to Dr. Campbellprown for his report on it. ; The sum,ner has been an extraordinary dry one, and the ; well is low, so that any extraneous matter finding its way iato the well would poison it more than when there was al larger quantity of pure water for it to mix with. She had died peacefully on the previous Wednesday. ASSABLTING A LANDLORD —SAMNA' Morris and Patrick Cannon, young man well known in the town, were sum- moned to appetr at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wedeesdey, to answer a charge of ass caking G. H. Fowler, landlord of the Millfield Inn, Appleton, and occupier of the Milltielet Recreation Crcounds,—.The Complainant said on the 13th Octobers sparrow shooting match was taking place on the liecreetien Grounds, when aiout 30 or 40 rough fellows passed the man who was receiving money at the gate with- out paying. They had not been inside long before they created a disturbance, and a fight commenced. The comb t- tants etipped to the waist, and Morris acted as second to one and Cannon as second to the other, wiping blood off the feces of the men, and getting them reedy after each round Complainant did all be poesibly coald to prevent a distur- bance, and blew his whistle for the police. He went in between the combatants, when Cannon and Morris seized kold of him and pulled him about. Cannon kicked him savagely onthe thigh, and be closed with him and threw Cannon on the ground. Cannon said he would be quiet and go off the geld if he would let him get up. Complainant allowed him to rise, and wee walking away from him when be received a severe kick on the leg, and various blows on the head and face. Cannon was the nears who kicked him. Afterwerds,Morris entered the Inn, and complainant ordered him out, wherespan Morris cursed him, and struck him on the chin. He had since been unable to eat solid food in consequence, and had to walk with the aid of a stick. He was very ill from the usage he received. He wished the men to be made an example, as this was not the first time he had been attacked.—Thomas Heaps. plumber, Penketh, corroborated.—ln reply to the Bench, Supt. Barker said the complainant kept a very respectable house.—Mr. Hall (the chairman) said as the complainant kept a respectable house the Bench would try to put down this rough conduct, and sentenee each defendant to a month's hard labour without the option of a fine.—Neither of the defendants were in court during the hearing of the case.—At the conclusion of the business Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, appeared and said he was instructed by the friends of Morris to ask for the case to be re-heard. Morris had not received his summons until late the previons evening, and when the case wag being heard he was searching for his witnesses. His friends were willing to pay for a warrant for his apprehension.--After some conversation, the Bench decided to try the case again, and issued warrants for the apprehension of both defen- dantse—Morris'a friends paid the costs.

Mr. R. Shaw was voted to the chair, and there were preeent the It :v. W. Preston. Messrs James Wilson, William Leach, W. Handley, T. Bowyer, Thomas Boote, P. Speakman, P. Briscoe, A. finest, D. Barker. The Chairman said : The rights of the freeholders in the common lands were very greatly interfered with because there was no organ,zed aesocration to protect them from en- croachments, and toe OimmissiOners thoughe it advieable that the power should be placed in the hands of a properly constituted body, so that the freeholders might bare the benefit of the common lands, and so that they might be set set apart for the public good. It would be necessary, there- fore, for that purpose to take certain steps, and no resolution of teat meeting would do more than express the feelings of the freeholders. If It was thought desirable, the Commis- sionere might get the requisite number to sign a petition for enclosidg and regulating the lands. After that there would' have to be an inquiry, and persons interested would have the opportunity of attending t ) take whatever course they thought proper. He thought it was of the utmost import- ance that the common lands should be secured for the benefit of the town, and he was sure it would be a great blessing te the rising generation if the lands were reserved as a place of recreation and for breething space in years to came, when they hoped the towa would pover a very large portion of tbe district. It was for those interested to say whether they Were willing that steps should be taken to secure this object, I and he tibould b 3 gta t to hear the ohs xv.ations of any gen- tleman before a resolution was salenitted. ALLEGED ROBBERY OF BANK NOTES AND CHEQUES BY RUNCORN MEN. Before Captain 0. W. Hezleburste at Runcern Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, George Bushell, of Lock-street, and Thos. and Elizabeth Bosworth. of the Holloway, were brought up, on remand, charged with having, on the Ist instant, stolen or received knowing to bt,stolen, eight £5 nntee, three £lO notes, and four cheques, one for £6, two for £5, and one tor £3, the monies of Richard John Jones, draper, Station-road, Llanfairfechaa —Mr. T. H. Hitchen appeared for the priso- ners, and asked that the male prisoners sbonld be tried separately, bat Superintendent Leah objected, and the magistrates decided to take the cases altogether.—Mrs. Jones, wife of the prosecutor, said on Wednesday, the let instant, she left Llanfairfechan by the 7-18 p m train for Manchester, and she had in her possession cheques and bank notes te the total value of £39. These were pinned together and placed in a piece of paper in a small basket. At Chester she hid to avail an hoar, and about eleven o'clock she en- tered a train she believed was going to Manctaster. In the carriage were the male prisoners, and a little boy and a girl. She placed her basket between herself and the prismer Box- worth, and ooened it to take out a neckerchief. Just at title moment a porter told her she was in the wrong train, and she hurriedly left the compartment to catch the train to Manchester. At Manchester she opened her baeket and dis- covered that the cheques and notes were gone. She returned to Chester by the first train next morning and informed toe railway officials—Mr. James B. Holland, caehiee at the 'Runcorn branch of Parr's Ranking Company, Limited, said on Monday, the 6th instant, the female prisoner entered the bank and produced a £5 note, for which she said she wanted cash. In answer to his inquiries, she said she had received It from her husband who was a fiatmin, anal hart obtained it from hit master for wages.—A clerk identified the woman, and he placed her name and address on the back of the note. —Mr. R. She remarked that that was for herself.—Mr. DAVid Widders, et the Nel- sen inn, Rutland-street, said on the 7th instant floxworth west to his house end said he had drawn £2O for hie freight. The prisoner handed him a £5 note, and re- marked that he had been knocking about the Atlantic, and now intended to settle at home.—Mr. John Coolant, of the Masorete Hotel, Devorishire-square' deposed to changing the prisoner Bosworth a £5 note on the 6th instant, in the pre- sence of Busbell.—By Mr. Flitchen t Bushell was talking to another person and might not have heard what passed.— Inspector Roche said he received information of the loss of , the notes and cheques on the 3rd instant, and he ceased handbille efferine a reward of £lO to the finder to be circu- lated. _ Mr. Handley held that the freeholders ought to know something of the scope of the Act under which it was in- tended to proceed, aod what betvfl's would accrue. Ha thought some of the Commissioners had been studying the Act during the last few weeks, and he quite thought they would have bean prepared with some information. The Chairman did not think that any Commissioner would undertake to lay down any ruler, or that he would express any opinions which might lead to controversy. It wit really a questinn iwhether the freeholders would place their rights in the hands of the Commissionera as a body, and they, having authority to proceed under the Act, would deal with the rights of individuals as the Act provided. Mr. Lighthuin said he represented a freeholder who was quit, willing to fall in with the decision of the meeting, and he thought the only issue before the meeting was whettor they should sur lender their rights in order that the ,cornmon lands might be preserved by a responsible body for the public good. Mr. Speakman said the question had been raised five or six years ago. He (Mr. bike Litman w s then appointed chaiFman of a freeholders' cotnmittee ; but, as described by the law-clerk the other day, they were an-irresponsible sat (4 people, and, in fact, no one would be responsible for any- thin gthat took place. It seemed to him that to place their rights in the hands of thee munissioners was a proper step to take; and in his opinion the most practicable way of dealing with the m Ater was tn appoint a committee, which could gather all information, ;and lay the whole question clearly before auaa Ijournel meeting. Toe Unarm an said he was afraid that if the steps sug- gested by Mr Speakman WAS taken they would be in a similar position to that in which they found themselves six years ago. So long as only the freeholders moved the free- holders would have to provide all the money required, whereas if the rights of the freeho'ders were acquired by the C)mmiss:oners, all charges would be paid out of the rates. • Mr Leach was selling that the ratepayers should have equal rights cv,th the freeholders, and Mr Pritchard described some of the provisions of the Act. Mr P Speakman was quite willing that the matter Amid be dealt with at once, and moved "That this meeting of freeholders of the township of Runcorn approve of an appli- cation to the Enclosure Couunlesionere being made by the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners for a provisional order to be issued for the enclosure and regulation of the common lands within the said township." Mr C Littler seconded the motion. .

Mr Handley said this seemed a very haphazard way of Oeeling with a very important geestion. He (Mr Handley) had perused the Act several times, and It was more import- ant than at first sight they would be led to believe. It was a very proper thing that theie rights should be ceded and put into the hands, of the local authority, seeing that the Act of 18713 was pissed for that particular purpose, tend if they had had section 8 read at the beginning of the meeting it would have cleared the way very materially: Stated shortly, Glen in his copy of the Public Health Act, said that by the Commons Act of 1876, urban authorities a-a authorised with the consent of the Inclosure Commis- sianers to c ;ntribute out of their funds in certain cases to- wards the maintenance of recreation grounds, or of paths or roads, or doing any Other matter or thing for the benefit of the town over which they have jurisdiction in relation to a common, situate either wholly or partly in such town, or within six miles of it; or they may acquire any such com- mon by gift with A view to the benefit of their town and the improvement of the common. It was the last part of that they were met to consider, that they might eoable the Commissionersr to acquire by gift the common lands. so that they Might be used for the benefit of the public. The Act was divided into two parts, the first' part of which was that an application can be made for the regulation of a common, and an application can be male for an enclosure. He had been asked several times of late, he supposed because he had had to do with the question before—" What was the differ- ence between regulation and eoclosure ?" The Act defined that o regulation" included the adjustment of rights and the improvement of the common, which had to do with the rights of turbery and the rights of atone, gravel, or other mineral underneath; and if it was the waste land of a manor, these rights 'could not be done sway with, except by the consent of the lords of the . manor. The improvement consisted in the giving powers for the draining and planting of trees, and also the making of proper oys-laws, so that the property would in future be cared for. Enclosure was a different thing, end referred to any object of histprical interest that might happen to be on time groand. They had one object of historical interest on Runcorn Hill which he should be sorry to see removed, '1 and already the stone-getter's hammer had got very near. It was a mark of a past civilisation by which the country was roused almost as quickly as the electeic telegraph spread news in these days, when the Danes were coming up the Mersey; and Beacon Hill he thought should not be inter- fered with. Mr. Handley then referred to the fact that the enciosure gave powers to form field gardens for the use of the poor, and also power to deal with any portion that lay precticaPy outside the limits of the common by sale, and using the money in the improvement of the remainder. It also gave power to enclose portions for recreation ground, which would make it very useful for the juvenile popula- tion of Runcorn. Before a Provisional Order coLlil be ob- tained the consent of one-third in valn^ of the freeholders in the soil of the common would have to be ob- tained, and he thought if some of the lacger land- owners were seen and their consent obtained it would almost settle that part of the question. When an inquiry was held the consent of two-tbitds of the freeholders, nether by presence or aesencts—the latter term implying consent —would be required. In closing, Mr. Handley said he was sure it would give'every freeholder the greatest pleasure in giving the necessary consent to the Commissioners, so that they mieht proceed as hastily as possible in the matter. Referring to the works of the Mersey Brine Company, be statsd that the Freeholders' Committee had come to an agreement with them that when the steps now proposed to be tilts° were completed, and the common vested for the public, they would conform to such terms and conditions, and pay such acknowledgments as might seem reasonable for their Interference with the cotnmon lands, and the fact that they had encouraged a new industry in the neighbour- hood would recoup them for any damage that might have been done. Be had great pleasure in supporting the mo- tion—After a few observations from Mr. Lightburn and the Rev. W. Preston, the resolution was carried unani- mously, atd the meeting concluded with a vote of thenks to . the Cbairman.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

IThe political situation is almost unchanged, except that bitter feeling has certainly increased. The Standard turns out to have done but poor service to its patty by proving that the Conservative peers won't accept even a Conserva- tive scheme of redistribution. The Tories are now begin- fling to see that the publication of the paper was a great mistake for them. It roles them or any little sympathy which tolerant people might have had with their prejudices. And now they are whispering about that the promulgation of the draft was a Government job. Liberal papers were not to be allowed to publish it, lest there might be a suspi- cion, but the Stondard succumbed to a very ready tempta- tion. lam told it is known how the paper got into the hands of the printers, and that probably pofics proceedings will be taken next week. But this is not likely. As yet the breach of duty involves no criminal offence. The question was practically settled when another Conservative paper created a precedent for the Standard. The truth is that where printing is adopted secrecy is almost impossuble. It may be that we dealt have some new legislation to create a new offence, bat as yet there is no crime. You cannot have larceny without proving the animus. furuncli, and that is very unlikely to be proved. The " undutiful" clerk or messenger will probably be dismissed, and perhaps the Stan. third would give him a handsome annuity. The Kensington Museum has opened a new Gallery which is devoted to such a collection of casts as London should have had years ago. The Gallery is very lofty, and lit with the electric light, and the decorator ha a had the courage to reject the old Pompeian red as a colour, and chosen a tint many shades lighter. The collection has the choice bits from all the galleries. At the end of the room are the famous full lengths of Eaeschines and Demostheoes, the one from the Naples Museum, the other from the Vati- can. Nearly all the Venuses are here, some very familiar, as the Venus of Milo, and some, like the beautiful statue lately discovered at alma, new friends to many Londoners. Curiously mixed up with these (for they are all in the same gallery) are Egyptian and Indian casts, so that all schools of sculpture may be compared. We are still at our old muddle and confusion about the lights of London. Every system seems to get its trial gives the most unbounded satisfaction to all parties, and when the period of trial is over, the Vestry, or whatever may be the authorities, go back to the old dingy gas burners that made London a disgrace ten or a dozen years age. The Embankment was somehow the most hopeful bit of what may be called experimental London. Certain of the gas- lamps were cancelled and every fourth or fifth bracket held an electric light. The result was not a failure. One might have wished a warmer illuminant, but at least there was light enough. But now they have gone back again to the gas, except in the case of sorne thirty or forty Jablochkeff's that make the rival illuminant look queer. So soon as the closing of the Healtheries releases our large and increasing body of pickpockets from their profitable labours in the West end we may expect the Thames Embankment scare to set in. Indeed, there has been already one case of garOtting, but the Embankment under the new conditions of seam. obscurity is expected to afford admirable sport. The Lon- don rough may well be proud of cover as no other city in Europe can provide. What Mrs. Kendal said the other day about the vulgarity of theatrical advertisements is fairly illustrated at the pre- sent moment. Passing down Regent-street to-day, I met two processions. One was of about a dozen tricycles in single file all largely labelled" Polly " and the Novelty," I suppose there is a difference between a tricycle with a top to it such as the Postmaster-General proposes to introduce in rural districts and a van on four wheels drawn by horse. Thirty years ago this method of advertisement was declared to be a nuisance and peremptorily pat down, and yet Re- gent-street was not then as full as it is now. A littlel further I met my other procession. This consisted of a lot of fresh ruddy cbeeked charity girls in the most old-fashioned get- up. They were quite little children, and they marched along ander the control of a sandwich-man, each of them stoutly producing to a puzzled public the programme of the Babes in the Wood. While I am on theatrical subjects, let me say what I have heard about the Garmoyle trial. There have been all sorts of rumours, reports, statements, and contradictions. Thus we have heard that the case has been compromised at a very large figure, Lord Garmoyle preferring that any sum should be paid rather than that he should submit to the ordeal of cross-examination. And then all this is indignantly core- tradicted as being without a particle of foundation. i shall venture to prophesy and events will show whether or not I make a good guess. In the middle of next month the case will come on. There will have been no compromise. The Court will be very full, the public very much interested the case called on, the jury sworn, and the facts opened b toe plaintiff's counsel. Miss Forteacue will go into the hr and be asked a few‘questions, and I think it is not wank A.. —judging from what I have often seen in actions of this kind—that the judge will say something, and then the c nun- gel will say something, and thenthe solicitors will say some- thing, aad that all these somethings taken togeth et. will amount to a verdict for the plaintiff for an agreed sio n. miss Fortescue will look very pretty in the witness box, and the public who have pushed into seats will look vet y &sup- Pointed when the next ease is called on. As every yemehas its fashion, so I suppose ev ary season has its flowers. Single dahlias were a rage atw eive months ago, and they only succeeded the bronze pe males, which followed the sun flowers. This year we seem to have had nothing. But the novelty has only to be vrai ted for, and it is sure to appear. At last it declares it jell. It is the ebysanthetnum. The Temple Show ie bsth earlier and ener this year than it has been for many years, and the e gardeners seem to be able to do anything .• ley lik with the , plant. The old-fashioned—the methetie —colours are still popular, but the triumph is produced by brilliancy. The new variety is flame coloured, with lo AZ pendulous petals. The lawyers—like the chrysantheree anes—show up at the Temple this year unusually earl' Term begins next Friday, a week before its wont, and am amused to see how steadfast Mr Justice Hawkins is to . his favourite bench at the Old Bailey. Other judges hay their predilections, some choosing and sonic avoiding their : old circuits, but Sir Harry is true to his C.O C.

There has been great trump, kblowing about the under- ground lines. At first there were inconveniences and de- lays, but now things work m are smoothly. loan only give my own experience. The C /days are great, and the uncer- tainty is greater. It i° , impossible to tell when your train, your particular train, may be fitted into the long necklace of crrrieg as that keep up the perpetual round. be no irregularity though there Previouslymigh t be d e layf there Tookn mt whole system might be brought to a dead leop for a few l ninutes, bat the sequence of the trains was observed. It is not so now, and the cause is this. A certain porti on of the line is common to all the companies, ,and whichever can get its train on, gains very soli?e advantages. No doubt bye-and-bye the system will be. organised, but for the present the Under- ground is alo .4. and irregular. The companies have certainly bad to der.t with great difficulties. October is the excursion month with the Healtheries. Extraordinarily cheat) tickets are issued by the South Eastern, the Chatham and Dover, and the Brighton Companies, giving their customers a day in London to see this exhibition, and this has flooded the Underground with thousands of third-class passengers. 'I he Brighton line took people from Brighton to Victoria and on to the Exhibition and into it and beck again to Brighton half-a-crown. The result is that South Kensington is as full as if there were a fair or a race being held hard by. The pickpockets are doing a roaring trade, and the Underground is besieged by traffic which the offi- cials takes no pains to control. These third-class passengers throng the first-class carriages without the slightest remon- strance, and the thing has been going on all through Octo- ber, and will go on to its close.

FIRE AT CROTT.-011 Monday morning. shortly bet Ore eleven o'clock, smoke was discovered issuing from some hay On the premises of Mr. Reginald Owed, jun Heath Farm, Croft. So rapidly did the fire spread that before water could be brought to the spot, it heel got firm hold of one stack and also commenced its ravagss on another. Five other stacks were for a time in imminent danger, but for. natelv the wind being in the opposite direction, and a large number of willing hands available, the danger was averted. The fire engine from Messrs. McCorquodale and Co.'s print. log works at Newton was soon on the spot, in charge ef Mr. McCorquodale, J.P., and Mr. Wood. Notwithstanding the difficulty in procuring a good supply of water, the fire was soon got under, and thus a large quantity of produce saved. How the fire originated is a mystery. The hay was insured in tha Scottish Union Fire and Life Ineciance Company.

div.p: FOOTBALL.

Seeretar!es of Football Ciuns are requested to note that rep ;rts of matches played oa Saturday mot be sent to the head office. Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

EARLESTOWN ALBIONS 'V. WARGRAVE TEAM.—This match was played on the ground of the former, and aeaulted in a drawn game by two goals each. WARRINGTON TRUE BLUES (2ND TEAS!): V. Sc CROSS AILITETHS, WIDN'ES.—A match was played between the above clubs on the ground of the former on Saturday and remelted in an easy win fur the home team by 2 goals, 10 tries, 4 minor points to 1 dead ball. RUNCORN RECREATION V.VULCAN.—PIayed on the ground of the latter. The bell was started by the Recreation cap- tain, playing against the wind, and was well kept in the home 25. Soon after the kick out Lunt got bold of the ball an.! ran a try in from near the half-way flag, which W; Ri.ey nicely landed over the bar. Shortly after half time a touch in goal was obtained by the Recreation, and the Vul- can had to touch down several times. Faulkner then got over the line and placed a try to the credit of the Recrea- tion' when Riley again added the major point. Soon after the ball was kicked out Lunt got possession, and after a grand run got another try. No goal being the result, time was called, the Recreation being victorious by 2 goals, 1 try, ant 6 minor points to Vulcan nil. WARRINGTON TRUE BLUES V. HALTON VIEW WAN- DERERS —The True Blues paid a visit to Widnes to play off their fixture with Helton View Wanderers. Warrington won the toss and elected to play with the wind. Milton pet the ball in inction and play was kept in the home " twenty-five " until Nevins secured the first try for the visitors. Acton made a very good attempt, but failed. The bail was again started, but by good play of the visitors it was returned, when Bibby dropped a neat goal and half- time was then called. When the ball was again started good play was kept close to the home goal and Evans se- cured the second try. A short scrimmage ensued when Peers made a good run aml secured the third try. Evans afterwards secured a try, but it was disputed. Score for the visitors, 1 goal, 3 tries, 1 disputed try, and two minor pints to nil. True Blues team :—Full back, Clegg; three-quarter backs, Evans, Bibby, D Won; half-backs, Nevins, Peers (captain); forwards, Acton, Coine, Andron, George IR,It, Warhurton, Furnival, Holt. Halton View Wanderers team :—Fall back, Horibin: three-quarter backs, Milton (captain), Humphrey, Barber; half-backs, Besivick, Moore; forwards. Rirlyard, Shuttleworth, Bate, Dutton, Collins, Burgess, Wilding, Leatherwood. RUNCORN V. WALKDEN (2ND Tgams).—Played at Run- corn on Saturday. The Walkden captain having won the taco, Lewis kicked off for Runcorn, Jones failing to return it, the first scrimmage was formed in the visitors' territory, when the ball was kicked over the goal line. Whitby being on the alert secured the first try for the home team. Wood's was entrusted with the kick at goal, and succeeded in regis- tering the major point. After the kick-off from the centre some good play was shown on bath sides, when the home forwards carried the ball to the visitors' "25," and the hall again travelling over the visitors' line, Whitby succeeded in obtaining the second try, which, however, was not improved upon, half-time being directly afterwards celled. After the interval the ball was taken to the home "25," when T. Yates was successful in dropping a goal for the visitors. Walkden, being favoured with the elements', had considerably the best of the play for a lengthened period, and scored several touchdowns. Ultimately, however, Runcorn. bed a turn, and some severe scrimmages were contested, and when "no side "was called victory rested with the home team by one goal, one try, and two minor points to Walkden one goal and five minor points. Teams :—Rurcorn : Woods, back ; Whinyates, Wainwright, and Jones, three-quarter backs; Whitby and Antrohus, half-backs; Clarke scaptain), Lewis, Gittens, Orme, Cox, Andrews, Dugdele, Jackson and Abrams', forwards. Walkden : A. Yates, beck; A. Jones, Holmon, and Hurst (captain), t'•ree-quarter backs; W. and T. Yates, half-backs; J. Yates, Leach, Green, Hoskins, Cook, Archorn, Shepherd. Wilcock. and Haves, forwards. EA ULESTOWN V. PRESTON PARISH CHI:ECM—Me Fades- town first teem joure eyed to Preston on Saturday if ternoon and met the Parish Church team on the ground of the latter at Penwortham. Both clubs turned out good elevens and the result was a capitally-played game. Having won the toss the visitors' captain chose to play with the ground in his favour; and Preston kicked off shortly after half-past three. For some fifteen minutes the home team held a decided advantage, and it was not long before Sharpies scored a goal for the Prestonians. The subsequent play was of a more even character, the Earlestonians repeatedly endangering their opponents goal, but the score was not equalised until ten minutes before half time, when Dagnall with a good shot secured the first goal. On the change of ends some splendid play was shown by the visitors, who though playing uphill severely pressed the Prestonians up to the call of time. Ogden scored a second goal; Rich a third; Duxbury added a fourth, and Dagnall made the total into five ; while the home eleven never made a dangerous attack on the E erlestown goal. The Earlestown team played up well to the finish, and the result was a well-earned victory by five goals to one. Teams : Earlestown :J. Ap- pleton, goal ; R. Green and J. Green, backs; R. Boveker, S. Whalley, and F. Emmett, half-backs ; W. Rich and J. Ellison, right-wing; A. Dagnall. centre ; J. Duxbury and J. Ogden, left-wing; umpire. Mr. D. Davies Preston Parish Church : Clarke, goal ; liodgkinson and Newsome, backs; Green, Brindle, and Worthington, half-backs; Poole and Sb arpl es, right-wing; Arkwright, centre; Leach and Dalton, id '-wing. RUNCORN V. WALEDEN.—The Runcorn first fifteen played off their fixture with Walkden on Saturday, on the ground of the latter, a very even game being witnessed. Dean started the ball uphill, to which Grundy replied, transfer- ring it back to the centre. Stubbs was here smartly collared before he could get away. Scrimmages were formed fre- quently, in which both teams apparently held their own. By a little effort the hcme team gained the Runcorn half, where W Hughes very wisely dropped in touch. Welsby and Grundy made strong attempts to make headway, bat the back play of the visitors being safe, Grundy preferred to kick the ball going dead. A similar point was gained through an attempt at goal by Welsby. On change of ends the play assumed the same bard forward play, Speakman , now and then livening up the monotony of the pack scrim- moves by sharp runs, which proved of 'good value to his coileagues. Galley, Dean, and Stubbs showed frequently in good forward play. Wright did a lot of hard work at half, stopping the frequent rushes of the home players. In the Walkden team Grundy and Yates played a safe back game, Isherwood, Urmson, and Simnister doing a lot of hard work forward. Score :—Walkden, four dead balls, Runcorn, nil. ' Teams :—Runcorn W Hughes, full back; H Hughes, Broady, and Speakman, three-quarter backs; Wright and ' Andrews, half-hacks; Dean, Barns, Mason, Gatley, Light- burn, Stubbs, Roberts, Janion, and Cox, forwards. Walkden: Grundy, back; Yates", Grundy, and Welsby, three-quarter backs; Cook and Harper, half-backs; Urtnson,Oldred, Sim- aieter, Preecot, Isherwood, Jones, Riley, Barns, and Rush- ton, forwards.

, - ST. HELENS RECREATION V. Strrrox. —Representatives of these clubs met at Sutton. on Saturday, in favourable weather. After the kick off the Recreationists were soon busy, and carried operations well into their opponents' ter- ritory; from a scrimmage near the goal line Langley got hold and ran the first try in. After the kick out the ball was neatly dribbled back by Green, and after a few scrim- mages in the Sutton twenty-five, Langley again rounded his opponents and gained the second try; both tries, however, produced unsuccessful attempts at goal. Sntton now warmed to their work, and mainly through the exertions of A. Pres- cott registered a touchdown, and shortly afterwards by the aid of a long run from R.llcCully a second touchdown ac- crued, which unfortunately was destined to be their only score, although Prescott by repeated runs tried hard to make some headway. In the sccond half with the wind in their favour, the Recreation completely outplayed the Sut- ton men, who had to act mainly on the defensive ; business i was entirely conducted n the home quarters. A. Prescott tried bard by plucky runs to alter the aspect of the game. Although the Recreation played fairly well, still there was a tendency in the team to play individually, and the ball i was certainly pot passed as much as t should have been. Score :—Recreation, 1 goal, 4 tries, 11 minor points; Sut- ton, 2 minor points. Teams—Recreation Full back, J. Hankinson ; threequarter-backs, J. Spddon, R. Valentine, vv. Taylor; half-backs, P. Roberts, R. Langley; forwards, W. Parr, H. Gregson, T. Rankin, W. Dean, J. Fletcher, T. Green, W. Highland, P. Finn, and A. McLungblin. Sutton Fall back, J. McCully' threequarter-backs, R. McCully., E. Nicholls, J. Wilson; half-backs, A. Prescott, S. Simpkins ; forwards, H. Unsworth, J. Hampton, W. Morris, G. Pres- cott, J. Corrigan, W. Critchley, P. Critchley, A. Mclonnon, W. Martland. WIDNES v. SALFORD. Great interest was taken in the meeting of these clubs at Salford on Saturday. Widnes had but a moderate team, being weak in the back division. Sal- ford won the toss, and elected to play downhill. Soon after Roulette kicked off. Several packed scrimmages took place In which Widnes had sligbtly the advantage. Farrell bay- mg got possession, put in a useful and dodgy ran, which enabled Johnson to secure a try, the kick at goal by Farrell being successful. After some very even but fast play, Roberts downed the ball almost on the line, the Borough

club claiming a try, hut it was overruled. A line-out was I formed, Farrell making a run which took play into neutral ground, where half-time was callei. On recainmencing the Borough men made a great rush, and almost immediate y Roberts made a grand run and secured a try, from which Bullock kicked a goal, Salford thus scoring their first major point. On the ball being brought out, Brown :led Corns for the " chemicals," and Eagles and Ottewell for Salford, showed up well in forward play. At length Ottewell man- aged to scramble over the line, and secured the second try for his side, Bullock tailing at goal. Later on, a try was claimed by Salford, but Widnes did not charge, and on the call of no-side, Salford were winners by one goal, one try, one disputed try, and one minor point, to Widnes a goal aria one minor point, Widnes having done much better than was, expected with their weak hack team. Teams :—Widnes: S. Bingham, boot; W. Longton, J. H. Smith, and J. Par- kinson, threequarter-backs ; E. Farrell and R. Johnsan, half-backs; A. Brown, S. H. Kenrick, W. Meagher, P. Corns, T. Fogg, W. Wilkinson, J. Goulding, W. bole, and T. Ridyard, forwards. Salford : Sherlock, back; Ro- berts, Walmsley. and Radcliffe. threequarter-backs; Buck- ley and Pratt, half-backs ; W. H. and J. Bullock, H. Eagles, Shaw, Vickers, Worthington, Yeate, Winnard. and Otte- well, forwards. WARRINGTON v. LEIGH —The Warrington Football Club on Saturday last received a visit from the club representing Leigh. A late arrival prevented a start until four o'clock, ,and near 400 spectators assembled to witness the match. The visitors started, and before they could properly realize their position Barnes made two ineffectual drops at goal. Trying to clear the line, Lees punted into touch. Danger threatened the Leigh citadel for a time ; eventually Jolley got in and Turner kicked the premier point. Massey , returned along touch, Lees responding aided by Boyle, I though their efforts were futile, as Jolley again go,. in. The try being disputed, the ball was replayed at 25 flag. The wind materially aided the home team, but the backs dis- played splendid form. A scrimmage on the Leigh line saw . Gilbert emerging with the ball, which be carried over. The place failed. At half-time ends were changed. The visitors 1' now had the wind with them. They made the best use of it, still the defence of Barnes, Massey, and Walsh could not be broken. A good run was made by Boyle, who looked dan- gerous until Barnes stopped his career. Time was rapacity approaching, when some good passing enabled Speakman to score try No. 3. Walsh missed at goal. The call of time • showed Warrington were victotiou's by one goal, two tries. and nine minor points to Leigh nil. Warrington team :—T ; Walsh, back ; J T Massey. T Barnes, W Warburton. three- quarter backs; E Gilbert. W Speakman. half-backs; II Ash- too (captain). W Hayes, F Turner, J Robinson, J R Calvert, W Povey, T Davies, L Humphries, and J Jolley, forwards. Warrington v. Leigh pal Teams): The 'Warrington Juniors visited Leigh on Saturday, and to their credit played the Leigh Juniors, assisted by several first-team players, who ought to have been playing with the first at Warrington. After a somewhat naisy game the visiting team scored their third successive victory by one try (Ap- pleton) and four minor points to three minor points. %Vat- rington team :—T Hewitt, back; A Appleton, H Boardman. T Balshaw, three-quarter backs; E Lightfoot, W Bashford (captain), half backs; R Littlewood, W Brimelow, W Potter, J Whittle, J Jones, J Ashurst, T Waywell, W Duanhell, and J Savage, forwards.
