div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

On Saturday, in the Football Association Cute competi- tion, at Oswestry, Crewe Alexandria beat Oewestry by one to none; in the Scottish Cup competition the Glasgow Rangers and 3.d Lanark again played a drawn game, no goal being scored ; in the Ayrshire Cup competition Ail- marnock beat Kilwinning Monkcastle by five to none; at Westminster the old Corthueians beat Westminster School by two goals to none ; the Old Westminsters beat litent- wood by three to two; at Paisley Queen's Park beat St. Mirrens by five to none; Bolton Wanderers beat Astley Bridge by seven to three; at Dumbarton Glasgow and Dum- bartonshire played a drawn game, three goals each ; at Wal- sall Liverpool was defeated be Walsall Association by four goals to three ; at Upton Somerset were beaten by Upton Park by five to none; Wednesbury Old Athletic beat Stoke- on-Trent at Wednesbury by four to two; Aston Villa and Nortliwich Victoria played a drawn game, three goals each, at Perry Barr ' • Notts Rangers beat Wednesbury, on the ground of the latter, by four to one. The professional difficulty in football is fast coming to a crisis. The recent action taken by the Association commit- tee held on the sth inst has called forth almost unanimous disapproval in Lancashire. Immediately the resolutions were made known, steps were taken to ascertain the opinions lof the leading Lancashire clubs. The result was that a meeting has been held at the Commercial Hotel, Bolton,l when it was decided to await definite actien on the part of the Association, and in the event of anything being done, to stand by one another. The Lancashire Association has also taken the matter up, as it is considered that if the resolutions are carried out they will clash with the county association's arrangements, inasmuch as some of the clubs who are members of the Lancashire Association will not be allowed to play, even in cup ties, others who are or certainly will be disqualined by the Football Association. The Blackburn Rovers on Saturday and Monday consid- erably improved their record, beating effieffield Park Grange by 17 to none and Rossendale by 11 to none. As on Sat- urday week they beat the Walsall Swifts by five to none, the aggregate score for the three matches played this month is 33 goals to none. The Earlestown Club secured another victory on Satur- day, when they met and defeated Preston Pariah Church by ' five goals to one. The match was played at Preston, and the result was extremely creditable to the Earlestown team. 'The clubs met at Earleetown last season, when the result was a draw; and a tight game was expected on Saturday. I;he Leigh let team, after being "sat upon " by the Blackburn Olympic to the tune of 18 goals to none on tbe previous Saturday, visited Eerlestown last week and met the 2nd eleven of the Earlestown Club. The latter at present appear in "line fettle," and they displayed their ability by defeating their Leigh opponents by five goals to one, exactly the same score by which the Ist team of the Earlestown Club disposed of Preston Parish Church. The meeting of the Haydock Sr. James's and Golborne Clubs, which took place at Haydock, on Saturday, was an exciting affair. Local rivalry was an inducement for both clubs to turn out their full strength ; and the result was a hard-fought game. The Golbornites secured a victory by two goals to none; but, it is stated, bad it not been for the excellent goal-keeping on behalf of the winners the result would have been different. The Rugby adherents at the Vulcan were thrashed, on Satutday, by the powerful fifteen representing the Runcorn Recreation; the latter showing themselves superior to their opponents in many respects. The Vulcan men, however,are not to be despised ; for when they are determined and work unitedly they can display some skill and science in the " handling " game. The St. Helens Recreation let team proved far too strong for the Sutton representatives, although the match was played on the ground of the latter. The contest evoked Iconsiderable interest. The home team, it was evident, I were overplayed by their opponents ; but the Recreationists displayed a tendency for individual play instead of collec- tive work—a tendency which does not in the long run im- prove or benefit the club.

div.head: ALLEGED _ASSAULT BY KISSING A
div.p: ALLEGED _ASSAULT BY KISSING A
MARRIED WOMAN.

A singular case was heard at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, when Mr Charles Mellor, a butcher carrying on business in Bridge-street, was summoned by Mary Dakin, a married woman, for an asssult alleged to have been committed on the Bth inst.—Mr P Davies, solici- tor, Warrington, appeared for the complainant, and stated that she was a manageress for Mrs Broughton, a tripe seller having a shop in Market-street and a branch shop in Bridge- street; Mrs Dakin managed the latter. On the Bth October defendant and some other persons entered it, the defendant going in by the back door, which he had no right to do. When inside the shop he placed himself in such a pasition as to barricade Mrs Dakin behind the counter, which he banged with a poker whilst giving an order for tripe and trotters. He partook of three trotters and kept the com- plainant in great fear and trembling, much to his satisfaction and amusement, behind the counter. He made jokes that were very distastefel to her, and although she asked him to behave himself, instead of doing so be, while she was com- plying with an order given by one of his companions, fol- lowed her behind the counter, put his arms round her, and gave her a kiss. Complainant was a respectable woman, and, Mr Davies said, the defendant must be taught that such behaviour was not to be allowed. The defendant and his party also went into the kitchen, where they had no right, and tossed some clothes about, put chairs and tables before the fire, and actually barred the woman out of her own house. That was, however, the subject of another action, and they should simply ask the Bench to convict the defendant for assault.—Complainant, in her evidence, said that the defen- dant came to the shop with a small fire shovel in his hand and banged it on the counter, saving. "Some small trotters, please." She asked him not to do that, and he then placed the shovel on some glasses and repeated, "Some trotters, please." Afterwards the defendant got hold of her and gave her a kiss, upon which she said, "Don't do that, that sort of work won't do for me." He also asked her to come and sit by him, but she refused. The clothes in the kitchen were thrown on the floor.—The defendant denied having com- mitted the offence, and called several companions who were with him on the day in question, who all swore that they never saw Mr M;;11or kiss Mrs Dakin.—Mr Davies then called Mrs Broughton, who spoke to seeing the defendant about what he had done. She asked him what right he had to kiss another man's wife, and he said, "I'll pay her any- thing she requests," and put his hands into his pockets. Witness said, "We don't require pay, and if you don't go and apologise to her for what you have done I shall take you before your betters." He replied, "I neither care for you nor your betters." A summons was then taken ont.— The Mayor, who presided, said that although they felt it to be an extremely strong case of suspicion—in his own mind he had little doubt that Mrs Dakin had spoken the truth—at ' the same time the evidence against complainant's evidence was so preponderating that he was afraid they must COTIO to the .conclusion to dismiss the case in accordance with the Saying that if there was any doubt the prisoner was entitled to it.—The case was then dismissed.

POACHING AFFRAYS. - Two desperate fights between gamekeepers and poachers are reported. In one case 24 men were surprised whilst " netting " land near Moreton Ham cpugleton, and after a sharp struggle, in which serious injuries were received on either si4e, two poachers and their apparatus were captured. The others escaped. Five keepers in the service of Lord Middleton were or. Monday attacked by ten poachers near Nottingham, and thoroughly disabled. The men got clear away, and have not been arrested.

THE LUNCHEON. The luncheon, which took place in the Assembly Room at the Lion Hotel, commenced at about two o'clock. Sir Gilbert Greenell presided, and he was sopported by Sir S Northcote, who ,eceived a hearty welcome, Sir R Cross, Lord Winmarleigh, Lady Greenall, the Hon. Miss Wilson. Fatten, Colonel Blackburne, M P ,Mr and Mrs J C Parr, Mr P Stubs, Captain Reynolds, Miff.) Blackburn's, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), and Mr Beamont. There was also numerous other ladies and gentlemen present. At the con- clusion of the luncheon, The CHAIRMAN gave " The Queen," after which Lord WINMARLFIGH rose amidst cheers. He remarked that he had been requested by the committee of the War- rington Conservative Association to offer to Sir Stafford Northcote, on their behalf, some words of welcome and of thanks for attending to assist at the ceremony of opening the club that afternoon. (Loud applause.) This was a very pleasant duty to him, because he was thus welcoming a friend with whom he had been associated during nearly the whole of his (Sir Stafford Northcote's) political life. The gentleman to whom he referred, however, needed no testimonial from him, as his character was well known throughout the length and breadth of the land. (Applause and hear, hear.) Their distinguished guest was engaged in endeavouring to refute the very serious misrepresentations that had been made by their political opponents. (Hear, hear.) In doing so be had to meet men- of great ability end high station, who,. from some cause or other—and he be- lieved the cause was not far to seek—were crying to with- draw the public attention from the main question now under discussion. So far as he could gather from reading the account of the Birmingham meeting, Sir Stafford Nortbcote had come out of it, as he had done on every other occasion, with honour and credit to himself. He had pleasure in ask- ing them to join with him in passing to Sir Stafford North- cote a hearty vote of thanks for attending at the ceremony of the day. The proposition was carried by acclamation and awarded musical honours.

Sir STAFFORD NORTITCOTE. on rising to acknowledge the compliment was received with enthusiastic applause. He said he was asked the other day by a foreigner who was pre- sent at a ereat meeting which he attended in Edinburgh, whether that which they had just been singing ("For he,s a jolley good fellow ") was not our national anthem, ow- ing to his having heard it so often. (Laughter.) Well, without saying that we have as yet dispensed either with "God save the Queen " or "Rule Brittania," be ventured to say that the little air with which they had indulged them was a very good supplementary piece of music. It testifies very much to the good humour which ought always to exist amongst those who are engaged in public life, even if they differ in their views as to promoting various good and liudable works. At this moment he just happened t) come from a part of the country where it was a little diffi- cult exactly to understand what their position was. (Laugh- ter.) Apparently the gentlemen whom he last had the hon- our of addressing, or trying to address, belong to the section of whom it is said— They prov'd their doctrine orthodox By apostolic blows and knocks. (Laughter.) Undoubtedly the appeal made to the power of "capable citizens" was very remarkable. It may be diffi- cult at times to know what is meant by capable citizens, but he had arrived at the conclusion that it means able- bodied citizens. (Loud laughter.) When they had got hold of a body of able-bodied citizens you may dispense with other arguments, which are hair-splitting and pedantic. It was a very great pleasure to him to be able to come amongst them. He felt that the visit which he should be able to pay that day was far short of the visit he should have been glad to pay to a place of such importance, (Applause.) Though lie had not time to talk to them upon many sub- jects upon which one would have been glad to have dilated, yet he bad the opportunity of meeting them and seeing face to face a considerable body of men who are working in the Conservative cause, and who are the support of the cause in this town. (Hear. hear.) He hoped before long, and pre- vious to going on to Liverpool, that he should have an op- portunity of seeing a good body of the working-men of the town. (Hear', hear.) This is a time when, although there may he many questions upon which there will be differences of opinion, vet there ought to be no such difference amongst those who love our constitution. There ought to be no diff- erence of opinion on the fact that they ,must all stand

THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY. OCTOBER 18, 1884 OPENING oF THE NEW CoNSERVA- MITE CLUB, WARRINGTON. The new club which has been built in Sankey-street for the use of the Conservative party in Warrington was opened on Wednesday. The new building, which occupies a site near the post office and opposite the Town Hall is, looking at it from Sankey-street, an attractive looking building, al- though its real purposes are somewhat disguised by its front floor basement being adapted for lockup shops. It is built of a free Gothic design, having a tiontege to Sankey-etreet of 70 feet, and a frontage to Winmarleigh-street of 112 feet —the whole covering an area, including the bowling green, of 3,000 superficial yards. 'rho main entrance to the club is from Sankey-street, which is entered by a pair of mas- sive and ornamental doors into the porch, which is about 10ft by Oft. Here are a pair of ve-y handsome pitchpine vestibule doors and screen into a vestibule about Oft by Oft. Passing through the vestibule we find ourselves in the hall, which is about 241 t by Mt. Is the left bend corner stands a massive stone ebimney piece with tiled back and hearth, acd fitted with a dog grate. The hall is supplied with a lavatory, a cloak room being formed in the spandrel of the stairs Passing from the hall, another pair of beautiful pitchpine doors, which lead into the inner hall, about 201 t by Bfl. At the far end of this hill is the bar for first-class members who do not wish to enter the billiard room. The first door on the right hand leads to the luncheon room, which is 28ft by Mt. This room is well lighted from the centre by a ceiling light. The first-class billiard room, which is 50ft by 23ft is next entered. The architects ap- pear to have made a special feature in the work of this room, there being a well-treated open timbered roof with ornemeetal principals, the whole of the joiners'work beim: of selected pitchpine. The whole of the light is obtained from I the roof, with ten skylights, each about 9ft by Oft. The space between the spars is plastered, thus materially contri- buting to the light of the room. At each end is a chimney piece in fumigated oak with the motto "Fair play is a jewel," intended no doubt as a reminder to those engaging in a same of billiards or cards. These have been specially designed by the architects, an I carefully mode by Messrs S. and E. R. Johnson, cabinet makers, Bri4ge-street. Near the centre of the room is a handsome bar window with em- bossed and stained glass. Leading from this room are the Private smoke rooms, lavatory, and water closets. A door leads from the hall to the second-class billiard room, the di- mensions of which are 60ft by 30 feet. This room will be fitted with four billiard tables. At the end are the lava- tory and urinals for the use of the 48 members only. At the top of a splendid stone staircase which leads from the ball is the reading room, 22 feet by /9 feet. In the main corridor the club secretary's office is situated, and from this office is a door leadingeto the balcony, which will be used at election times for the purpose of addressing the electors. We next come to the office of the Secretary of the Associa- tion, a room 18 feet by 12 feet, and adjoining this is the committee room, 22 feet by 22 feet, which takes the corner facing Sankev-street and Winmarleigh-sireet. Afterwards we enter the large meeting hall, 60 feet by 40 feet in extent. This room has also an open roof. At one end is a raised and permenent platform for speech making, eithe for which purpose it is admirably adapted. In the centre of the room, on the Winmarleigh-street side, is a splendid circular stair- case leading into Winmarleigh-street, so that this hall may be used separately from the club if required. It is also pro- vided with lavatory and water closets. At the end of the room is the servery, with serving hoist from the kitchens, so that in the event of dinners and parties being held, the good things of life can be conveyed from the manager's kitchen to the large hall At the back of the building are the rnanaem's quarters, an excellent house containing four good bedrooms, sitting room. aed two kitchens. Underneath the house are the beer cellars, dec., belongirg to the club. Be- hind the building, and facing Arpley-street, is the bowling green, 40 yards by 37 yards, fitted with shed, tool, and bowl house. There is also a tower, which considerably adds to the imposing effect of the building. It contains two rooms, to be used as offices for the club. Each of the numerous rooms is supplied with electric bells; in feat, nothing has been omitted which is likely to conduce to the convenience and comfort of the members, the premises including an as- sembly room, committee rooms, n we room, smoking room, two billiard room., dining room, manazer's residence, and kitchen, &c. Mr. Porter has been the sole contractor for the whole of the work. Mr. Ephraim Auckland has held the sub-contract for the stone work. Messrs. Williams and Clay have supplied the erates, ranges, and tiling, and Messrs. Johnson the wood chimney pieces. The heating has been done by Messrs. Bradford, of Manchester, and the ventilating by Mr. Edward Wood, of Manchester. The whole of the work has been carried out under the superin- tendence of Messrs. Pierpoint and Adams, the architects. The ornamental glass work has been designed and carried out by Messrs. Edmundson and Son, of Manchester. Great efforts had evidently been made to carry through the proceeding of the day in as successful and imposing a manner as possible. In addition to obtaining Sir Richard Cross to open the club, the managing committee had, though with some difficulty, been able to persuade Sir Staf- ford Northcote, while on his way be Liverpool, to make a call at the town in honour of the occasion. In the town itself some attempts at decoration had been made. In Bridge-street and Sankey-street there was a considerable dis- play of bunting, but in scarcely any other part of the town was there anything out of the ordinary in the way of decora- tion to be seen. The active proceedings of the day were initiated by the receptions of Sir R. Cross and Sir S. North- cote at Bank Quay station. Sir R. Cross arrived there shortly after one o'clock, and was met by Captain Litton. There was no display whatever at Sir Richard's arrival, and he was at once driven off to the new club, of'which he made an inspection. About two o'clock Sir Stafford Northcote arrived at the °WOO station from Birmingham, where he had been demonstrating with doubtful success, and was met by Sir Gilbert Greenali and Captain Reynolds. There were several other ladies anti gentlemen on the platform, and on t e right bon, gentleman stepping from his first-class car- riage be was greeted be a hearty cheer. At the outside of the station a considerable crowd had assembled, and on Sir Stafford's appearance there as loud cheering, mingled, however, with a deep volume ol hooting. Sir Stafford was at once conducted to Sir Gilbert Greenall's private carriage and driven off to the Lion Hotel, where a luncheon was par- taken of. On the way there the party passed through Sankey-street and Briage-street. and were frequently greeted with mingled cheering and booting. On the arrival of Sir Stafford becoming known cannons were fired on the green behind the Conservative Club, and this kind of noise was kept up till late in the evening.

shoulder to shoulder against the dangers with which we are threatened. The great question which we are now called upon to try is not whether they should have a larger or smaller suffrage, or whether there should be more members here or more members there, but whether they were to proceed on a proposition relating to a re- vision of the constitution in a constitutional manner. It was quite certain taa: a very large proportion even of those wino are attackiog the House of Lords are in favour of what is called a second chamber, but they do not tell us what they would do if the House of Lords were abolished, or front where they are going to get their second chamber. In one respect he thought he saw what those persons meant by a second chamber. Those persons who are calling out so much against a limited electorate, which, of course, must mean any electorate short of universal suffrage, because' any electorate must be limited by some lines—are in a certain sense depreciating the House of Commons, which is the pro- duct of a limited electorate. They would not have a second chamber in the House of Lords. Where Would they get it, then i Evidently in the streets—that was their second ctram- ber—(loud applause); and if they did not take care, those per- sons who were making the opinion of the people gathered to- gether in the streets powerful would gain a very great advan- tage over them. He said to th-un as he said wherever he went, 4i You do your part" You have here got a seat to retrieve. He had al ways associated the name of Warrington with his friend in the chair—Sir Gilbert Greenall—(hear, hear, and cheers); but he was quite certain of this, that if they were to carry their principles to success they must stand to- gether, and be determined to win back the seats which they lost, and lost under false impressions, some-four or five yea- ago. (Hear. heir) He was convinced that amongst three, whom be saw before him there was that spirit of determina- tion and, let him hope, of thorough unity and concord upon the question which will lead to a successful result whenever the struggle may 'come to a head. (Hear. hear, and ap- plause.) He took that opp ortunity of saying that he looked upon all persons, ladies as well as gentlemen, as being equally interested in the preservation of those great institu- tions which have made England what she is—(applause)— and which, he trusted, they should be able to maintain, in order that England may not fall in the seals of nations. (Load applause )

, The CHAIRMAN gave "The health of Sir Richard Cross and Colonel Blackburne," whom he hoped might long con- tinue to represent the division of South-West Lancashire. Sir RICHARD CROSS, in replying,retnarked that he always looked uoon Warrington as practically his native town. (Applause.) He bdieved that he and his friend Colonel Blackburne would combine to repres ,rit the division of the county so long as they adhered to the opinions which they held when they last appealed to the electors. When the next election came—and it might arrive sooner than many of them expected—Warrington must return a Conservative member to Parliament. (Loud applause.) They knew that they possessed a majority on the register, and it would be their own fault if they did not win. He hoped that before long he should be abl. to propose in that room as a toast " The health of Sir Gilbert Greenall, your Borough Mem- ber." (Loud applause.) Colonel BLACKRURNE also acknowledged the toast, and spoke 0 very strong terms of the machinations of evil speaking, which he said, distinguished many members of the Liberal narty.

Mr. BFAUMAT proposed "The health of Sir Gilbert Greenall," and said that England was now very much in the position which she occupied at the close of last century, when one of her poets said of her— eh l has but one foe, and that foe!, the wmid. The action of the Government reminded him of a writer in Hollas's great work, who said "I am for Old Noll, I freely declare it, though his rule made tyrants tremble; for he also made England great and her enemies tremble." Could they say that any enemy of England was made to tremble by any action of her Majesty's present Government ? (Cries of " No, no.")

The proces.ion must be pronounced as a failure as a demon- stration of strength, for there were less than 120 persons in it; and there was besides a noticeabl) absence of some who are looked upon as leadinz Conservatives. A numbers of people hid in the meantime gathered a- long the route of the proc2Biion, and as Sir Stafford North- cote and the lading members of the party passed along a mingled chorus of cheering and hooting was raised. In front of the club there was a great cruel] of people, and here the party met with a very cordial reception, though even here a very powerful body of dissentients made their pre- sence known in an unmistakeable manner. At the front en- trance to the club

Captain REYNOLDS, on behalf of the Conservative Club, welcomed Sir R. Cross, and said they considered themselves fortunate in havins, one to open the club for them who had been so long associated with Warrington, and who had al- ways been such a kind friend and neighbour. They consid- ered as an association that they should extend Conservatism in Warrington in opening that club, both as regarded the borou.,Li and the county. He then presented a gold key to

Sir R. Cnoss who said that the Conservatives of War- rington always looked upon him as one of themselves. (Cheers) He had lived long enough among them to know the kindness of their hearts and how much they were to be trusted. (Hear, hetr). Sir Richard then unlocked the door, and the company having traversed the lower floor of the building, proceeded to the meeting hall which htd for some time been filled with people. On appearing on the platform, Sir S. North- cote and those who accompanied him were received with prolonged applause. Sir H. Cross having briefly de- clared the club open _ .

Captain REYNOLDS read the following address : "'l,O the Right Honourable Sir Stafford Henry Northcote, Bart., G.C.8., M.P.—Sir,—We, the members of the War- rington Conservative Association, beg to offer you a hearty welcome, and tender you our thanks for having honoured us by coming to Warrington on the occasioa of the opening of the Conservative Club. We desire to express our entire confidence in you as the leader of our party in the House of I Commons—(cheers)—and to say that we believe the man- ner in which you have upheld the Constitutional cause in Parliament has won for You the esteem of your fellow- , countrymen. (Cheers.) We congratulate you upon the effectual resistance you made to the attempt of the Liberal Administration to change the law for the purpose of a•lmit- ting an avowed atheist into the House of Commons. (Cheers, and a Voice: "Watch Bradlaugh "—laughter.) We believe that the action of the House of Lords in insist- ing upon a fair re-arrangement of the constituencies being made a part of any plan for referrning the electorate meets with the approval of the country, and we trust that the leaders of the Conservative party will not permit any mea- sure of Parliamentary reform to become law which will not secure a fair and equitable representation of all sections of the community. (Cheers.) We also desire to express our concurrence in the criticisms you have at various times passed upon the foreign and colonial policy of the Liberal ministry, the erratic and vacillating natuze of which has lowered the influence of this country, and destroyed the concert of Europe. (Hear, bear.) It is our hope that as a result of an early appeal to the constituencies • you will again be called upon to take part in the Executive Govern. rnent of this country, and that you will shortly be again in a position as a Minister of the Crown to give effect to the great principles of the Tory party, of which you are so dis- tinguished a champion.—Signed for and on behalf of the Warrington Censervative Association, GfLBERT GREENALL, President.—Warrington, October, 1884."—( Loud cheers). Sir STAFFORD NORTIICOTE, who was loudly cheered, said he could assure them that it was with no small feelings of geratificetion and gratitude that he received that address, and it would afways give him a great interest in the future of Warrington colitics to think that he had had the privi- lege of being present upon the occasion of the opening of that club, and of seeing his friend and colleague, Sir Richard Cross —(cheers)—perform the duty of opening it, and to have had also the advantage of being allowed to in- scribe his name at the head of their visitors' book. (Hear, hear.) Now they knew he had only a very short time to spend in Warrington—he wished it were longer—(hear, hear,)—but in the few minutes that remained to him he wished to ex- press to tbein his great gratification at the spirit which is indicated in the proceedings in their important borough. Above all things he liked any ceremony that has to do with unlocking and opening doors, because it seemed to him that that is what they ought to do—that they ought to open in every pbssible way, the entrance to political knowledge and study, that they ought to invite all persons to come as freely as possible and obtain and study for themselves the infor- mation that was valuable upon political questions, and that they should put as far away from them as pos- sible, and condemn as utterly detestable the idea of keeping people in the dark and shutting them up. (Applause.) When Parliament was adjourned or prorogued—it might ae well have been adjourned— (laughter)—but when it was prorogued in July or August by the Prime Minister there was an impression prevailing in Ministerial and Liberal circles that nothing more was needed than a theatrical stroke of policy in the dropping of every measure before the house, making a great display of the de- struction of things which the Government knew perfectly well would come to an end all the same but throwing the responsibility upon the action of the same, party, and especially upon the action of the House of Lords ; and he had no doubt that there was a strong impression on the minds—and a real impression—of the Goverament and of their immediate supporters that nothing was needed beyond that theatrical stroke in order to bring the whole country to their feet and enable them to carry their policy. (A Voice : "They have not done it.") Well, they bad net done it yet. That showed that his friend puts his finger on the real source of the mischief and trouble the other day at Birmingham. (Laughter.) Every- where they had found that there was a great spirit among the Conservative party, that they were not deluded by those representations of their opponents, and that whilst there was of course a great difference of opinion amongst men of different shadee of politics, everwhere there seemed to be a disposition to give a fair hearing and a candid considera- aion to our arguments. As the results developed themselves before the eyes of those gentlemen, who had thought they were going to carry all before them by the theatrical display —as that appeared they found they were losing ground, and that place after place was either declaring against them or . showing a much greater or stronger minority against them than they were at all prepared to anticipate, and they were also finding that the language that bad been used and the arguments which they compelled the country to hear open a hundred platforms—that these argnmants were telling, and

were producing an effect which they had not e.spected. What was the result ? It was at all events in a certain quarter what it had not unfrequently been. Our opponents, tindiog that they were getting rather worse than they ex. pected, lost their temper. (Laughter.) That was the whole history, he believed, of the proceedings in Birmingham this week. They tried what they could do by an outside demon- stration, and then, when they found that in spite of that we were going on with our preparations, they first of all tried forged tickets, and so endeavoured to get into a meeting to which they had no business to come ; and, secondly,- when there was a diffculty about admitting the forged tickets, they found a way "'over the gar- den wall." (Loud laughter and cheers.) In conclu- sion Sir Stafford said he had told them that he had only a very few minutes to stay at Warrington. (Cries of "Go on.") It was all very well for them to say "go on," but he could assure them be did nothing but "go on." (Cheers and laughter.) He hoped he might in due time have an opportunity of again coming amongst them. (Cheers.) He trusted that they were doing their part for the good cause, and that they would again return a Conser- vative member to the House of Commons. (Loud cheers.) That 10739 the Erst time that he had had the pleasureof visit- ing their town, but he hoped it would not be the last. (Loud cheers, during which the right hon. gentleman resumed his seat)._

Sir R. A. C2oss, M.P., who was cordially received, said the opening of the club was a complete answer to the state- ment that the Conservatives were the "stupid party." They wanted the people to study for themselves, to have the case put h4ore them, and make up their minds on the question. [tie Radical party had chine all in their power to push for- ward their own nostrums, and there was moth in.; they wished tnore than to abolish the House of Lords ; but, as Sir Staf- ford Northcot2 had said, they found that the opinion of the country was against them on that point. This attempt to rouse up the country had miserably failed, because the House of Lords was stronger in the estimation of the country than ever it had been. (Applause) And why 8eC41.188, he believed, it had stepped forwarct in the cause el freedom, in the cause of the people, and in order to pre- vent the tyranny of one man dominating over all others. (Applause.) He believed that when the question was thoroughly fought out the country would support the House of Lords in the action which it had taken. (Applause.) Colonel IRELAND BLACKBURNE, M.P., then addressed a for words to them, congratulating them on the opening of th at g,ne club.

Sir GILBERT GREENALL having responded in a few words, the proceedings terminated. EVENING RECEPTION. In the evening the Club premises were thrown open to ticket-holders, of whom there were a large number present. In the meeting hall a meeting was held, which was presided over by Captain Reynolds. There were also preeent Sir Gilbert Greenell, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Mr. Robert Davies, Captain Litton, Mr. R. Pierpoint, Mr. Mat- , tioson (Conservative candidate for Carlisle), Alderman Kean, Councillor Burgess, dm. The CHAIRMAN, in his opening remarks, gave an account of the proceedings which had led up to the erection of that club. He then went on to say that although the Conserva- tive parts' had now got a new club they bail net yet had the opportunity of haying a newspaper in Warrington. They . all knew that they had in the town a very spicy piper called The Examiner. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) They would I not say a great deal about it, because it was not worth it. I (Laughter.) They also bad got a paper that was one of the !great wonders of the day—they were almost from hour to hour provided with the political questions of the day in a , paper called the Echo which was not in their favour, and these papers were poured into Warrington. Now he did I hme when they bad got their club that a newspaper would: follow in Warrington in which they would get their views stated strongly and very much more truthfully than they did in another paper. He then mentioned that a third way for their party to recover the borough was that in tip several wards they should at periods not ex- ceeding three months have meetings to which they would ask the people of those wards to come and support them' and hear what they had to say. There seemed to have been, Captain Reynolds went on to say, in the minds of some of them a doubt as to who was to be the candidate for War- rington. Now that night there was no doubt about who was , the candidate for Warrington. ("Sir Gilbert," and ap- plause.) He dare say it may be thought that he (Sir Gil- bert) was getting old, but if they looked at him they would consider that he was still a very young mane and from the way in which he goes in and the way in which he went out be (the chairman) really saw no difference in him for the last 20 veers. He (Sir Gilbert) might have bad some cliff"- dance, but the working-men of Warrington, not content but they must send a deputation to say that age was nothing, and that they wished that he might again represent lVar- rington and wipe away the sting and disgrace of the date it that occurred to them in 1980. He knew he was only speak- ing the minds of those around him when he said that there I was no man that they should so much wish to wipe that dis- grace away than their friend Sir Gilbert, and with him they meant to do it. (Loud applaue Sir GILBERT GREENALL, who was received with loud ap- plause, said : Captain Reynolds, ladies and gentlemen, my old and ancient friends I venture to call you, I should indeed be ashamed of myeelf if I arose upon this occasion and attempted to address you without some emotion. It is q.nite impossible, or it ought to be impossible, to any man who has any sentiment of feeling or community with his fellow- ' men, it ought to be iMpossible for him to address you under these circumstances wi:hout some emotion. (Hear, hear.) I do think that we are indebted to my most esteemed friend Captain Reynolds for his speech. (Applause.) His speech has contained very much indeed to instruct us, and more it has contained oy which we ought to profit. To Captain i Reynolds the erection of this clui, is mainly doe. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The success of Captain Reynolds is founded not more upon his industry and determination than, it is founded upon the uprightness of his purpose for which he advocated this club. I am anxious, b store I address you at more length, again tp repeat my obligation to Captain Reynolds for what he has done, for what he has said, and to assure you that there isno man in this room more grateful than myself to Capt. Reynolde. And now, gentlemen,let the first , septence I utter with respect to this club be a natural utter- l ance. It is that I rejoice with you that we have this club; and I rejoice daily more and more when I consider from whence the main part of the funds to erect this club, have come. A large proportion of the money which has built this building has come from you, my friends. (Hear, hear.) It has come from you, my friends, the working-men. (Hear, hear.) As far as this building is concerned, it is not more mine than it is your,. I any sum up what I mean by say- ing this: That in this club what is yours is mine, and what is mine is yours. Now, then, we have a clear understanding about this club, we have a clear understanding that it bed longs to all of us, and I hope we have a feeling in the di- rection of the recommendation of my friend that this club is to be of real utility and real service; that it is to be a place where we can meet' together and in which we shall have the various supplies of information which we can read together. And I hope that whenever I come into this club I shall come and approach those with whom I can confer and whom I feel to be partners with myself in this building. (Ap- plause 1 Well, now, I will pass to another subject. I will try to speak plainly and I will try to speak definitely. (Hear, bear.) Now, then, with respect to my years. I do not intend to tell you that I feel to be an old man. (Laughter and ap- plause.) I intend to represent my own Case by what has been facetiously told to me as the text of a celebrated travelling itinerant preacher. The text was this : " I have been old, I am now young." (Loud laughter.) That is what I intend to say to myself. (Renewed laughter.) Politically, I am young enough, thank God, for the help He gives me; I am young enough to be associated with you, and I intend, as long as God gives me the present vigour which I possess, to be with you, to belong to you, in the Parliamentary sense. (Applause.) Well, my friends are here with their pencils—(addressing the reporters). I am rather sorry for you, because I believe that you are putting down every word that I utter. (Laughter.) Now, gentlemen, you with the quick pencils and pens, try to make better than it is all that I say. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) But I wish to speak of myself. ( Laughter.) I believe that a man is not what he may describe himself to be. (Hear, hear.) I believe that a man is what be mikes himself. If a man by good condect and high principle makes himself worth anythieg, the well- judging part of our community always know well enough what he is worth without his being obliged to extol him- self. (Hear, hear.) I have always avoided speaking of my- self, but there are occasions when a man is obliged to speak, and if a man when he is obliged to speak is worth anything he will always speak plainly and in a manner that be can- not be misunderstoed. I say this, that there is nothing mere useful, nothing more honourable in ally man than plain speaking. (Hear, bear.) And now with respect to my pre- sent position, and with respect to what I am going shortly to utter, I have never since the last election, a which I know a good deal, and of which I can tell you a good deal, bnt I do not wish your hair to stand on end. (Laughter.) That is past and gone ; it is of the present that I have to , speak. T have not declared until this day nay intention and purpose of again offering myself to be a candidate for your suffrage. Now,! speak plainly and directly that I shall, if my life is spared,—l tepeat the words, if my life is spared— 11l speak both English and Irish—(laughter)—l will come 'seforo you asking the favour of your suffrages. (Apolaose.) Now there are many that I see before me who, I will sup- pose ready to say, "Why, have not you said that before; me have been at various meetings ; we have expressed our con- fidence in you ; you are rather shady in what you have said; you have never said positively you would be our ' candidate." I could give you many and good reasons why I did not give expression to that conctusion, but the matter is now decided. I shall ask you for your eutlfrages. (Ap- plaase.) "And why," yOll may ask, "did you ceme to that positive conclusion Y" I came to that conclusion be- cause I was asked to come to that conclusion, and askod by those, who, I think, are the most intelligent and powerful body in this comraunity—l was asked by largemumbers of

working-men, who came to me repeatedly. They hare I come to rite in a deputation, but numbers and numbers have spoken to me privately and quietly. I have determined at the invitation and urgency of the working- men to become a candidate for this borough. (Applause.) And now I feel this, and I want you to feel it, that I have i come forward on the urgeemy of the working men, PO 3o ' I depend upon what the workingmen can do. I believe the working men; I trust the people; I believe the working man never puts his hand to any matter which he does not intend to accomplish. (Hear, hear.) I believe that the working men both can and will return me as the member for Warrington. (Hear, hear.) I am confident that what the working men have told me they will do they can do, and I bslieve that if life and strength taste I shall become the member for this borough—(applause)—a member chosen and elected by the most honourable body of men in the community—the working men. (Hear, hear.) To those who hear what I say is this: Suppose I were in Parlia- ment now, where I ought to have been—(laughter)—do you think I would support the preseat Government '1 ("No.") I reply no. (Applause.) They are a Government who have not verified their nromises; they are a Government who have distracted everything, and made trade almost unprofitable. (Hear, hear ) They are a Government who said "Peace, I peace, peice," and they have deluged a large part of the world with war arid blood. They had said they would be economicil. and had spent more money a great deal than I they ought to have done. We shall often tneet,and if you wish me to speak to you I shall always be willing, and I , shall always be ready, if on the passing events of the day I you wish to know what I feel and what I think, you shall ' know. If you wish my views on the conduct of the administration you shall know. Now, I think I have had Imy saw. I hope I have not detained you. (A Voice: "I wish we had a barrel of Wilderspool ale here," and roars of laughter.) lam very sorry indeed that my friend may be ; a little thirsty. Ido not think I could supply him ; but I I am very glad to hear that let has a favourable opinion of Wilderspool ale. (Laughter.) I thank you very much in- deed. (Applause.) The Chairman then called for three cheers for Sir Gilbert, which having been given Mr. ROBERT DAVIES addressed the meeting, and criti- cised the foreign policy of the Crovernment„ after which addresses were also given by Mr. Mattinson, M.P., Mr. R. Pierooint, and Councillor Burgess. A vote of thanks, moved by Sir Gilbert Greenall, to the chairman closed the I proceedings.

PH CSOOT. BOARD OF GUARDIANS —The fortnightly meeting of the Guardians of the Prescot Union was held on Thursday, at Whiston Workhouse. There were present : Mr. J. T. Hall (chairman), ReTS. Thomas Chambers and J. Barnacle, Meseta W. Newsome, J. Jackson, J. Buckley, W. Gerard, J. , Fisher, W. Tyrer, J. Fidler, E. Syder, J. Griffiths, J. Ken- wright, W. Leigh, E. Johnson, T. Betook, T. Dobell, H. L. Hulme, F. Hill, R Tueon, W. Gilbody, J. Leatherb,rrow, and Mr. H. S. Hartley (clerk) —The iVorkhouse Master's Report: Mr. Hale reported that there were 432 inmates this week, against 423 lag week, and 420, in the corresponding period of last year. Vagrants relieved during the week 46, against 56 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 78 imbeciles in the Workhouse, and there were also 18 boys and girls chargeable to the Union, 47 being at Kirk- dale and 31 in Pantasaph Orphanage.—The Late Rate Col- lector for Eccleston: The Clerk read correspondence between the Local Government Board and Mr. F. A. Harrison, late rate collector for Eccleston township, with reference to the surcharges made by the district auditor upon Mr. Harrison. The latter wrote to the Local Government Board stating that with reference to the balance- of £l4 153 id which the auditor found against him he had tickets in his possession showing that he had paid tradesmen to the amount of a greater part of the balance against him, and he asked if they would allow the tickets to stand against the balance. In reply, the Local Government Board stated that they would require a cloy of the auditor's certificate, with his reasons for making a surcharge; and they also asked for the tradesmen's tickets to be forwarded to them with an explanation why he (Mr Harrison) did not charge the payments in his accounts. On the 6th October the Local Government Board wrote to the Guardians stating that Mr Harrison had not replied to their letter, and a sub- seqnent letter they had sent to him bad been returned, marked "Gone—no address." They inquired if the Clerk to the Guardians could inform them of ois present address. —ln the course of a discussion which ensued, the Clerk said ' he did not consider it hie duty to find out Mr Harrison's address unless the Guarelians gave him authority to do so ; and Mr Fidler expressed the opinion that Mr Harrison ought to be prosecuted. Die subject ultimately dropoed.—Death of the Registrar : A letter was reed from Mr James Kirk- man, of Ormskirk-steeete St Helens, announcing that his father, llt R Kirkman, registrar of births and deaths for the St Helens district, had died on the 15th inst. Some discussion took place as to the filling up of the vacancy, the Clerk stating that it was in the power of the Guardians to elect a successor to Mr Kirkman, but they must do it within a fortnight, or the Registrar-General would fill up the vacancy. Mr Fidler gave notice that at the next meeting he would move the rponintment of a successor to Mr. Kirkman.— Vote of Condolence : On the motion of the Rev. T. Chambers, se- conded by Mr. Gerrard, a vote of condolence with the family of the late Mr. Basil Cane, Poor-law Inspector for the Nor- thern District, who recently died, was passed.—The Supply of Water to the Workhouse : The Clerk reed the following letter from the Liverpool Corporation "Town Cleilee Office, Dale-street, Liverpool, 3rd October, 1864. Dear sir, —Water supply. Referring to your letter of the 23rd Sep- tember last, the Water Committee are willing to extend their pipes and to give a supply of water to the Whiston Work- house upon the usual terms—that is that the Guardians should enter into a 10 per cent agreement under which they will for a period of tea years pay to the Corporation such annual sum as with the water rent upon the Workhouse, and upon any other buildings supplied by the earns extension, will be equal to one tenth the total expense incurred by the Corporation in extending the pipes. The committen supreme that the workhouse for which you require a -supply is the one situate on the road from Present to Rainhill at its junction with Dragon-lane. Is that so ?—Yours truly, G. J. ATKINSON, town clerk." The letter was referred to the Committee.—lnerease of Salaries, and Bad Trade.—The Finance Commit ee recommended that the salary of Mr. James Parkinson, relieving officer for the Prescot district, should be increased from £1.26 to £llO per annum.—Mr. Hill moved, and Mr. Fidler seconded, a motion to that effect. In the course of a long discussion, several members expressed the opinion that the present was not the time to raise salaries and increase rates, considering the bad state of trade and business in the Union.—Mr. Johnson called attention to the depressed state of-trade in St. Helens, re- marking that there were a number of shops closed in the heart of the town—a thing which had not been known for many years past. Large numbers of people were out of employment and could not get work, and on those and other grounds he considered they would not be justified in in- creasing sal eries.—An aineedrnent was subsequently passed almost unanimously that the application for an increase of Salary be considered six months hence.—This was all the business of interest.

Wanontom Cauncu. —On Sunday, two sermons. 5n connection with the harvest thanksgiving services were preached in the Emmanuel Church, Wargrave. The church was devoid of any decoration, but there were large c ngre- gations at each service. The sermon in the mornhar was preached by the Rev Canon Whitley, D.D., vicar of Bed- lingtm, and in the evening by the Rev R 0 Greep, assistant chaplain to emigrants. Collections were made in aid of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts, realising £l5 12s.

TILE-EAHLESTOWN GOSPEL Dirssros.—The Erst an- niversary services of the Earlestown Gospel Mission and Blue Ribbon Movement were preached in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Sunday afternoon and evening, by Mr. Thomas Benson, of Wean% who Is better known as " Bishoo " Benson. There was a large congregation at each I service. A selection of anthems were nicely rendered by the choir and a few friends, under the leadership of Mr. H. Grundy. The instrumentalists were Lysons, of Pen- dlebury, Mr. Gee, 0 Liverpool, Mr. John Tripp and Master B. Tripp, of Esrlestown (violins) ;. Mr. G. Birks (violon- cello), and Miss Lysons, of Pendlebury, efficiently accom- panied on the harmonium. The sum realised by the collec- tions was about £3.

THE BENEFITS OF GOOD TEMPIADISTI.—A Meet- ing of the members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tempters was held in the Lodge Room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance, and Brother John Taylor, W.C.T.,. presided. One new member was initiated, and one restored to membership, after which i committee was appointed to make arrangements fol the anniversary tea meeting. In accordance with the pro- gramme, which was headed "Sacred melodies," a selection of hymns and melodies were sung, and were interspersed with the discussion of severer, questions left over from the previous evening. The most important was, "What benefit does a Good Templar receive more than an ordinary abstainer " and in the consideration of this topic a :cry interesting discussion took place. The meeting throughout was of a very pleasant character, the. discussions beir.g of an instructive character. The ‘ Closing Ode," which was sung about 9-45, concluded the proceedings. Ensuc-nousE DIsTURDSNCE.--- A somewhat serious disturbance, which occurred in one of the principal public. houses of Earlestown, on Saturday night, created some ex- citement on the following day or two, and the statements made even went so, far as to the effect that the depositions of an injured 1113.1 had been taken, The latter, however, turned out to be inaccurate. It seams that a man stat9d to ,be under the inauence of °rink, visited the public-house in question, and because the manager refused to supply him he created a disturbanv. The manager recuested him to leave and he slid so for a short time, but he again returned, and renewed the disturbance. Upon the manager again wir- ing him to go out of the houee the man seized him by' the legs and kicked him several times, and it is alleged that he was " backed up" hy one or two of his friends. They continued to struggle near the " bar " and as the assailant again kicked the manager, the latter took down a some- what heavy stick hanging against the wall, and, struck his opponent on the head. In the meantime the police had been communicated with, and when P.C's. Parker and Hunt put in an appearance they found the man with a severe wound on his bead from which blood flowed pro. usaly. The injured man was subsequently taken home, and on the way he turned upon the police who had some difficulty in getting him horns. It is stated that the DM has since recovered. There will be some proceedings in the pollee court arising Ql,lt of the affair.

DIELE=TO•97,I WEPLEYATT miecellaneens concert in aid of the fund for the purchase of an organ for the Brunswick Wesleyan Chapel, Cross-lane, will be held in the Viaduct Institute on Monday see OUT advertising columns. evening. For particulars "THE POLITICAL LIVE oF ME. GLADsTONC.r'—On Weclneeday evening at a meeting of the members. of the Earleetown and District Liberal Club, held in one of the rooms of the club-, Mr. Walter McEvoy read a second Pinar on The Political Life of Mr. Gladstone." There was!. fair attendance. and Mr. M. Birkleead presided. The essayist ID a carefellv proper:eel and instructive paper reviewed Mr. Grledstme's career since the year 1836, pointing out the dates upon which be was appointed to the various offices he had filled, and the main points of the great speeches he had delivered. The meeting was also addressed by Messrs. Howard, Holyocke, Waywell, and Bturgess, who stated thit Mr. Gladstone was the greatest politician and financier land ever ever posseseed, and be was far beyond comparison !with Lord Salisbury or Sir Stafford Northcote. The proceedings were of a very enjoyable character. COSTLY BTioNE TIIROWING AT NEWTON. At the Newton Petty sessious ou Zaturdav, before Messrs R. Houghton, Pearson, and A. C. McCorquoilale, Charles Naylor, a lad, was summoned by the Rev. Charles cotter- ill Ward for unlawfully smashing a pane of glass and doing damage to the amount of 13s. The defendant was reme- sented by Mr. Moore. solicitor, Warrington. The corm:dew; ant is the conductor of a boarding school near St. Peters IChurch, and on the 2ed inst a number of lads wale in an adjoining roadway throwing stones at a chestnut tree- Oee of the windows of his house was smashed, and on a glazier being called in he estimated the darneee at 131. Teo/ lads named Spencer and Squire stated that -the defendant I had thrown the stone which broke the window. Tbe defence I was that the defendant had not broken the window.—On the defendant's fattier promising to pay the oosts and the dam- age the summons was dismissed. PaEsENTATTON AT TM BAPTIST CIIE;TEL gather- ing of a very interesting character was held in the Baptist Sunday School, Marketectreet, Earlestown, on Tuesday evening, when the scholars in the senior male and female classes, taught by Mr & F Aveline and Mr T Howard respectively, sat down to a nice tea provided by Mrs Jack- son, of Bridge•street. The company numbered about 50 persons, and the subsequent proceedings were presided over by the Rev W C Tayler,. pastor. As a memento of the marriage of Mr G F Aveline, that gentleman was presented with a handsome biscuit box, which bore the following appropriate inscription: "Presented to G F Aveline, on the Occasion of his marriage, by the members of his class." The presentation was made by Mr Edward Eckersey on behalf of the subscribers; and Mr Aveline, in response, stated that when he was invited to the meeting he heel no idea that he was to be the recipient of such a gift, whichwould always be highly prized by himself and his wife. "Tag ARTFUL DODGER " APPEERMMED.—A week or two age we reported that an overcoat had been stolen from a house in Tamworth-street by an individual who ap- plied for lodgings, stating that he was employed by the London and North-Western Railway Company to paint and decorate the station. He slept at the house one night, but disappeared on the following Morning, taking with him a valuable overcoat. Nothing, further was heard about him until a few days ago, when he fell into the hands a the Leigh police. It appears he attempted to carry on the ear dodge in that town. He visited a house there, and agaT, stated that he was a "painter.' He manage Ito "pick up a watch belonging to the tenant of the house, but when at- tempting to pawn it he was suspected, and afterwards given into custody. It has since been found that he was the same person who was " wanted " at Etrlestown, and in due time he will, no doubt, receive the punishment he deserves. THE VICAR OF EARLESTOW.N AND HIS L&TE CHEM= CLEANEll.—surne weeks ago a case was tried at the War- rington County Court in which Mrs. Stacey sued the R'. T. R. Matthews, vicar of St. John the Baptist Church, Earlestown, for tne recovery of an amount alleged to he due on a " washing " and cleaning account. The claim was disputed by Mr. Matthews, and the judge gave•hie decision in favour of the latter. The matter, however, has not been allowed to drop here. The bishop of the diocese has been communicated with, and the circumstances of the case laid before him. Writing on the Ich Met, he stated that be could not decide who was responsible for the sum owing to her, but if Mr. Matthews declined to pay the account the only course for Mrs. Stacey to adopt was to sne Mr. Mat- thews in the county court. On Thursday Mrs. StaceY visited Liverpool for the purpose of having an intervieW with the bishop and laying the accounts, receipts, &c., be- fore him. It is probable that a further claim will be made against the vicar. THE PRIMITIVE METHODIST: NEW SCHOOLS. The sPeciel services in connection with the opening of the Pri- mitive Methodist new schools, Lord-street, Earlestowne I were continued on Sunday, when two sermons were preached Iby the Rev. William lIICO3O, Of Patricrofr, and formerly of ISt. Helens. In the afternoon the choir of the chapel, under the leadership of Mr. W. Banton, gave a service of sacred song entitled" Poor Mike; the story of a waif " ; the Rev. S. K. Hocking being the author. There was a crowded con- gregation, and the greatest possible interest was manifested in the service. The connective readings were given by Mr. John Worsley, in the unavoidable absence through illness of Mr. James Woods. The musical selections were impres- sively rendered ; several quartets,. duets, atc, by Miss S. J. Woode, Miss A. Thompson, Miss S. Thompson, Miss Clara Jackson, Mr. T. Dickens, Mr. Ji Potter, and Mr. J. Spree - ton being especially well given. The morning and evening Services were well attended, and the sermons by the Rev. W- illman were attentively listened to. The collec•ions which were hi aid of he new school fund realised a little over £2O.

SAD STORY OF DOMESTIC LIFE AT NEWTON. Before Messrs R Houghton and J Pears in at Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, Samuel Rlininer, a respectably dressei loan, was charged under a warrant with assaulting his wife Maria at Newton, on the 24th September.— rhe de- fendant pleaded not guilty.—Mrs Rimmer cried piteouslY• throughout the proceedings, and seemed to ea pear suffering great pain. She said that or, the 24th September she had been in the house all morning, and in the forenoon she sent her daughter for a chop for her dinner. She also asked the little girl to go for a glase of beer, but she would not, as she. said her father had told her he would not allow her to fetch beer. She (the complainant).then went herself for the beer, and cooked the chop. There was no bread to eat, and after dinner she felt very, tired. When her husband came in sne was lying on the 'sofa, and, he asked her why she was lying there, to which she replied that she was very tired. He then sent for a loaf and some sugar and tea, and she there- upon said, "I will have half of anything you buy." Com• - plainant. continuing her statement, said : He tnen flew at me with borh his fl.ts, and he die give me what for. He made me black and blue all over, and if you don't believe it Dr Watkins' assistant will tell yea. My husband has been for Mr Caldwell to take ine to Haydock Lodge Asylum, but Mr Caldwell said he could do nothing in the matter. I asked Dr Watkins' assistant if I was a lunatic, and he said, "Who says so P" I told him my husband said I was, but he said, "No, my good woman; you are only excited." He won't give me any money, and he says I am a drunkard. But lam not a drunkard lam too proud to get drunk. I like my children to be nice. I have suffered for a great many years.—The Clerk (Mr White) asked the complainant if she did not get the warrant at Warrington.—The com- plainant replied that she did.—The Clerk: Did you not say that Mr McCorquodale had sent you for it ?—The com- plainant: He said I could either have a warrant or a sum- mons, but I had no money.—The Clerk: You said Mr McCorquodale had sent you.—The complainant: I said I had seen hina—The Clerk: This warrant was simply given out on the understanding that Mr McCorquodale had sent her to apply for it, as. he would not sign it because the hus- band works at their works.—The husband: How long have. you been carrying on in this way P—Complainant : I cannot answer.—How long is it since I gave you any money ? Seven weeka.—What is the reason I stopped the money? cannot tell you—you Paid I was a drunkard.—Did you go to. Liverpool? Yes.—How long did you stop? • Never mind —the doctor ordered me away.—Did you not tell me you. were going to a Mrs Hughes—some one I don't know ? No, I dal not.—Did you stay ten days? I stayed a week.--How did you come borne? No answer—Did you come and knock at the door at one o'clock in the morning? No, it waa twelve o'clock.—Are you sure ? Yes.—Did you come to the door or go to your aunt's? I went to the door and then wen', to my aunt's and slept there.—When you taok the sugar ont of my hand did you push againstme? No,. I did not.—Did you take the sugar? I snatahed it from you.— What did Ido ? You thumped me with both your, fists.— The defendant said his wife had driven all his children away from home with the exception of two little ones who were staying with him. Their mother had never made.a.meal in the house for the last eight or nine weeks, and he (defen- dant) got nothing from her but blackguardism.—ln reply 10 the clerk,the defendant said he had his two children to call as witnesses. He called one girl forward, whereupon the Chairman said : This is a very disagreeable case, bringing children against their parents. Could not we suggest that you allow your wife something to live apart and separate ?-- The defeadant said there were two sons in court, and per- haps they would do their share. When a mother kicked a child because they would not go for drink, it was time for husband to do something. During the last six months his wife had run him in debt up to £2O, and previously be al. ways. paid for everything. There was a creditor for a big sumin, court.—Mr Pearson, as'aed if he could not suggest anything with regard to the future.—The defendant : I will only be too happy if she will keep away from the door. But if I have to pay all these debte I cannot give her more than 53. I will give her ss, and she can keep away freely- -The Chairman aCannot you give her moa•?—The defera- , dant : She has stripped my house completely, and she bas some of the goods at Earlestown.—The Chairman agam asked if he could not give her a little more—say 103 Per week.—The defendant: No, sir, and not take the children. She has nothing but herself to keep, and she is as strong as any woman in the town.—The Chairman: You will keep all the children ?—Defendant: Yes.—The Chairman (to the wife): It will be muala better if you will take this 5a Per week and live apart from him.—The complainant : That would not take me to the hers ital and keep me. lam not strong enough to work.—The defendant: That is not the truth.—The Chairman: I think the Bench are quite satis- fied that you shoald give her a little more.—The defendant : I have seven children, and two are too young to work.—Tl's Chairman: The Bench suggests that you should give her da per week, and if she is willing to separate from you we svili grant a separation order,—The defendant will give tier .es per week, then.—The Chairman (to the wife): Are you will; tug to take 6s per week P—The wile :. Yes, sir.—The Ilene said the case would be dismissed cn those terms, anti thel would grant a separation order.

POLICE INTELLIGENCE. i WARRINGTON BOROUGH roma, COURT. SATuamay.—Before Alderman Chandley. DauNsENNEss.—The only case was one in which Michael Dowd, labourer' last from Gosport, was charged with haring been drank and disorderly, and was fined se. and costs. MoNaAv.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), in the chair, Alderman Davies, and Mr. John Fairclough. DRUNBENNESS.—Androw Stephenson was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street.— Mary Knockton, a young woman, was similarly deal with for being drunk and disorderly in liaydock.street.—For 1 being drunk and disorderly in Sankey-street, Thos. Moore was fined ss. including costs.—Charlotte Marsh was fined 55.. including costs. • KEFRACTORY VARmorr.—George Barcroft was charged with refusing to break a given quantity of stones whilst a caaual inmate of the vagrant ward at the Union, and further with doing damage to a cell to the amount of Ls.—Prisoner said he broke as many stones as he was able to. He denied having damaged the cell, but admitted having removed a brick that had been previously loosened.—ye was dismissed on promising to leave the town. A DRUNKEN Datua.—George Claybrook, a respectable- looking man, was fined 5s and costs for being drink whilst In charge of a horse and omnibus on Saturday.—ln extenua- tion defendant p.eaded that he had on Saturday come to Warrington from Liverpool without food, and to make matters worse he was afflicted with the toothache. He therefore took a little tram, which had an unexpected effect upon him. He bad since had the tooth drawn and ptoduced it in court.—Alderman Davies: We had better imprison the tooth for a month:—The Mayor: You have got rid of your refractory tenant. however. ILL-TEEATING A IdOnsk.—Patriok Weleby, cab driver, was fined 20s. and costs for ill-treating a horse on the 24th September by working it in an unfit condition.—The case was proved by Inspector Greenwell, Altrincham, who stated that there were raw wounds order the collar which caused the animal great pain. TIIESDAY.—Before Councillor Broadbent (in the chair)

and Aldermen Burgess and Chandley. DRUNNENKESS.—Thomas Kelly was tined ss. and costs, or seven days ; and John Scott, 53. including costs, or seven days, for drunkenness. Wm:mum:ay.—Before Alderman Chandley. A DESERTER.—John Murphy was charged on the evi- dence of P.S. Bowen with being a deserter from the South Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks. Ho was found in a lodging-house by the sergeant. Prisoner seas re- manded to the military authorities. DRIINEENNESS.—EIiza Davies, charged with being drunk In It.lam-street, was cautioned and discharged. INDECENT Coaruncr.—Annie Hodgson was sent to prison for 14 days for indecent conduct the previous evening. THIIRSDLY.—Before Captain Litton. DRUNKENNESS.—Sarah Burns was fined 5s and costa, or seven days, for being drank and disorderly in Buttermar- kat-street on Wednesday night. She is 20 years of age, and has been in Olson nine times for similar offences. Farr,AL—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), in the " chair, and Alderman Chandley. A DISOBEDIENT SwayAra.—Jeffery Worthington, a boy, was summoned by Joseph Birchall for the sum of 5s as compensation for neglect of work. He was ordered to return to work and pay the amount due at 6d a week. AVOIDING DISTRAINT.—John Fryer, a sergeant stationed at Orford barracks, was summoned for removing his goods from a house near the Blue Coat School in order to avoid a distraint for rent, he being indebted to the owner, Ann Cragg, to the amount of EL Lie vets ordered to pay the money, or, in default of dietress, to'lae sent to prison.

Fon SOCIOLOGISTS.—When a man takes your hand with a firm cotdial grasp, it is a sure sign that his heart is fall or his purse is empty. "How does Pat propose to get over single blessedness ?" said the priest to Pat's friend. "Why, he proposes to ' Bridge-it !" replied the friend. • An observing man has discovered a similarity between a young ladies' seminary and a sugar-factory, since both refine what is already sweet. IT MADE HIM HOT.—An absent-minded St. Louis parson asked a disaonsolate widower whose wife he had buried the week before, "Well, Mr. Brown' how does your wife stand the heat ?" They do not speak now. "I have lost my dog," said Mrs. Rarity. "Why doesn't your husband look for him ?" some one asked. " Who— Jim ? Why, you know Jim's in the detective force ! Be can't find anything." A young lady, on bsing asked at a musical examination, "What is. an interval? judiciously replied, "It is that space of time allowed for refreshment between the acts of an opera or the two Darts of a concert." HOW BILLS OF FARE ARS MADE UP. Restaurant Keeper: "John, what kind of meat did you order to-day ?" Steward: Veal, she" " Only veal?" "Yes sir." Then he at down and wrote on the bill of fare, "Chicken pie, Irish ostew, roast veal, beef a la mode, corn beef hash, veal pie." - An Irish gentleman was recently attended by an eminent London physician, who, pausing and looking at him with an inquiring glance, said, "I should like to know, sir, if your family have been long-lived ?" "Long-lived, is it ?" responded the patient thoughtfully. "Well, doctor; I'll just tell You how it is. Our family is a West of Ireland family, said the age of my ancestors depended entirely on the judge and jury who tried them !" THE INTELLIGENT COMPOSITOR.—Professor Milne, of Tokio, in Japan, has constructed a pair of pendulum seismo- graphs, - instruments for the automatic delineation and registration of the earthquake-disturbances so frequent in that country. He wrote describing them as "conical pendu- lums," each consisting "of a heavy mass suspended by a string." The printer of a local paper improved the original i by describing them as "comical pendulums," consisting of "a heavy man suspended at the end of a string." The coronet's ihquiry as to the cause of the fatal explo- sion in Hall End Colliery, West Bromwich, was concluded on Wednesday. The jury found that the seven men were killed by an accident, but some observations were made on the danger of working the mine with open lights. Mr/. BURT, M.P , ON AMERICAN LABOUR.—Replying to a correspondent on the subject of the prospect of American labour, Mr. Bart, M.P., writes :—" I was in' America last year, and took special note of the condition of the working classes in the mining centres. My observation leads me to the 'conclusion that though, on the whole, labour is better paid in America than in this country, the position Of the man who has only his labour to depend upon is most uncer- tain in many parts of America. The chief advantage in that country is afforded by the openings and chances of ob- taining land. The best and most accessible land is fast being appropriated, and I do not think the outlook for labour is exceedingly attractive. A CHESTER TRADESMAN GOING TO MARRY THE QUEEN. —At Chester, on Saturday, Joseph Crawford, who until re- cently carried on the business of a shoemaker in Grosvenor- road, was charged with doing wilful damage to the windows of the shop and of the adjoining establishment, occu- pied by Mr. Delaney, draper. It was stated that the pre- vious evening prisoner, Who had been ejected by a sheriff's warrant, visited the premises and smashed six panes of glass in the window and four in the window of the next shop.
