THE WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. you nermit me to sav,through the medium of your paper, that in consequence of the unsatisfactory ter- mination of the proceedings of the Town Council last Tuesday evening, it is my intention at the next meeting again to move the same resolution respecting the removal of air., sir, your obeleat servant, W. J. BURGESS. 13, Palmyra-Flame, Warrington, 9th Oct., ISB4. "STRIKE" OF THE WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH CHOIR. _ . . _

Sir,—The choir of the Warrington Parish Church are apparently well versed in the art of making mole-hills into .mountains. Chagrined at some, no doubt, imagined slight of the worthy rector, these gentry hold a meeting, or ac- : cording to your account, a series of meetings, and pass a bumptious resolution to go out on strike. They claim to have approached the rector in a proper manner, and say that their overtures have not been fairly met, but I think that most of the se-called sligh,s they appear to lalaenr under are fancied, and that all might have worked smoothly had they not been so touchy. But now that they are our, let them remain out, and no doubt the rector will soon be able to form quite as efficient a choir.—Yours. &c, C hIURCEIMAN.

October 17, 1884. Sir,—l was pleased to read your account of the above strike, in last Saturday's Examiner, as I had seen the several officials mentioned doing duty the previous Sunday, and had also seen in three different Liverpool papers tat the 'Warrington Parish Church choir had struck. Ido not often invest in a copy of your neutral contem- porary, but as that was the first local paper published after the event I purchased a copy, bein4 anxious to glean fuller particulars, but to my astonishment found no mention of an affalr that was evidently going the rounds of the county press, and probably of the entire country, as such items of news generally travel a long way. I may say that I have spoken to several members of the late choir, and they agree that your account is a very good and fair one. and for it as a parishioner I thank you. It seems some remarks were made by a clergymen at some chance meeting miles away from here praising the rector for ni3 services in East Loudon about thirty years ago. I can't Leila thinking it would have been no bad job for War- rinzton if he had stopped in East London. Some months ag, I sew in one ' daily " a peragraph stating that the rect-r of Warrington had resigned his living, but since then he has got shut of two as h srd-working curates as ever entered the town, also the organist, and now the choir. Still he remains with us, evidently as self-setisfied as ever.— Yours, &c., A DISGUSTED PARISHIONER. read

S:r,—" How these Christians love one another! " I in the last issue of your journal an account of the " strike " of the choir of the Warrington Parish Church, and being somewhat interested in such matters, for reasons best known to myself, I took the trouble to inquire into the matter, and found that the statement given by you was generally fair and impartial. If there was in it a tendency to a failing, it wa, in that the Rector, whose conduct seems to have been ex:remely arbitrary, was too easily spared. Such disputes as have in this and other instances in the neighbourhood arisen I think very deplorable, as being calculated to bring contumely on the church itself, which, whilst preaching humility, forbearance, and charity, eiVES us such glaring instances to the contrary. I have been many times dis- gusted with the Atheistic ravirlgs of an occasional writer in your columns, but I mast admit that the more I hear and sec of church disputes and petty bickerings the more I am inclined to lose such disgust. It is, Sir, becoming a bye-word that the Church will be sooner disestablished by her own ministers than by any efforts of outsiders. But in the case of the Parish Church choir, I must say that I think the singers in refusing to continue their services took the only course open to them without abandoning a great portion of their self-respect. When a choir that has for years given able and gratuitous services is systemetic illy snubbed by one who ought to treat its members with the greatest possi- ble consideration, it is time that they rebelled and averted their independence. I hear that the Rector is trying to !Orr.: a new choir, and it will serve him right if be fail 3 in the effort. In my opinion, as an impertial observer of the course of events, the choir are undoubtedly right, and they hive my cordial sympathy.—Yours, (kc., Warrington. OBSERVER,

div.head: DISESTABLISHING A CHOIR.
div.p: DISESTABLISHING A CHOIR.

Sir,—The persons, or rather parsons, who cry Out 93 loudly at the enormity of relieving them of State aid and patronage seem to be wonderfully adept in the arts of die- establishing other people. We have already bed plenty of Instances in this pert of Lancashire of the cynical disregard which these " nrou I priests" have for what may be celled the "vested interests" of others; but it seems we are to have another. The choir of the Pariah Church of War- rington are being thrust out of their places without a tittle of compensation or acknowledgment for " unexhausted im- provement'," or anything else, because, forsooth, they will not releinit with unquestioning docility to the autocratic will of the reverend Qnekett. Now, sir, lam inclined to contend that if we were to be guided by the strict ru,es of equity it would he decided that this choir he as much to do with the church as the rector who is now putting them aside with such contemptuous ease. Is it with regard to the fabric of the church itself? It will be very different from meet cases if the choir have not done more than the priest to erect and maintain it. Or is it with regard to the con- gregation who worship in it ? I will be bound to say that if a poll were taken it would he found that in a mejority of instances the choir acted as an attraction, while the uncon- scionable dullness and emptiness of the sermons was the , deterrent. It would be affectation to expeess surprise at what has taken piece. The law as it is creates, as it were, an inap7reunt in inznerio wherever a branch of the Est-eh- ili i shed Church s set up, n which the priest is absolute and almost irresponsible, and acts of petty tyraney such 33 these are the inevitable outcome of ouch a sye'em. All we can hope for is th et when this state of things comes to be amended an oft-quoted but much-neglected precept will be had regard to, and that the clergy will be done by as they have done by others.—l am, sir, SPECTATOR.

div.head: "A VILLAGER" AND "CAPTAIN CUTTLY,"
div.p: "A VILLAGER" AND "CAPTAIN CUTTLY,"

Sir,—lt may savour of te nerity that an obscure villager should attempt to assail the fortified position of "Captain Cnttle," who has such resources in the words which command him. Evidently he cares little for logic, and vet attempts the art of reasoning. From his "simple standpoint" Christianity is a failure. By what line or argument? Not by endeavouring to show that there is nothing in its teaching to furnish the highest standard of duty or of morals. He endeavours by extracts, wrenched from their context, to show that Christianity has been (not a failure) but abused by some of its followers. Such abuse is no argument against it. Some men abuse their health. Well, "Captain," is health of no value? Some people are dishonest. Do the laws of the land cause dishonesty? The -examples to which he gives such prominence in his letters on:y show what a depraved thing is human nature; that " Vde heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked." To charge Christianity as producing this bad fruiti s a monstrous assumption. He might as well main- tain that the art of healing is the cause of disease, because 30 many are afflicted. The wheat and tares must of neces- sity grow together till the harvest, the time of final separa- Veil. Seriously, I ask, does not Christianity teach what is true, honest, lovely, just, and of good report ? Is not this the essence of the moral law, which forms the foundation of the civil law of this country? Christianity a failure— absolutely and universally! such the logical inference frcm "Captain Cuttle's " statement. I maintain that it is not a corrupt tree. If it does not destroy every evil, it is not because it is corrupt in itself; but it encounters so much that is corrupt in the heart that its influence is checked and impeded. Will "Captain Cuttle " point out any precept in Our Lord's sermon on the mount that is evil and pernicious in its tendency? What good fruit has "free thought" prckinced ? Where is to be found the list of its benefactors, philanthropists. self-denyinq labourers among the poor, the and dying? I shall be glad to be furnished with such a list To me it will be a pleasure to know if its disciples are seking to improve the condition of the " over-crowded poor," for whose wafa. e my opponent is evidently very solicitous. Secularism and Christianity claim to produce the moot beneficial influence in the world. It ought not to be difficult th decide which. With papers read at the Church Congress, or elsewhere, or the doings of individual religious profeseors, I have nothing whatever to do. The question is: Does Christianity as a system produce evil in the world? Let Captain Cuttle " prove that it does. Bishop Butler, in the "Analogy," says a writer, remarks that "the merits of systems are often more to be judged by their essential ten- dencies than by their actual achievements." When the rival schools-of "free thought," as represented by Bradlaugh and Holyoake, are agreed as to what is best for the world, it will be time enough for Christianity to retire into obscurity. By the. way, he says. "Villager charges Atheists with being swindler." This is a garbled extract—a wilful perversion— of my statement, viz .that "some infidels were swindlers," but net as a class. When "Captain Cattle " next gives a que.ation. from my letter, will he give it as it is written ; this I claim as due to me.—Faithf ally yours. VILLAGER. [We must 0099 this correspondence with this letter, as it has now occupied as much space as we can afford to give It—ED. Ex.]

(practical). 26 While it is disappointing to alt concerned that none of the students in the Art Class succeeded in obtaining a certifi- I cete, it must not be forgotten that an examination in art can scarcely be considered a fair test of the work done dur- ing the session. The stendard of examination is so high 1 that only a very sm ID per centage of the cendidatee who attend the examination ever pass. In a small class such as I ours, meeting only once a week and consisting chiefly of very young students, we are placed at a great disadvantage as compared with schools of art which meet from three to five times a week; and the per centage of pastes in the country, including schools ot art, is only about 30 per cent. A more reliable test of the work dune by the students during the seetion is the amount of Government grant on the drawings sent to South Kensington for inspection. This greet, which is awarded according to merit, amounts to 78 per student, which is considerably above the average. A failure therefore, at the examination, ought not to deter students from following up the study, as it is by perseverance andcon- tinned study only that power in art can be gained and suc- cess accomplished. The results of the examination in the science subjects is very satisfactory, and the committee are glad to notice a great improvement in machine and building construction. The chemistry classes have been exceedingly well attended, 45 students attended the theoretical class and 31 the practical class, and the results are quite up to the average. Althoagh the per centage of passes is in the ag- gregate slightly less than last year, more first-class certiti- cites have been ebtained. This manifests itself in a -very substantial Manner, for, while our earnings from Govern- ment in 1883 amounted to £73 Gs, this year we base earned £lO6 12s. The library, which contains a very valuable col- lection of science and art works, will be open to the public every Saturday evening, from October to March inclusive, from six p.m. until nine p.m., and the committee, in order to make it more attractive to the working claeses. have arranged to provide the following papers :—Graphic. London 2i'em3, Punch, Judy. Fun, The Spectator, Saturday Review, Engineering, Illustrated Science Month! y, A-note/edge, Magazine of Art Monthly, Nineteenth Century, Contem- porary Review, and local papers. The committee are anxious to promote the success of the library in every way they possibly can, in the hope that ultimitely one of a more extend-d and permanent character will be provided for the inhabitants of Widnes."— Mr. Morrison added that he had just received the Govern- ment report for all the schools in the kingdom, and he found that the average earnings per student was 12e 6d, while the average earnings per student at Widnes had reached LI Is 4.1. (Applause.)—The Chairmen said they must be all gratifiei with the report which the hon. secretary had just read. They lid been at work ten years, and he thought the results obtained during that time would bear comperison very favourably with those of any similar undertaking. He 1 wished to draw Attention to the t ict that the committee of- ferea a prize of 5e to any student who Ateined a pass in art, or who obteined a first-class certificate ire the elemen- tary stage of any science subject. The fee for each student being 3e for the course, the student who showed ordinary diligence and attention might by winning the committee's prize obtain lois instruction gratuitously. He thought that spoke well for their ecience and Art Cl ewes. He did not know whether they adopted a similar system in other science and art classes, but he thought it was a feature which ought to be remembered by those who intended to avail them- selves of the instruction to be there obtained. (Hear, hear.) He, as one of the committee, attended one or two of the examinations during last May and Jane, and he was dieap- pointed to find that some of the students had not even taken suffieient pains to qualify themselves for the examinations by attending twenty lessons. When students joined a class of this kind, and when they agreed that they would make those 20 attendances, he thought the least that could be expected of them was that they would carry out their contract. As a rule the majority of the students did so, but still there were some who seemed to think they might come and go when they pleasea. If students would not show by their attendance an apprecia- tion of the trouble taken by the committee it was a Ttestion whether the classes should be continued, but he hoped they should not have any students who thought so lightly of the benefits that were offered hy the classes as not to de their very utmost to attend all the lessone. During the last few weeks he had bad an opportunity St visiting the greet coun- try on the other side of the Atlantic, and he had hoped very much that he mioht have had time to make some inquiries into science tea, hing there, hut he was sorry to say his time war so much ttken up by travelling about, and business en- gagements, that he wee not able to invrstigate the subject as he wished to do. From inquiries he hid m ide, however, he was quite convinced that the young men on the other side of the Atlantic were fully alive to the advan- tages of a thorough scientific edacition. Tuey were taking advantage of the educational oppor- tunities afforded to them, and these opportunities were of a very excellent character in most of the large towns of America. He was very much impressed with the mag- nificience of some of the museums and schools of both art and science. The American people had not th et exclusive regard for the "Almighty dollar" which they were some- times credited with. He was informed on most credible authority that the students attended the higher schools not merely for the opportunities the science might give them in after life to get a few more dollars, but to cultivate their minds. He whould like to impress upon the students pre- sent that the young men and young women an the other side of the Atlantic were pressing them very hard in the race of life—they were fully aware of the advantage ef culture of the mind; and unless they in England took care to take advantage of the opportunities they had they would in- vitably be left behind in tho race. He had now great pleasure in introducing Professor Boyd Dawkins to distribute the prizes. Professor Boyd Dawkins having distributed the prizes, a list of which has been published in this journal, delivered an address. He said he was pleased to see that the prizes showed that the students were not giving attention solely to those subjects in which they had proved their preeminence, but had tastes which extended in other and different directions. It seemed to him that the narrowing tendency, the intensifyiug ten- dency of modern education had comparitively little roomn in that place. The chemist had a bout which was not tied and fettered by chemistry, the person who had given his mind more particularly to engineering was a man who cared for such things as remote from engineering as, to say, the keeping of bees. That to his mind was very encouragine. Speaking to the unsuccessful students he said the very fact of training for the intellectual race in which they had been competing would enable them to fight more successfully in the battle of life, although they have not at the present time carried away a prize in that particular line in which they had laboured. He would, as far as he could, put be- fore them the present position of natural science. They all, he thonzht, at the present day acknowledged the value of the study of nature, and he supposed in Widnes they really appreciated that study at its proper value, fer the very existence of Widnes WAS essentially de- pendent upon it. In the old days and when he spoke of the old days he was speaking of times no further back than something like forty or fifty years ago—the greater portion of knowledge and of cultiva- lion of the mind was locked up in what Was known under the name of the classics. He alluded to the study of Latin and Greek in the past, and proceeded to say that during the last 40 or 50 years an entirely new branch of kntwledge had sprung up. He alluded is natural science. They found the knowledge of chemistry, for instance, spreading and developing and assuming proportions which were simply extraordinary. What might be said of chemistry might be equally said regarcling the development of other sciences; for instance, such subjects as geology and biology. Now-a- days the old and the new learning were competing, the one with the other. The success of a man in life—and here lie was putting things on a comparatively low platform—de- pended essentially upon his mastering the difficulties by which be was surrounded, and by obtaining the capacity for seizing opportunities. (Applause.) But while striving to master nature as well as they could, those who could should heard a little Latin and Greek, and make teemselves ac- quainted with the manners of men and the modes of thought in the days before there was any natural science at all. Commenting on the study of art, Professor Dawkins said there were two corner stones, as it were, which it was most important for them all to bear in mind. Tire first thing I they had to do in order to cultivate art was to ' cultivate the power of seeing natural objects, and the second corner stone was the faculty of representing natural objects as true to nature as possible. In conclusion, Professor Dawkins said in this country there was a great antagonism between hand work and head work, which Was wholly uncalled for and which was absolutely unreasonable. This wrong distinetion, this separation of the hand and head had been the cause of the almost total extinction of the sculptors' art in this country. lie would say that all work was equally noble when it was done with a good intention. (Applause ) If the tendency of modern education wee to unfit men for those handicrafts by:which the world went od, then he thought the less they bad of educetion the,barter. The proper view to take of education was that it should fit a man better for his surroundings; that it should milts

THE RAINHILL SEWAGE FARM The Local Govern- ment Board forwarded for the Board's consideration a letter ' dated the 22nd September, from Mr. S. H. Hartley, elet k to the Prescut Rural Sanitary Authority. The letter stated that the authority on the 11th inst. instructed their sur- veyor to again inspect the Rainhill sewage farm. Attention , was drawn to a statement contained in the letter of the clerk to the Widnes Local Board, dated the 21st ult , that he was instructed by the Chairman of the Health Commit. !tee of that Board to repeat the request made be that Board ! on the oth July, that the Local Government Board should , send down an inspector to examine, take evidence and re- port. The authority questioned the right of any individual i member of a committee or board to give such instructions. ! The authority felt they had just cause for complaint , j against the Widnes Local Board, as that Board had no right ! to trespass on the Rainhill Sewage Farm, the property of ; the sanitary Authority. As to the samples sent to the Local Government Board it would appear that there WAS no evidetice as to where they were obtained or by whose direc- tion. The report of the inspector was attached, and it stated that although there were no tanks there was a complete system of sewerage for the Rainhill Sewage Farm. The sewage as it Caine from the mains was distributed along open carriers on to land provided for that purpose. After perculating through the soil into underground drains, it joined the watercourse on Wilmere-lane, near the IVidnee Boundary. Until it had passed through the soil it was al- , most an impossibility for any to escape into the stream. At the present time, owing to an accident which is being re- paired, sewage does not flaw on to the land at all. Conse- quently, there was no effluent water other than that from ordinary land or drainage. Wkailat the repairs were in hand the sewage escaped from a storm outlet, into a watercourse fi awing altogether in another direction to the one com- plained of by the Widnes Local Board.—The Clerk said by the instructions of the Health Committee, he had written to the Local Government Board inquiring whether they purposed taking any action in this matter, as the Board felt that no good could be done by continuing the correspon- dence between the two authorities.—Later the B )ard went into committee to consider the matter, and decided to send Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Carey, Wright, and Midwood, as a deputation to the Local Government Board. THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.—A letter from Mr. A. D. He coupled with the toast the name of the president, to whom he referred in complimentary terms.— The toast was received with musical honorue, the company singing "For he is a jolly good fellow."'—The Chairman, in responding, .seid he was proud in being connected with a club which had under nets difficulties done so much during the past year. (Hear, hear.) He had been connected with cricket something like 40 years and he knew a little about the game, and be had been very much pleased with the dis- position shown by many members in the club to unite to- gether in'overcoming the difficulties as they had arisen, and aseist in the work of the club. He spoke df the indefatig- able labours of Messrs. Pickthall,. Adams, and Weight, and to the generosity of many friends outside the club. Thev had got on through the year with great success and with only a sin ill deficit which he hoped to see wiped off before the commencement of another season. (Applause.)— Mr. F. J. Adams gave the toast of the'" Runcorn Football Club," although he was a cricketer and thought cricket pre- eminent above all other games, and beyond measure the most minty game of the coil ntry ; still he felt the same re- gird for athletic sports of all descriptions, knowing thee they bad made England and Englishmen what they were. He believed that England that day was as far above all other nations as ever it was. (Applause.) He therefore looked upon the Foothill Club with the same pride as he did the Cricket Club. (Appleuse.)—Mrl H. Johnson responded. Mr. R. J. Weight proposed the health of "The President " in felicitious terms, and the to est was honoured with enthu- siasm—The President responded in a suitable manner, con- gratulatinz the club up in the ettecesees of the sateen. (Au. platiee )—The to est of "Our Captains," proposed by Mr. J. M. Beguley, responded to by Messrs. Weight, J. R. Frith, and H. Wright; the " Hon. Sec. and Treasurer and Coin. mite," proposed by the Chairman, and responded to by Messrs. Adorn, J. M. Frith, and F. Bate; and "The Town and Trade," proposed by Mr. F. Fairhurst and Mr. G. Anderson followed. Before the conclusion of the proceed- ings, Mr. Adams, who ha e performed the duties of secretary for the pest two years in an admirable manner, was pre- sented with a valuable gold pencil case in taken of the esteem in which he and his services are held by the club.

div.head: IVIDNES BREACR OF PROMISE CASE.
div.p: A IVIDNES BREACR OF PROMISE CASE.

On Thursday, at the Court of Passtge, St. George's Hall, Liverpool, before Mr. T. H. flails, judge, and a common jury, an action for breach of promise of marriage was tied, in which Helena Nicholas, formerly of Widnes, and now of 29. 1C:0)ton-street, Liverpool, was the plaintiff; and Carl Achard, pork butcher, 14, Scotland-road, the defendant.— Mr. Taylor (instructed by Mr. Quelch) appeared for the plaintiff ; and Mr. Mulholland (instructed by Messrs. Bart- lett and Berry) for the defendant. According to the case for the plaintiff, both parties were Germans, and when chil- dren in their own country knew each other. Three years ago DI ai n tiff came to England and occupied several places as domestic servant, the defendant at the same time being in Liverpool. A few months ago she went as servant to a Mr. Bower, pork butcher, Widnes, whose business she bought. When the business had been bought, defendant went over and spoke to her about it, finishing up with a promise to marry. Plaintiff accepted the offer, aud a few days afterwards went to Liverpool to see defendant, but returned to Widnes in disgust because she found him drunk. Neat day the defendant went over to Widnes and apologised for his conduct, at the same time renewing his promise to marry her. At the request of the defendant plaintiff, on the 29th March last, packed up her goods and went to the defendant's shop, where she stayed seven weeks. During the time she remained with him de- fendant was guilty of misconduct towards her, and she asked him to carry out his promise to marry her, but he would not do so. He offered to pay her wages as a servant, but she refused to accept payment, remarking that she came to be his wife and not his servant. The damages were laid at £3OO. The defence was a total denial of the promise Defendant alleged that he engaged plaintiff as a house- keeper, and paid her fis a week. They quarrelled about domestic matters, and this led to separation,—The jury found a verdict for the plaintiff—damages £3O.

div.head: RUNCORN CRICKE CLUB-A.NNUAL DINNER.
div.p: RUNCORN CRICKE CLUB-A.NNUAL DINNER.

The annual dinner in connection with Runcorn Cricket Club took place list night at Wilson's Hotel, Bridg?-street, Mr. H. Jackson being the caterer. There was a good attend- ance of members and friends. Mr. J. R. Frith, president of the club, occupied th, chair, and there were present: Lieut. Joule, Messrs. R. J. Weight, F. J. Adams, F. Fairhurst, J. J. Speakman. H. Wright, J. E. Langshaw, J. H. Salkeld, W. Timmins, T. D. Timmins, W. Frith, J. A. Frith, J. B. Frith, P. Smieh, J. Potter, W. R. Earp. W. Stubbs, T. Junes, J. Poole, Connor, J. D. Widders, F. Savage, T. Baguley, C. Dutton, A. B. Hawkins, F. Bate. The repast concluded, " "

Mr. F. Adams, the hon. secretary, read the annual re- port, which stated that another seassn having passed they, a second tims since the resuscitation of the club, met to com- pare results, and this time he was glad to be tole to say that these results were in every way very satisfactory, and that they had not allowed the honour and dignity of the town suffer in the slightest degree in the matter of cc icket. Ifie prognostications at their last reunion had been to a great degree realised. He then ventured to hope that with a better ground and more liberal support they would be able to take a more prominent position, and soon have a club worthy of the town. This support a number of gentlemen resident in the neighbourhood had fully accorded to them, enabling them to rent a ground much more suitable than the one they had ia 1883, but which, unfortunately, was still very much behind what a cricket ground ought to be ; and also to build if not a'very handsome, yet a very useful and commodious tent, Their best thanks were due to these gentlenpn, who would, he trusted, renew their goneros:ty in the forthcoming season. In 1883 both elevens played 23 matches, winning 7 and losing 13. In 1894 they had played 29 matches, winning 14, losing 10, being 1, and drawing 4, two of the latter being virtually victories. The number of victories and defeats were exactly divided between the two elevens. The number of runs scored by the first eleven were 1,031 and 6 wickets to 141, and by their opponents 717 and

div.head: MR. GLA.DSTOi‘iti_ANo__Tai WIRRAL'
div.p: MR. GLA.DSTOi‘iti_ANo__Tai WIRRAL'
RAILWAY.

The first sod of the Wirral Railway, which will when com- pleted give direct communication between. Birkenhead and North Walv, was cut on Thursday by Mr. Gladstone The ceremony took place on the outskirts of Birkenhead, and was witnessed by about 15,000 people, who had assambled in I the show ground of the Wirral Agricultural Society for that purpose. Very great interest was exhibited in Mr. Glad- stone's visit to Birkenhead, for a large crowd gathered in front of the railway station at which he arrived, and the route to the place where the ceremony was per- formed was lined by many thousands of persons, who cheered him most heartily. The welcome which he re- ceived at the showground was of an extraordinary enthu• siasti: char toter. In their eagerness to show their personal regard for him a portion of the multitude broke down the barriers surrounding the enclosure where the sod was cut, and by doing so made ib difficult for the right lam. gentle- man to discharge the formal part of the ceremony. Subse- quently he delivered a speech, in which he pointed out the advantages likely to accrue to North Wales and to Liver- pool by the construction of the proposed railway and the completion or the Mersey tunnel. At a luncheon which followed the ceremony Mr. Gladstone spoke in reply to the toast of his health and drew a vivid picture of the material , progress of Liverpool, from his personal recollection of the town, during the last half century. He anticipated, when adequate communication by tunnel was established between Liverpool and Birkenhead. that the dock system on the Cheshire side would become to all intents and purposes a part of the Liv..rpool dock system. Concluding his speech by a reference to the increasing wealth and power of the country, the right hon. gentleman asked his hearers if they ever heard weak-minded peoplespeak of the actual or pos- sible decay of this empire not to listen for a moment to " such dreams and such fables." nut strength of the British Empire was increasing, and, so far as human judg- ment can anticipate, would increase. If other European countries had grown in power this country bad yet more grown in power. They might rely upon it the day had not come, and it was not about to come, when they need fear, with justieeat their hack, to look in the face of any Power of any country in the world.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

During the course of his speech Mr Gladstone made the following allusion to this district :—Look at the disadvantage under which they are with ferries to cross over the Mer- sey, and no power at all of °toning the Dee except by going round by Chester. Now, it would be no small advantage to the people of Liverpool seeking rest from their arduous oc- cupations. which they pursue with an intense activity sur- passed nowhere on the face of the globe, to come among us over yonder—(cheers)—for fresh air if they want it, as we know they do. I say it would be no small advantage to them to be able to go a diatanoa of 25 miles which would place them in North Wales country and North Wales scenery, rather than dragging round as they have now to do admiring the scen2ry of Runcorn Gap—(laughter)—and not only admiring the scenery of Runcorn Gap, but inhaling in their nostrils those balmy gales which always proceed from the works at Widnes. (Renewed laughter.) I hope they will not poison you at Conn th's Quay when you come into Nfirth Wales, but at any rate it will be a long time before Connah's Quay is as bad as Widnes. (Laughter and cheers,)

Husband, deputy-coroner, held an inquest at the Boir's Head Inn, Warrington, respecting the death of a farm labourer, aged about 45 years and name unknown, who was found dead in bed at a lodging-house is Angel's-yard under circumstances previously reported. A verdict of "Natural causes" was returned.

Bowrarra.—On Saturday afternoon a match at bowls to be played on two greens took place between Joseph Gloave, of the Bank Quay Bowling Club, and Win. Bolton, of the Padgate Club, the first part of the game being played on Mr. Mellor's green, and the second on the green attached to the King and Queen, Padgate. There was only a moderate attendance on bath greens. As was expecred, Gleave showed his superiority on the Bank Quay green, and at the conclusion of the half game the scores were :—Gleave, 31 ; Bolton, 17. On restlming play at Padgate Bolton made a run of 13, but was unable to get level with his opponent daring any part of the game, who ultimately won by five points. The scores at the finish were :—Gleave, 01; Bol- ton, 56.—0 n Monday, a main at bowls took place at the Cemetery Inn Manchester-road, when the proprietor (Mr. W. Grundy) added £1 to an entrance fee of 24 each. Four- teen competitors entered, and the first and second prizes were won respectively by James Shaw and W. Grundy,

Two men, were killed, by the Great Northern express in a tunnel near Barnet, on Thursday niglat. DEATH OF' MR. A. M. SULLIVAN.—Mt.. A. M. Surivan died in Dublin on Friday morning. His prospects of re- covery had improved since the recent oberation WaS per- formed on him, and his medical attendants were confident of his restoration to health ; but a sudden change set in on Thursday, and he breathed his list on Friday morning at the residence ot a friend with whom he had been staying at Upper Rathmines, a suburb of Dublin. He resigned his• seat in the Hones of Commons in 1882 on account of ill health. He was only 55 years of age. • FATAL GAS. I- XPLOSION. EIGHT' PERSONS &MIK')

----- Arava.—A terrible gas explosion occurred on Thursday night in Londonaby which a loss of life was caused, as well as serious injury to-some fifteen or sixteen persons. It ap- pears that a strong smell of gas was detected in Edward-• - street, Bermondsey, and two men from the South Metro- politan Gas Company were sent to ascertain the cause. One of them went into the house, it is alleged, with a piece of lighted tar roperelespite the warnings of the owner, and a terrific explosion ensued ; the front and back walls of the dwelling being forced, outward, while the roof and flooring fell in, burying eight persons in the house: including the three children who were in bed. Help was promptly rendered, and it was then found that some persons who bad been standing near were lying insensible, and these were im- mediately conveyed, to the hospital. In the course of an hour those buried- were extricated. The. youngest child, named William Jonesoged four years, was so injured that it died shortly afterwards, and the death of two other children is expected: Tne other persons escaped with slight injuries, but two lads-outside were very seriously hurt. - SERIOUS FIRE ON AN ATLANTIC: LINER. The Guion LinerNevade, from New York, arrived at Queenstown on Friday morning on fire. The flames burst out on Wednesday last;. but had been kept under by the efforts of the officers and crew. Great excitement prevailed on board, but the passengers and crew are safe. The tire on the Nevada is believed to have been caused by sponta- neous combustion, a portion-of the cargo of eotten being in close proximitvto the eogine room. A quantity of the cargo was thrown overboard, and an immense quantity of water poured on the burning material.. A. tender sent to assist returned to Queenstown and landed a number of passengers who had booked for Irelaed. Nar- ratives furnished by passengers state that a hasty ex mina- tion, after a cry of fire on Wednesday, showed that sense bales of cotton and hops stored in a compartment by them- selves were well 'alight.: Great excitement at once pre- vailed amongst the passengero, and a number of women rushed about the deck 'with their children in their arms, imploring the officers to save titer% and they were pacified with difficulty. Meantime the crew, ably and cooly directed by the crptain and officerserverired with a will on the nam- ing hold. Huge quantities of, water were poured down the hold, but for some time it apparently lead no effect, for the fire managed to spread to the ether side of the engine-room and burned so fiercely that some of the outside plates of the vessel became red-hot. Ultimately, however. tne enormous volume of water began to tell and at length the fire was partially subdued. All the passengers speak in terms of the most enthusiastic praise of the conduct of the officers and crew. Bridget McCune, a consumptive steerage pas- senger, bound to Ireland, died of fright and excitement. The Nevada left Queenstoven for Liverpool on Friday evening, the tire having been completely subdued.

div.p: THE SEIZURE OF BRITISH TUGS BY AMERICAN
REBELS. AN ENGAGEMENr AT SEA.

PANAMIL, THITIMILY.—A party of rebels seized the B-It- ish tagoott Morro on the 14th inst and compelled the cap- tain to taw them to Costa WA. The steamer Alajuela was also captured by rebels, who put to sea it her on the follow- ing day. The Government thereupon seized the Morro and sent her on an expedition in pursuit of the Alejnela. On corn- ing up with her an engigement took place, during which the Morro was rammed and• forced to return. Several of those on board were killed and, wounded but the loss of the rebels, who escaped, is unknown. To-day the British en- sign on the Morro was hauled down and the Columbian en- sign hoisted in its place. The foreign residents here de- nounce this step as an insult to Great Britain, but they are powerless in the matter as no-. British vessel is on the spot. TRE NILE EXPEDOTION.—REPORTED SAFETY OF COLONEL STEWART.

CAIRO, FRIDAY.— the following is the text of the tele. grain received on Friday morning from the Sub-Mudir of Dongola :—The special messenger has returned from Wadi- garna, where the steamer from Khartoum ran aground. The inhabitants declare thatthe steamer was conveying money belonging to the Greek consul, and that there were forty persons on board, including Europeans and natives. The steamer, which was armedotlso carried the booty captured by the party in their engagements with the rebels, al well as the heads ef some of the insurgents killed at Khartoum. When the steamer ran aground at Salamat the inhabibinta were much terrifled.l The messenger then repeats the story of the treacherous hospitality offered by the Sheikhs, and of the massacre, as aleady known,addiog that the only ptison- ere in the hands of the rebels are blacks.

WADY HALFA..--TraitlM are again working regularl7. The special boats are-to be carried by road around the gate of the Great Cataract. The natives persist that all the steamers returned to Khartoum after bombarding Berber, and only a native craft descended the river. Colonel Stewart's safety is thus believed assured. Sir Charles Wilson has reached Debbah.

The Foreign Office. receired a massage on Friday morn- ing from Lord•Wolesley,. stating that Sir Charles Wilson telegraphs to him that there is no evidence whatever that Colonel Stewart was on board the steamer wreckad on the Nile. Sir Charles Wilson left Dongola last week is a steamer to search for demils of the reported massacre, and to ransom the prisoners if possible.
ALLEGED. SERIOUS ASSAULT AT HALE-WOOD.

ACTION FOB £5O DLI&A.OES. Before Mr. P. P. E Thompao,,, judge, and a special jury, I at the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Charles Sutton, of the Mill-house Farm. Hale, sought. to recover damages, which he assessed at £5O, from Edward'Grace, son of Mr. Robert Grace, whose farm adjoins that of plaintiff for an alleged assault committed on plaintiff by the defen- dant.—Mr. W. I'.. Husband, of Widnes,' appeared for plain- tiff. and Mr. J. 0. Swift defended.—Mr. Husband said that on the morning of Friday, the 29th August, plaintiland another man named William !••utton went to Liverpool market, and returned by the 5 30 p.m. train, reaching Speke at 6 p.m. They had then three or four miles to walk, and they called at defendant's to talk over,some farming mat- ters_ The elder Grace asked them to have a glass of t eer. and they did so. During this convivlal time defendant with some instrument struck plaintiff two.or three blows on the head, which inflicted several large wounds and " dazed " him. He was attended by n•loctor, and still suf.- fered from the wounds.—Plaintiff, being called, said he was bigger in stature than the defendant. The latter, was sub, ject to fits, and was not a man that he (plaintiff)mcald ;tight with—la fact he treated him as a woman. In Mr. Grace's house at the time mentioned, there pereMr. and Mrs. Grace, William Simon, plaintiff and defeadant. 7hey were talking about harvesting matters, when all at once de- fendant proposed to tight him, and came and hit him about the head with his fists. Plaintiff got out of the room as well as he could, but on returning far his- hat defendant came behind and struck him with a, weapon on the head. He was chant for a few moments and stooped down, upon which defendant struck hint again, He had four scalp wounds. which wore all bleeding. Plaintiff produced a scarf which he had that day purchased in Liverpool and put on there. It was saturated with blood. He went to Police-sergeant Cola's, at Mtton, mull afterwards to Dr. Booth, at Widnes, where the wounds were dressed. He was in bed from Friday night to Monday, was attended by a doctor for a fortnight, and frequently had headaches and pains. In reply to Mr. Swift, plaintiff said that both he and Wm. Sutton were sober.—Wm. Sutton, P.S. Coutts, of Dittonond P.C, Clarke having riven evidence, Mr. J. O. Swift said this masa peculiar case, and he should show in evidence that plaintiff was drur.k, that he began to curse in the house, that he snatched a stick out of the hands cJ Mrs. Grace, and struck her across the shoulders with it. Defen. .fendant then interfered in self-defence.—The jury returned a verdict in favour of the defreadant.

BOROUGH OF ST. HELENS. TO THE ELECTORS OF WEST SUTTON WARD.— LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—The term of three years, for which you did me the honour of electing me as one of your representatives in the Council for the West Sutton Ward, will expire on the Ist November, and I therefore beg again to offer you my services. Should you again honour me with this mark of your confidence, my best efforts shall be exerted in the in- terest of your ward, and of the borough generally.-1 remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, your obedient servant, ED WARD JOHNSON. Elephant-lane, Sutton, October 17th 1884. TO THE BURGESSES OF PARR WARD. As the period for which you re elected me to represent you in the Council has almost expired, I hasten ts inform you that Ido not intend seeking re-election. The claims on my time are such that of late I have not been able to devote that time and attention to your interests I should like to have done, and which you have a right to demand from your representa- tive. As a member of the Council, it has always been my aim to merit the confidence you had so unreservedly placed in me, and to discharge my duties faithfully to all. I thank you most sincerely for the honour so long c inferred upon me. Your obedient servant, THOMAS WALKER. Merton Bank Alkali Works, St. Helens, Lancashire, 14th October, 1884. BOROUGH OF ST. HELENS. TO THE BURGESSES OF ECCLESTON WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—My present term as one of your representatives at the Town Council will shortly expire, and I beg again to offer myself as a candidate for a renewal of the honour. During the 12 years for which I have represented you many very important matters have been dealt with ; in these]: have taken an earnest and active part, and I trust that my actions have met with your approval. While a great number of important questions concerninit the health, the sanitary con- ditions, and the general interests of the town have been delft with, many still remain tor disposal, and my wish and hope is that, as your representative, I may assist in their considers, tion by the Town Council. My sole desire has been to secure the true interests of the town, and if I should again be returned by you my best energies sha'l be given with the same object in view. lam, L soles and Gentlemen, Your obliied and faithful servant, RICHARD PILKINGTON.
